questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 23-year-old patient came with complaints of non-scarring alopecia in the vertex region of his head. Histological examination shows loss of hair with haemorrhage into the follicular areas and mild perinuclear lymphocytic infiltrate. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Trichotillomania

The clinical scenario depicting a young adult presenting with non-scarring alopecia in the vertex region and histology showing perifollicular hemorrhage is suggestive of trichotillomania (trichotillosis).

Trichotillomania has to be differentiated from alopecia areata (Option A). Trichotillomania presents with incomplete hair loss within a patch with varying lengths of hair whereas alopecia areata shows smooth hairless patch with sparing of white hairs. Regular pitting of nails and exclamation mark hairs are seen in alopecia areata. When the diagnosis is uncertain, a scalp biopsy can be done. Perifollicular hemorrhage is characteristic of trichotillomania while peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate is diagnostic of alopecia areata.

Trichotillomania is classified under obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. It is characterized by recurrent body-focused repetitive behavior (hair pulling) and repeated attempts to decrease or stop the behavior. It is commonly seen in females. The hair loss is commonly seen over the vertex but can involve eyelashes, eyebrows, and beard.

The most effective treatment for trichotillosis is habit-reversal training (HRT).

Other options:

Option B: Telogen effluvium is diffuse hair loss resulting in non-scarring alopecia due to loss of telogen hairs due to fever, pregnancy, hypothyroidism or anemia.

Option C: Tinea infection shows patchy hair loss, resulting in non-scarring/scarring alopecia. Easy pluckability, broken hairs and wood's lamp positivity are features.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female came with complaints of bone and joint pain. NSAIDs were prescribed. After a few days, she presents again complaining vesicobullous lesions healing to give a brownish discoloration over the face (upper lip area) as shown in the image. This most probably suggests a diagnosis of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fixed drug eruption

The patient has a history of consumption of NSAIDs, following which there is an appearance of vesiculobullous lesions on the lips, evolving to give a brownish discolouration. The most probable diagnosis is fixed drug eruption (FDE).

A strong differential diagnosis is post-chikungunya pigmentation (PCP) of the face seen on the nose and cheeks (chik sign). However, this is not the answer because there is no antecedent history of fever, myalgia or other symptoms suggestive of chikungunya. PCP often appears as the fever subsides and may persist for about 3-6 months. PCP mimics melasma and may be misdiagnosed if proper history is not taken.

The image below shows chik sign:

Fixed drug eruption (FDE) is a type of delayed hypersensitivity reaction. It is characterized by well-defined brown, hyperpigmented plaques that may follow vesiculobullous lesions. They occur on lips, hands, legs, face, genitalia, and oral mucosa, and can cause a burning sensation. They usually present 30 min to 8 h after drug exposure and recur at the same location on re-exposure. NSAIDs, Paracetamol and Co‐trimoxazole are the most common drugs causing FDE.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presented with hair loss and itching of the scalp along with mild discharge. Which of the following is useful for diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. KOH mount

The patient has a history of itching and mild discharge and examination shows a well-demarcated patch of alopecia, with scaling and broken hair shafts. This is characteristic of tinea capitis. Though the diagnosis is clinical, a KOH mount is used for confirmation.

Scrapings from the edge of a lesion are transferred to a slide, to which KOH is added. It is then examined under the microscope for the presence of hyphae, as shown below.

Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte infection primarily occurring in children. Clinical features of tinea capitis are patchy hair loss, scaling, tender lymphadenopathy, and in severe cases, there might be pustules and crusting of the affected area along with sinus formation.

The clinical variants of tinea capitis are:

• Endothrix - a non-inflammatory type in which multiple black dots are present within the areas of alopecia. It is most commonly caused by T. tonsurans and T. violaceum.

• Ectothrix - a mild inflammatory type in which single or multiple scaly patches with hair loss are seen. Microsporum audouinii, M.canis, M.equinnum, and M.ferrugineum cause ectothrix infection.
• Kerion - a severe inflammatory type that presents with an inflammatory mass with thick crusting and matting of hair with pus and sinus formation. It is commonly caused by T. verrucosum and T. mentagrophytes.

• Favus - is characterized by the presence of yellowish, cup‐shaped crusts known as scutula that develop around hair follicles. It is caused by T. schoenleinii

Treatment:

• Terbinafine: <10 Kg- 62.5 mg; 10-20 kg - 125 mg; >20 kg- 250 mg, all given daily for 4 weeks.
• Itraconazole: 2-4 mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Dense irregular collagen is found in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dermis

Dense irregular collagen is found in dermis.

Irregular connective tissue is of three types: Loose, dense and adipose. Dense connective tissue is located in regions which are under consistent mechanical stress and where protection is required for the ensheathed organs. The abundant collagen fibres in the dermis run in a haphazard manner. This protects the skin.

It is usually present in :

• Reticular layer of the dermis
• Superficial connective tissue sheaths of the muscle and nerves
• Adventitia of large vessels
• Capsules of various organs and glands (e.g, testis, sclera, periosteum, perichondrium)

On the other hand, dense regular collagen fibres are found in tendons.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the condition shown below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Congenital melanocytic nevus

The image shows a child with a well-circumscribed, black, heterogenous lesion covered with hair. This is characteristic of a congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN). They may be present at birth or develop shortly thereafter. They are benign and can be brown, black, purplish, or red, and are usually a palpable lesion.

They can be classified based on size: small (<1.5 cm), medium (1.5-19.9 cm), and large or giant (>20 cm). Larger CMN have a higher risk of developing malignant melanoma.

Management of CMN depends on the size and location of the lesion. Smaller nevi may be observed, while larger nevi or those at a higher risk for complications may require surgical excision, particularly if there is a concern for malignant transformation.

Complications of CMN include neurological abnormalities (intraparenchymal melanosis is the commonest finding), malignant melanoma, and other tumors like rhabdomyosarcoma.

The images below show different melanotic skin lesions:

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the layer of skin (in the image given below) in which desmosomes are abundant.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. D

Desmosomes are abundant in the stratum spinosum (Option C, label D in the image) layer of the epidermis of the skin.

Desmosomes are adhesion complexes in epidermis which link adjacent keratinocytes. They appear like spines on microscopy and hence this layer is also called the prickle layer. Defects of desmosomal proteins, inherited or acquired, result in blistering disorders.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The following image depicts:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scabies

The given image shows raised, brownish thread-like lesions in the interdigital distribution (burrows), typically seen in scabies.

Scabies is an ectoparasitic infection caused in humans by Sarcoptes scabiei. It is transmitted by close personal contact. Pruritis with nocturnal exacerbation and contact cases within a family should raise the suspicion of scabies. Typical locations of lesions are the finger webs, the flexor surfaces of the wrists, the elbows, the axillae, the buttocks and genitalia and the breasts of women (Circle of Hebra). In adults, the face is often spared. Pruritic papules and nodules on male genitalia and breasts serve as valuable diagnostic clues in the absence of burrows.

Dermoscopy of the burrows shows jet‐with‐contrail appearance. Microscopy of scraping from burrows can be done to demonstrate mites.

A single overnight application of 5% permethrin cream from neck to toe in adults and from head to toe in children is the drug of choice for the treatment of scabies in all ages including infants (at least 2 months old) and pregnant women. All family members, even if asymptomatic, need to be treated simultaneously for this condition to prevent reinfection. Oral ivermectin can also be used.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The histopathological slide given below is suggestive of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pemphigus vulgaris

The given slide shows a row of tombstones appearance, which is classically seen in pemphigus vulgaris.

In this condition, there is a suprabasal splitting of the epidermis leading to blister formation. The basal layer remains adherent to the basement membrane and gives the resemblance to a row of tombstones as shown in the histology image below.

Pemphigus vulgaris is a chronic immunobullous disorder characterized by the presence of antibodies against desmosomal proteins, desmogleins 1 and 3 expressed in the skin and mucosa.

Clinically, the patients present with ill-defined, irregular, slow-to-heal oral lesions and erosions. Flaccid blisters filled with clear fluid may arise on normal skin or an erythematous base. The rupture of such blisters produces painful erosions and heals without scarring.

Nikolsky's sign is positive which is elicited by applying firm tangential sliding pressure with a finger on lesional or perilesional skin. This leads to the separation of the normal‐looking epidermis from the dermis, producing erosion.

Direct immunofluorescence is considered the most accurate confirmatory test of this condition. It shows intercellular IgG and C3 deposition on the surface of keratinocytes throughout the epidermis in normal, perilesional skin, in a characteristic fishnet/chickenwire appearance as seen below.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following diseases is unlikely to present with skin lesions on the shin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypothyroidism

Hypothyroidism is unlikely to present with skin lesions on shin. Myxedema (severe hypothyroidism) and pretibial myxedema are different entities. Pretibial myxedema is the infiltrative dermopathy (mucin deposition) seen over shin in Grave's disease, a type of hyperthyroidism.

Other options :

Option B: Diabetes: Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum is classically seen on the anterior leg.

Option A: Sarcoidosis: Erythema nodosum may be seen on the anterior leg.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 23 year old patient presents with lesions in the groin as shown in the image below. Which of the following cannot be a cause of these lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspergillus

The image shows a well-circumscribed, annular plaque in the groin region which is characteristic of tinea cruris. Tinea cruris is a dermatophytosis. Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton are dermatophytes whereas Aspergillus is not.

Dermatophytes include 3 genera:

1. Trichophyton species infect skin, hair, and nails and include T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, T. tonsurans, T. schoenleinii, and T. violaceum.
2. Microsporum contains M. gypseum, M. canis, and M. nanum. These infect only hair and skin (not nails).
3. Floccosum is the only species in the genus Epidermophyton, It infects only skin and nails (not hair).

Aspergillus spp. produce large necrotic lesions like ecthyma gangrenosum, and sometimes small papules and cold abscesses.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A disease associated with the occurrence of blistering and peeling of over >30% of body surface area is usually caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Drugs

Blistering and peeling involving greater than 30% of the body surface area points to the diagnosis of toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). TEN is primarily drug‐induced, with a culprit drug being demonstrated in approximately 85% of cases.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are both severe mucocutaneous reactions, characterized by blistering and epithelial sloughing. The two terms describe phenotypes within a severity spectrum, where SJS is the less extensive form and TEN is the more extensive

Disease
Epidermal detachment
Purpuric macules and atypical target lesions

SJS
<10%
Present

Overlap SJS-TEN
10–30%
Present

TEN with spots
>30%
Present

TEN without spots
>30% (large sheets of epidermal loss)
Absent

Common drugs that can cause SJS/TEN are:

• Allopurinol
• NSAIDs- oxicam group
• Anti-epileptics - phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine
• Antibiotics - penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfamethoxazole, sulfasalazine, nevirapine

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A mother has a pearly white papule on her forehead (as shown in the image below) which her infant also develops. What is the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pox virus

The image shows pearly white umbilicated wart-like lesions with a characteristic dimple at the center, suggestive of molluscum contagiosum, which is caused by pox virus.

The age of peak incidence is between 2 and 5 years. In children, it is mainly caused by the type I molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV-1). There is a relatively higher incidence of MCV‐2 type in adults and HIV infection. Sexually transmitted molluscum contagiosum may be present over the genital area.

It has an incubation period of 2 weeks to 6 months. Widespread and refractory lesions are seen most commonly in HIV or patients on immunosuppressive therapy.

It is characterized by the presence of intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusion bodies called Henderson-Patterson bodies or molluscum bodies. Pseudo-Koebner phenomenon is seen, that is, new lesions develop along lines of trauma.

Treatment is usually not required, and lesions are likely to resolve spontaneously. Stimulation of the immune response can be done after destructive or inflammatory therapies with salicylic acid, trichloroacetic acid, and imiquimod. Cryotherapy when done needs to be repeated at 3-4 week intervals. Extensive lesions are treated with an antiviral agent like cidofovir.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient came with a history of fever, body ache, and joint pain. He was given NSAIDs. A few days later, he developed brownish pigmentation over the nose. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chikungunya

The given history of fever, joint pain, and centrofacial hyperpigmentation points toward a diagnosis of chikungunya. Post chikungunya pigmentation (PCP) usually appears after the fever subsides and persists for about 3-6 months. Hyperpigmentation associated with chikungunya fever is macular and most commonly affects the nose and cheeks.

Another close differential is fixed drug eruptions (FDE). FDE has a shorter latency, usually presents 30 min to 8 h after drug exposure, and recurs at the same location on re-exposure. It presents with hyperpigmented plaques that may be preceded by vesiculobullous lesions.

Hyperpigmentation of the centrofacial region (nose and cheeks) mimics melasma and may be misdiagnosed if proper history is not taken.

Nose pigmentation is striking in cases of chikungunya fever and is termed chik sign. The image below shows chik sign on the nose:

FDE is a type of delayed hypersensitivity reaction.  They occur on lips, hands, legs, face, genitalia, and oral mucosa, and can cause a burning sensation. NSAIDs, paracetamol and co‐trimoxazole are the most common drugs causing FDE. NSAID‐induced FDE mainly affects the genitals and lips.

The image below shows FDE on upper lip area:

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with multiple nodulocystic lesions on the face. Which among the following is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Isotretinoin

The presence of multiple nodulocystic lesions implies that this is a case of severe acne. Isotretinoin is the first-line drug for the treatment of severe acne (nodular acne and acne conglobata).

Systemic retinoids are highly teratogenic and are absolutely contraindicated in pregnant women, those planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding mothers. Two negative pregnancy tests (on separate occasions) are required for females of childbearing age before starting acitretin or isotretinoin.

Baseline evaluation of serum lipids, transaminases, and complete blood counts should be done before starting any systemic retinoids. These values should be checked monthly for the first 3–6 months and once every 3 months thereafter. Monthly pregnancy tests should be done while on the drug.

Note: Female patients should avoid conception for 3 years after discontinuing acitretin treatment for cutaneous psoriasis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the type of connective tissue present in the area marked by the arrow in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dense irregular

The area marked is the reticular dermis. It is made up of dense irregular connective tissue.

It is found in the regions that are under considerable mechanical stress and where protection is given to ensheathed organs. It is usually present in:

• Reticular dermis
• Superficial connective tissue sheaths of the muscle and nerves
• Adventitia of large vessels
• Capsules of various organs and glands (e.g., testis, sclera, periosteum, perichondrium)

On the other hand, dense regular collagen fibers are found in tendons.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which component of cement causes allergic dermatitis among construction workers in India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chromate

Chromate is the most frequent allergen in cement causing occupational contact dermatitis. The most common allergen causing allergic contact dermatitis in India is nickel. It is commonly found in artificial jewelry. However, among construction workers, chromate is more common than nickel. The reported prevalence of allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) to chromate among construction workers is usually more than 10%.

Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is an inflammatory condition caused due to a delayed hypersensitivity reaction (Type 4 hypersensitivity) to a specific allergen that comes into direct contact with the skin. Some common allergens include nickel (found in artificial jewelry), PPD/Para phenylene diamine (in hair dye), chromate (in cement), rubber or latex, cosmetics, etc. Patch test is used for the diagnosis of ACD.

Patients usually present with pruritus, erythema, swelling, papules, and papulovesicles. In severe cases, large vesicles or blisters may form due to the disruption of the intercellular bridges. If exposure persists the affected area becomes dry, scaly, and thicker with lichenification and fissuring develops later. There is involvement of the covered areas as well as the exposed areas.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is a drug used in the treatment of tinea cruris for which widespread resistance is found to be developing?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Terbinafine

The use of terbinafine as the agent of choice for tinea cruris and corporis has been limited lately due to the development of resistance.

Tinea cruris (also known as jock itch) is a dermatophyte infection involving the crural fold. The most common cause is Trichophyton rubrum.

T. rubrum isolates have been found to exhibit resistance against terbinafine.

Note: The question is based on research papers about Trichophyton rubrum strains exhibiting primary resistance to terbinafine.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following nerves is biopsied for the diagnosis of pure neuritic leprosy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superficial branch of radial nerve

Superficial sensory branch of the radial nerve is most commonly used for nerve biopsy in neuritic leprosy.

Although any nerve involved would show the pathology, it is prudent to biopsy a branch of a sensory nerve, rather than a mixed nerve or major nerve trunk. So, the ulnar nerve will not be the best answer despite it being the most common peripheral nerve involved in neuritic leprosy.

The common nerves and sites where nerve biopsy is performed in leprosy are as follows:

• Superficial sensory radial nerve branch at the wrist
• Ulnar cutaneous nerve near the ulnar border of the base of the hand
• Sural nerve near the ankle

Note: Nerve biopsy is the gold standard for confirmation of pure neuritic leprosy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with hair loss. The hair loss is patchy as shown in the image below. Black dots are noted in areas of hair loss. Which of the following types of tinea is this child suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endothrix

The given clinical scenario depicting a young child with patchy hair loss and the image showing black dots is suggestive of endothrix type of tinea capitis.

Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte infection primarily occurring in children. Clinical features of tinea capitis are patchy hair loss, scaling, tender lymphadenopathy, and in severe cases, there might be pustules and crusting of the affected area along with sinus formation.

The clinical variants of tinea capitis are:

• Endothrix - a non-inflammatory type in which multiple black dots are present within the areas of alopecia. It is most commonly caused by T. tonsurans and T. violaceum.
• Ectothrix -a mild inflammatory type in which single or multiple scaly patches with hair loss are seen. Microsporum audouinii, M.canis, M.equinnum, and M.ferrugineum cause ectothrix infection.
• Kerion -a severe inflammatory type that presents with an inflammatory mass with thick crusting and matting of hair with pus and sinus formation. It is commonly caused by T. verrucosum and T. mentagrophytes.

• Favus - is characterized by the presence of yellowish, cup‐shaped crusts known as scutula that develop around hair follicles. It is caused by T. schoenleinii

Treatment:

• Terbinafine: <10 Kg- 62.5 mg; 10-20 kg - 125 mg; >20 kg- 250 mg, all given daily for 4 weeks.
• Itraconazole: 2-4 mg/kg/day for 4-6 weeks.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy had painful sores in the mouth with a rash over the hands along with fever. Which of these is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coxsackievirus

The presence of fever, along with painful sores in the mouth and small, tense vescicles with surrounding erythema on the palms and soles in a child point towards the diagnosis of hand-foot-mouth disease. The most common cause of which worldwide is coxackievirus A16.

Spread is by droplets or faecal contamination and the incubation period is 7 days. The fever is generally mild, and is followed by the appearance of lesions. The characteristic lesions are slightly oval, with a grey blister roof and a narrow rim of erythema. The oral lesions are aphthoid and are less painful than aphthous ulcers.

Only symptomatic treatment is given. The lesions generally disappear in 7 - 10 days.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with flaccid bullous lesions involving the oral cavity and the skin. He has lesions as shown below. Acantholytic cells are seen on Tzanck smear. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pemphigus vulgaris

Flaccid lesions, mucosal involvement, and the presence of acantholytic cells are suggestive of pemphigus vulgaris.

Option A: There is no mucosal involvement in pemphigus foliaceus.

Option C: Dermatitis herpetiformis presents with multiple small vesicles and no acantholysis.

Option D: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense bullae and no acantholysis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient was treated with steroids for psoriasis. On stopping the treatment, he develops fever, malaise, and lesion as seen in the image below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pustular psoriasis

The given clinical scenario points towards the diagnosis of pustular psoriasis.

Pustular psoriasis is a type of psoriasis characterized by tiny pus-filled lesions (pustules) having a characteristic lakes or sheets of pus appearance (seen in the image).

The patient presents with a history of fever and malaise along with the presence of pustules on a circumscribed, fiery red, edematous or scaling plaque. The pus is usually sterile. Sudden withdrawal of systemic steroids is usually the trigger for this condition.

Pustular psoriasis can be divided into:

• Localized pustular psoriasis
• Generalized pustular psoriasis:

• Acute generalized pustular psoriasis (Von Zumbusch)
• Subacute annular and circinate pustular psoriasis
• Acute generalized pustular psoriasis of pregnancy (Impetigo herpetiformis)

Treatment: Acitretin (oral retinoid) is the drug of choice for pustular psoriasis. However, it is contraindicated in pregnancy. Systemic steroids are used instead. Cyclosporine is the second-line drug.

Note: Systemic steroids are never used for the treatment of psoriasis except in the case of Impetigo herpetiformis where they are first-line agents.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient with fever and joint pain developed pigmentation on the nose after a few days of taking NSAIDs as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chikungunya

The given clinical history of fever and joint pain and the image showing hyperpigmented macules on nose (chik sign) is suggestive of Chikungunya.

Post-chikungunya pigmentation (PCP) most commonly affects the nose and cheeks. It often appears as the fever subsides and may persist for about 3-6 months.

PCP mimics melasma and may be misdiagnosed if proper history is not taken.

Another close differential is fixed drug eruptions (FDE). FDE is a type of delayed hypersensitivity reaction. It is characterized by well-defined brown, hyperpigmented plaques that may follow vesiculobullous lesions. They occur on lips, hands, legs, face, genitalia, and oral mucosa, and can cause a burning sensation.They usually present 30 min to 8 h after drug exposure and recur at the same location on re-exposure. NSAIDs, Paracetamol and Co‐trimoxazole are the most common drugs causing FDE.

The image below shows FDE on upper lip area:

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The following lesion is seen in a 25-year-old man who came to a primary health centre 5 days after he had unprotected sexual intercourse. On palpation the ulcers were painful. Suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy was present on the right side. The patient has no previous history of drug allergy. Which kit will be used for the management of this particular sexually transmitted disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Kit 3/white

The appearance of painful genital ulcers, along with unilateral suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy, 5 days after unprotected sexual intercourse best fits the symptom cluster of a non - herpetic genital ulcer. The treatment of which is kit 3 / white kit in case of no penicillin allergy.

The above-shown clinical image and the findings are consistent with a diagnosis of chancroid.

Soft Chancre/Chancroid:

• The causative organism is  Haemophilus ducreyi.
• The incubation period is 3 to 10 days.
• It presents with multiple painful ulcers on genitals.
• It may be accompanied by unilateral painful, suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy.
• Treatment: Inj. Benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units + tab. Azithromycin 1 gm single dose

Note: In the syndromic approach to sexually transmitted infections, kit assignment based on the identification of a cluster of symptoms rather than making an actual diagnosis is given emphasis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Topical steroids are most effective in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Eczematous dermatitis

Topical steroids are the drug of choice in the treatment of eczematous dermatitis.

Other options:

• Steroids cause atrophy and hence is contraindicated in patients with dermal atrophy.
• Herpes infection is associated with immunosuppression so steroids are not useful.
• Routine steroid use not recommended in rosea as it can worsen the condition.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which cell is not present in the layer marked D?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Langerhans cells

The layer marked as D is stratum basale. Langerhan's cells are not present in stratum basale. Langerhan's cells are predominantly present in stratum spinosum.

Keratinocytes, melanocytes, and Merkel discs are all seen in stratum basale:

(Option A) Keratinocytes are predominant cells of the epidermis and constitute the majority of the stratum basale.

(Option B) Merkel discs are type 1 slow-adapting touch receptors.

(Option C) Melanocytes are dendritic cells which are derived from the neural crest cells. The melanosomes synthesized by the melanocytes migrate to the adjacent keratocytes through the dendritic processes

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following does not present with maculopapular rash?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zoster (shingles)

A maculopapular rash is not seen in zoster (shingles).

Shingles cause vesicular lesions that are grouped together and specific to a dermatome.

Type of rash
Description

Macule
Flat lesion with a well-circumscribed change in skin color < 1 cm

Papule
Elevated solid skin lesion < 1 cm

Vesicle
Small fluid containing blister

Maculopapular rashes are seen in:

• Rubella
• Dengue (febrile phase)
• Measles
• Chikungunya (acute infectious phase)
• Erythema infectiosum
• Zika virus
• West Nile virus
• Infectious mononucleosis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: You have ordered a patch test for an 8-year-old boy with a history of allergic contact dermatitis. After the application of the patch, when should you ask him to return for removal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 48 hours

In patch testing, the patch is removed after 48 hours to examine the site of reaction.

Patch testing is a test to detect sensitivity to a specific allergen. A battery of suspected allergens is applied to the patient’s back under occlusive dressings or patches. It is allowed to remain in contact with the skin for 48 hours.

• 48 hours:  Patch removal for initial reading to detect delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
• 72-96 hours: Final reading done for confirmation.

Note: Since the question is regarding the timing of patch removal and not regarding the final diagnosis, 48 hours is the answer.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman who presented with complaints of fever and joint pain develops the following lesion on her nose after a few days of taking NSAIDs. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chikungunya

The given history of fever and joint pain along with centrofacial hyperpigmentation shown in the image point towards a diagnosis of chikungunya. Hyperpigmentation associated with chikungunya fever is macular and most commonly affects the nose and cheeks.

Nose pigmentation is striking in cases of Chikungunya fever and is termed as Chik sign. It appears as the fever subsides and persists for about 3-6 months.

Hyperpigmentation of the centrofacial face (nose and cheeks) mimics melasma and may be misdiagnosed if proper history is not taken.

Another close differential is fixed drug eruptions (FDE). FDE is a type of delayed hypersensitivity reaction. It is characterized by well-defined brown, hyperpigmented plaques that may follow vesiculobullous lesions. They occur on lips, hands, legs, face, genitalia, and oral mucosa, and can cause a burning sensation. They usually present 30 min to 8 h after drug exposure and recur at the same location on re-exposure. NSAIDs, Paracetamol and Co‐trimoxazole are the most common drugs causing FDE.

The image below shows FDE on upper lip area:

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A child presents to OPD with tense bullae over the torso. Biopsy of the lesion showed a subepidermal level of blistering and neutrophil infiltration. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dapsone

This clinical scenario with tense blisters showing subepidermal separation and neutrophilic infiltration at the basement membrane points towards a diagnosis of IgA pemphigoid or linear IgA disease or chronic bullous disease of childhood. The drug of choice is dapsone. It is bacteriostatic against M. leprae.

It also has an anti-inflammatory action by decreasing the action of neutrophil enzymes. Hence, it is useful in the treatment of IgA pemphigoid, linear IgA disease and chronic bullous disease of childhood.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female patient presents with active genital warts with a history of recurrence, but her husband doesn't have it. What advice will you give to prevent transmission?
options: Give continuous prophylaxis to the patient
Give prophylactic anti-virals to the husband
Give anti-virals whenever active lesions are present
Don't involve in intercourse when active lesions are present
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Don't involve in intercourse when active lesions are present

The advice to prevent transmission is to not involve in intercourse when active genital warts are present.

Genital warts are caused by HPV and transmitted through the sexual route. Antivirals are not very effective against anogenital warts. Biological treatment options like podophyllin, imiquimod, 5-fluorouracil are given. The best way to prevent transmission of infection is by avoiding sexual intercourse when active lesions are present.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A male baby born to a non-consanguineous couple develops blisters on areas of friction. Their previous baby also had similar complaints and died at the age of 2 weeks. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Epidermolysis bullosa

The clinical history given in the question points to a diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa congenita.

Epidermolysis bullosa is a mechanobullous disease characterized by blistering in areas of mechanical trauma. Blisters are commonly seen in trauma-prone areas like hands, feet, elbows, and knees. There are three types of epidermolysis bullosa:

• Epidermolysis bullosa simplex - defective K5/K14 protein
• Junctional epidermolysis bullosa - defective Laminin
• Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa - defective Collagen-7

The image below shows epidermolysis bullosa lesions on the foot:

Other options:

Option B: Chronic bullous disorder of childhood - It typically presents with bullous lesions having a string of pearls/cluster of jewel appearance (image below). It is an IgA-mediated immunobullous disorder. It manifests in early childhood and is not a congenital condition.

Option C: Congenital Syphilis - Syphilitic pemphigus presents as a vesiculobullous disorder. The investigation of choice is VDRL.

Option D: Neonatal Pemphigus - It is an autoimmune blistering disease caused by the transfer of maternal IgG autoantibodies to desmoglein 3 to the neonate through the placenta when the mother is affected with pemphigus. It is clinically characterized by transient flaccid blisters and erosions on the skin and, rarely, the mucous membranes.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient with a known case of chronic plaque psoriasis with more than 50% skin involvement presents to you. Which of the following will you not recommend?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oral steroids

Oral/systemic steroids are not used in the management of chronic plaque psoriasis. Topical steroids may be used.

Systemic steroids are avoided because the withdrawal of systemic steroids causes the development of pustular psoriasis.

The only indication of using systemic steroids in psoriasis is generalized pustular psoriasis in pregnancy (impetigo herpetiformis).

Other options maybe used in treatment of extensive (>30%) chronic plaque psoriasis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A rose gardener with a history of thorn prick presents with the following lesions. What is the possible causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sporothrix schenkii

The given image shows the distribution of lesions along lymphatics. This distribution along with the history of thorn pick is suggestive of the causative agent Sporothrix schenkii.

Sporothrix schenkii causes rose gardener's disease. It is a saprophyte that lives on grass and plants. Hence a history of thorn prick in farmers or gardeners is an important clue.

Other causes of skin lesion distributed along lymphatics is fish tankgranuloma caused by Mycobacterium marinum.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A school-going child who had applied henna comes to dermatology OPD with the following lesions. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dermatitis artefacta

The likely diagnosis in this case is dermatitis artefacta (factitious dermatitis).

Dermatitis artefacta is a psychodermatological excoriation disorder with a female preponderance, commonly affecting adolescents and young adults, where elaborate techniques (using sharp objects, cigarettes, lighters, chemicals etc.) are used to self induce skin lesions.

The morphology of the lesions are varied, with oddly linear, clear-cut and angular edges, surrounded by normal looking skin. These lesions appear with no prodromal stage or associated symptoms as they are self inflicted. They are distributed over easy to reach areas of the body and have a varied appearance based on the mode of injury.

• Option A: Contact dermatitis is due to contact with allergic agents such as paraphenylenediamine (PPD). Presentation can vary from erythema, swelling, papules, vesicles and in severe cases, blisters on the areas of contact with the allergen (henna, in this case). There exists a sequence of inflammatory changes here, unlike the lesions in dermatitis artefacta.
• Option B: Polymorphic light eruptions as the name suggests are seen over sunlight-exposed areas of the body. The lesions are polymorphic and are symmetrically distributed.
• Option C: Vitiligo is characterized by patchy involvement of skin with hypopigmentation.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the type of skin lesion.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Annular

The given image shows ring-shaped lesions with central clearing, which are characteristic of annular lesions.

In annular lesions, only the edges are active and appear raised, or in a different color. They are seen in tinea corporis, granuloma annulare, borderline leprosy, and psoriasis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Methylisothiazolinone (MI) in cosmetics is used as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Preservative

Methylisothiazolinone (MI) in cosmetics is used as a preservative to inhibit bacterial growth. It is permitted to be used up to the level of 100 ppm.

Several cases of allergic contact dermatitis due to MI were reported due to its presence in wet wipes, hair cosmetics, facial cosmetics, deodorants, and sunscreens.

Furthermore, cases of airborne exposure to MI causing severe airborne and generalized dermatitis from recently painted walls and even from toilet cleaners have been described.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The given condition is caused by which drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bleomycin

The given image shows flagellate dermatitis. It is caused by bleomycin.

Flagellate dermatitis starts as bands of pruritic, flagellate, erythema over the trunk, and extremities within few hours to 6 months after administration. The rash heals with persistent flagellate hyperpigmentation.

No treatment is necessary since the lesions usually disappear when bleomycin is discontinued. If the patient is itchy, managing pruritus with an antihistamine may limit trauma to the skin, and thus avoid further hyperpigmentation.

Another side effect that one needs to watch out for with the use of bleomycin is the development of pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis of this condition affecting hair?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trichothiodystrophy

The given clinical image of hair seen under polarising microscopy reveals tiger tail banding (alternating light and dark bands) characteristic of trichothiodystrophy.

Trichothiodystrophy is an autosomal recessive condition causing defective DNA repair. It causes brittle sulfur-deficient hair, photosensitivity, ichthyosis and systemic involvement. Unlike xeroderma pigmentosum (a similar condition with defective DNA repair), there is no risk of skin cancer.

Option A: Trichorrhexis nodosa is associated with node formation and fractures. The classic appearance, shown in the image below, is known as thrust paintbrush appearance as if two paintbrushes are rubbing against each other. It is associated with trauma to the hair shaft and arginosuccinic aciduria.

B- Trichorrhexis invaginata or bamboo hair is characterized by invagination of the distal hair shaft into the proximal portion. It is seen in Netherton's syndrome. It is also called golf-tee or ball and socket appearance as seen below.

Option D: Monilethrix, seen in the image below, is characterized by beaded hair and is fragile at the constricted sites. It occurs as an isolated condition or can occur in Menkes disease.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: 22-year-old primigravid woman at 8 weeks gestation comes to the office for her initial prenatal visit. She has no symptoms except mild nausea. She smoked a pack of cigarettes a day and drank 7-8 beers each week but quit after learning she was pregnant. The patient has a history of an allergic reaction to penicillin; she developed a generalized rash with intense itching that responded to antihistamines and corticosteroid cream. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. The screening VDRL test is positive, fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test is positive. Her HIV test is negative. Which of the following is the best next step in management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Skin testing and penicillin desensitization

This patient has serologically confirmed syphilis in early pregnancy (positive VDRL + FTA-ABS) and a history of penicillin allergy (mild rash).

Key points:

• Penicillin is the only proven effective treatment for syphilis in pregnancy and prevents congenital syphilis.
• Azithromycin and doxycycline are contraindicated in pregnancy or unreliable against maternal and fetal infection.
• Delaying treatment until delivery risks vertical transmission.
• The recommended approach is penicillin skin testing and desensitization, followed by appropriate penicillin therapy.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Azithromycin – Not reliably effective for preventing congenital syphilis.

B. Doxycycline – Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic).

C. No treatment until delivery – Risks fetal infection, congenital syphilis, and adverse outcomes.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presents with multiple, tiny, round papules over the trunk and flexor surfaces of the forearms. The lesions are discrete, smooth, shiny, skin-colored, and measure about 1–2 mm in diameter. They are asymptomatic and have been present for 3 months. Closer examination on histopathology caused by a dense lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the dermal papillae being encompassed by elongated rete ridges. Nails and mucosa are normal. No systemic complaints are noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lichen nitidus

Lichen nitidus is a benign, self-limited papular dermatosis seen commonly in children and young adults.

• Multiple tiny (1–2 mm), discrete papules
• Smooth, shiny, skin-colored
• Common sites:

• Trunk
• Flexor surfaces of forearms
• Genitalia (sometimes)

• Usually asymptomatic
• Nails and mucosa typically spared
• “Ball and claw” appearance:

• Dense lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in dermal papillae (ball)
• Surrounded by elongated rete ridges (claw)

Why not other options:

A. Lichen planus:

• Violaceous, pruritic, polygonal papules
• Wickham striae, mucosal and nail involvement common

C. Lichen striatus: Linear distribution along Blaschko’s lines

D. Pityriasis versicolor:

• Hypo/hyperpigmented macules with fine scaling
• Caused by Malassezia

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents due to sores on her feet. Since she took her first steps 3 months ago, she has had blisters involving the soles of the feet, which subsequently break down and heal slowly. The patient had failure to thrive as an infant due to frequent oral ulcerations but otherwise has been healthy and has achieved normal developmental milestones. Examination shows small bullae at the soles with faint erythema and no scarring. Biopsy taken at the margin of a blister shows an intraepidermal cleavage plane. Which of the following most likely contributes to the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?
options: Loss of function mutation in filaggrin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Impaired keratin filament assembly

• This infant has epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS). Key clues are blistering with minor trauma (walking), oral ulcers in infancy, slow healing without scarring, and intraepidermal cleavage on biopsy.
• EBS is caused by mutations in keratin 5 or keratin 14, which are critical for keratin intermediate filament assembly in basal keratinocytes.
• Defective cytoskeletal support makes cells fragile, leading to blister formation with mechanical stress.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Autoantibodies against tissue transglutaminase – Seen in celiac disease, not blistering disorders.

C. Loss of function mutation in filaggrin – Causes atopic dermatitis/ichthyosis vulgaris, not bullae.

D. T-cell–mediated hypersensitivity reaction – Seen in contact dermatitis, not congenital blistering.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl comes to the physician for a follow-up evaluation. She has multiple erythematous pustules and nodules over her face, for which she has received erythromycin and topical benzoyl peroxide. She is concerned that the therapy is ineffective. The physician recommends a drug on the condition that the patient agrees to use oral contraceptives. The molecular structure of the drug most likely recommended by the physician closely resembles a drug used to treat which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute promyelocytic leukaemia

This adolescent has severe nodulocystic acne refractory to antibiotics and benzoyl peroxide. The requirement for oral contraceptive use strongly points to isotretinoin, a highly teratogenic retinoid. Isotretinoin is a vitamin A (retinoic acid) derivative, and its molecular structure closely resembles all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which is used to treat acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) by inducing differentiation of malignant promyelocytes (PML-RARA fusion).

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. EGFR-positive NSCLC – Treated with erlotinib/gefitinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitors).

C. BRAF-positive metastatic melanoma – Treated with vemurafenib/dabrafenib (BRAF inhibitors).

D. HER2-positive gastric cancer – Treated with trastuzumab (monoclonal antibody).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 16-year-old male is started on oral isotretinoin for nodulo-cystic acne. His mother asks what routine blood tests to monitor during therapy. The most critical lipid abnormality to screen for is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Elevated triglycerides and total cholesterol

Isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid) most importantly elevates triglycerides and total cholesterol. Fasting lipid profiles must be monitored throughout treatment due to the risk of hypertriglyceridaemia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 19-year-old girl with severe nodulocystic acne is started on oral isotretinoin. After 6 weeks, she shows dramatic reduction in new lesions. Which one of the following mechanisms best explains the response?
options: Suppression of TNF-α and IL-17 pathways
Inhibition of keratinocyte proliferation and normalization of follicular keratinization
Direct inhibition of Propionibacterium acnes protein synthesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of keratinocyte proliferation and normalization of follicular keratinization

Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) is the most effective drug for severe nodulocystic acne because it targets the primary pathogenic event—abnormal follicular keratinization. It reduces keratinocyte proliferation, promotes normal differentiation, and prevents comedone formation. Additionally, it causes marked sebaceous gland atrophy and decreased sebum production, indirectly reducing Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes. These combined effects explain the dramatic reduction in new lesions seen within weeks.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents with fever and widespread sheet-like skin peeling. The Nikolsky sign is positive. There are no oral lesions. The causative exotoxin acts on which specific target?
options: Desmoglein-3 — causing mucosal and cutaneous lesions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Desmoglein-1 — causing subcorneal acantholysis

SSSS is caused by staphylococcal epidermolytic toxin targeting Desmoglein-1, causing subcorneal acantholysis. Since Desmoglein-3 is unaffected (maintains mucosal adhesion), oral lesions are absent — a key distinguishing feature from pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to 3 days of malodorous vaginal discharge and severe vulvar pruritus. The patient is sexually active and had a copper-containing intrauterine device placed for contraception last year. Pelvic examination shows a thin, frothy, and green vaginal discharge with marked vulvar and vaginal erythema. Vaginal discharge pH is 5.5. The intrauterine device strings are visualized and protrude through the cervical os. Microscopic examination of this patient's vaginal discharge will most likely reveal which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flagellated, motile organisms

This patient has trichomoniasis, caused by Trichomonas vaginalis. Classic features include thin, frothy, green discharge, malodor, severe vulvar pruritus, erythema, and elevated vaginal pH (>4.5). On wet mount microscopy, the hallmark finding is flagellated, motile protozoa with jerky movements. Copper IUD use does not cause this but does not protect against STIs.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Clue cells – Seen in bacterial vaginosis; discharge is thin and gray with fishy odor but minimal inflammation.

B. Filamentous, gram-positive bacilli – Indicates Actinomyces-Classic trapper associated with IUD-But will not show "thin, frothy, and green vaginal discharge with cervical inflammation"-Usually presents with PID! Presentation is classic for Trichomoniasis

D.Pseudohyphae – Seen in Candida infection; discharge is thick, curdy, white, and pH is normal

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 21-year-old college student presents with sudden onset of multiple symmetrically distributed targetoid lesions over the palms, soles, and extensor aspects of forearms. He had painful grouped vesicles over the lips 10 days earlier. Examination reveals classical target lesions with a dusky center, surrounding pale edematous zone, and outer erythematous rim. Oral mucosa is minimally involved. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?
options: The characteristic target lesion consists of only two zones and is typical of Stevens–Johnson syndrome
The most common trigger is HSV-1 infection causing a cytotoxic dermatitis
Recurrence at the same site after drug intake due to resident memory T cells is the hallmark feature
Lesions predominantly involve proximal trunk with sheet-like epidermal detachment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. The most common trigger is HSV-1 infection causing a cytotoxic dermatitis

| Feature | Erythema Multiforme (EM)

| ------- | ------------------------

| Pathogenesis | Cytotoxic dermatitis

| Most common trigger | HSV-1 infection

| Lesion | Classical 3-zone target lesion

| Distribution | Distal extremities, palms, soles

| Difference from SJS/TEN | EM has typical 3-zone targets; SJS/TEN has flat atypical 2-zone targets with epidermal detachment

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 22-year-old woman presents with progressive thinning of scalp hair. Hair microscopy demonstrates angulated hair roots, indicating active hair growth. The dermatologist explains the normal phases of the hair cycle. Which of the following correctly matches the hair cycle phase with its characteristic feature?
options: Catagen – Accounts for 80–90% of scalp follicles at any given time
Telogen – Active proliferative phase lasting several years
Anagen – Presence of angulated roots and longest growth period
Catagen – Resting phase lasting approximately 3 months
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anagen – Presence of angulated roots and longest growth period

The hair cycle consists of three major phases:

1. Anagen (Growth phase) ✅

• Longest phase
• Lasts 2–7 years on the scalp
• Approximately 85–90% of scalp hairs are in this phase
• Hair matrix cells actively proliferate
• Hair root is pigmented and angulated ("flame-shaped")
• Responsible for hair length

Hence, Option C is correct.

2. Catagen (Transition phase)

• Lasts 2–3 weeks
• Accounts for only 1–2% of scalp hairs
• Hair growth stops
• Lower follicle undergoes apoptosis and involution
• Club hair begins to form

3. Telogen (Resting phase)

• Lasts approximately 2–3 months
• Represents 10–15% of scalp hairs
• Hair is fully keratinized and forms a club-shaped root
• Hair is eventually shed during the exogen phase

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Catagen – Accounts for 80–90% of scalp follicles ❌

• Anagen, not catagen, comprises 85–90% of scalp hairs.

B. Telogen – Active proliferative phase lasting several years ❌

• This describes anagen, not telogen.

D. Catagen – Resting phase lasting 3 months ❌

• Telogen is the resting phase lasting about 3 months.
• Catagen is a brief involution phase lasting only 2–3 weeks.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 23-year-old man who notes recurrent severe nosebleeds is found to have pink spider-like lesions on his oral and nasal mucosa, face, and arms. The patient most likely suffers from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome

This patient’s recurrent severe epistaxis combined with pink, spider-like lesions (telangiectasias) on the oral and nasal mucosa, face, and arms is classic for Osler– Weber–Rendu syndrome, also known as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT). It is an autosomal dominant vascular disorder caused by abnormal blood vessel formation, leading to fragile telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations that bleed easily.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Von Recklinghausen’s disease (NF1) – Features café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas, not mucosal telangiectasias.

B. Neurofibromatosis type 2 – Characterized by bilateral acoustic neuromas.

D. Von Hippel–Lindau disease – Causes hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma, not epistaxis with telangiectasias.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 24-year-old man presents with pain and swelling of the right knee 3 weeks after an episode of urethral discharge. Examination reveals multiple hyperkeratotic papules and plaques over the soles and circular painless erosions over the glans penis. Laboratory evaluation shows sterile synovial fluid and negative rheumatoid factor. Which of the following combinations is most characteristic of this condition?
options: Palpable purpura with thrombocytopenia and IgM deposition in vessel walls
Circinate balanitis with keratoderma blennorrhagicum occurring after genitourinary infection
Painful genital ulcers with tender suppurative inguinal buboes caused by Haemophilus ducreyi
Symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis with rheumatoid nodules and anti-CCP positivity
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Circinate balanitis with keratoderma blennorrhagicum occurring after genitourinary infection

This patient has reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome).

High-yield features:

• Sterile inflammatory arthritis after distant infection

• Commonly urethritis or enteric infection

• Mucocutaneous lesions:

• Circinate balanitis → painless circular erosions on glans
• Keratoderma blennorrhagicum → hyperkeratotic papules/plaques on palms and soles

• Typically seronegative arthritis

Why others are wrong:

• A. Palpable purpura with thrombocytopenia and IgM deposition in vessel walls: Describes Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis), which has palpable purpura with normal platelet count
• C. Painful genital ulcers with tender suppurative inguinal buboes caused by Haemophilus ducreyi: Describes chancroid
• D. Symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis with rheumatoid nodules and anti-CCP positivity: Describes rheumatoid arthritis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 24-year-old sexually active woman presents with fever, migratory polyarthralgia, pustular skin lesions on the extremities, and tenosynovitis of the wrist. Blood cultures are pending. The physician suspects disseminated infection caused by a sexually transmitted organism. Which organism is the most likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neisseria gonorrhoeae

The constellation of fever + migratory polyarthralgia + tenosynovitis + pustular skin lesions in a sexually active individual is classic for disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI).

Causative Organism: Neisseria gonorrhoeae

• A gram-negative intracellular diplococcus
• Transmitted sexually
• Can disseminate hematogenously → DGI

DGI triad:

1. Migratory polyarthralgia
2. Tenosynovitis (especially wrists, fingers)
3.

Dermatitis → pustular or vesiculopustular lesions

4.

Certain strains evade immune response → bacteremia

5. Immune complex deposition contributes to joint symptoms

Why not other options:

A. Chlamydia trachomatis: Causes reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome), not pustular lesions

B. Treponema pallidum: Causes syphilis (rash involves palms/soles, not pustular + tenosynovitis)

D. Haemophilus ducreyi: Causes painful genital ulcers (chancroid)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of dysuria and urethral discharge. Upon further questioning, he reports recent unprotected sexual intercourse. A urethral swab is taken for Gram stain and culture. Which of the following organisms is least likely to cause urethritis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Haemophilus ducreyi

This patient has urethritis following unprotected sex. The most common causes of urethritis are Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonococcal urethritis) and Chlamydia trachomatis (most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis). Trichomonas vaginalis can also cause urethritis, especially persistent or recurrent cases.

Haemophilus ducreyi, however, causes chancroid, which presents with painful genital ulcers and tender suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy, not urethritis.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Chlamydia trachomatis – Leading cause of nongonococcal urethritis.

C. Neisseria gonorrhoeae – Classic cause of acute purulent urethritis.

D. Trichomonas – Can cause urethritis, particularly in sexually active men.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 27-year-old sexually active man presents with genital ulcers for 5 days. Examination reveals multiple soft, non-indurated ulcers with ragged undermined edges that bleed on touch. He also has a unilateral fluctuant inguinal swelling. Gram stain from ulcer exudate shows gram-negative coccobacilli arranged in “school of fish/railroad track” pattern. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the most likely diagnosis?
options: Genital ulcer is usually painless, transient, and absent when inguinal lymphadenopathy appears
Inguinal lymphadenopathy is typically absent, though pseudobuboes may occur
Tender buboes are associated with concomitant active genital ulceration
Tzanck smear demonstrates multinucleated giant cells and recurrence is common due to sacral ganglion latency
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tender buboes are associated with concomitant active genital ulceration

The patient has chancroid due to Haemophilus ducreyi:

• Multiple painful soft chancres
• Tender fluctuant unilateral bubo
• Concomitant genital ulcer present
• “School of fish/railroad track” appearance on smear

| Disease | Genital Ulcer | Pain | Ulcer Characteristics | Inguinal LN | Bubo | Concomitant Ulcer when LN appears | Key Diagnostic Clue

| ------- | ------------- | ---- | --------------------- | ----------- | ---- | --------------------------------- | -------------------

| Primary Syphilis | Single | Painless | Clean-based, indurated hard chancre, non-bleeding | Bilateral enlarged, rubbery, non-tender | Absent | Present | Dark ground microscopy; corkscrew motility of T. pallidum

| Chancroid | Multiple | Painful | Soft chancre, ragged undermined edges, necrotic base, bleeds on touch | Tender unilateral | Present | Present | “School of fish/railroad track” arrangement of H. ducreyi

| Genital Herpes | Multiple grouped vesicles → ulcers | Painful | Superficial ulcers with polycyclic margins | Bilateral tender | Usually absent | Present | Tzanck smear: multinucleated giant cells; recurrent disease

| LGV | Single transient ulcer | Usually painless | Small transient ulcer often unnoticed | Tender inguinal/femoral LN | Present | Absent | Groove sign of Greenblatt; Chlamydia trachomatis L1–L3

| Donovanosis | Single/multiple | Painless | Beefy-red highly vascular ulcer, bleeds on touch | Usually absent | Pseudobubo possible | Present | Donovan bodies in macrophages (“closed safety pin”)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man comes to the OPD to discuss hair loss. He has hair loss primarily around the temples, which began insidiously 3 years ago. Physical examination shows moderate thinning of hair at the anterior scalp, temporal region, and vertex. An oral medication is prescribed to treat the hair loss. After the initiation of therapy, which of the following changes would most likely occur in this patient?
options: Testosterone low, Dihydrotestosterone low, Estradiol normal
Testosterone high, Dihydrotestosterone low, Estradiol high
Testosterone high, Dihydrotestosterone low, Estradiol low
Testosterone high, Dihydrotestosterone high, Estradiol high
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Testosterone high, Dihydrotestosterone low, Estradiol high

This is androgenetic alopecia (bitemporal recession + vertex thinning). The oral drug used is finasteride, a 5-α reductase inhibitor (type II), which blocks conversion of testosterone → dihydrotestosterone (DHT). So DHT falls. Because less testosterone is converted to DHT, testosterone rises slightly, and some of that extra testosterone is aromatized to estradiol, so estradiol can increase (explains gynecomastia/sexual side effects in some).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 28-year-old pregnant woman develops cauliflower-like lesions in the perianal region. She asks about treatment that avoids systemic drug exposure. What is the first-line treatment in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen

Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen at -196 degrees C) is the first-line treatment for anogenital warts in pregnant patients. Podophyllin and imiquimod are avoided in pregnancy due to potential teratogenicity.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 28-year-old sexually active man presents with high-grade fever followed by large, deep-seated vesiculopustular lesions with central umbilication. Examination also reveals prominent cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which feature best differentiates this condition from varicella?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Prominent lymphadenopathy with deep-seated lesions

This is Monkeypox (Mpox).

High-yield distinguishing points:

• Emerging sexually transmitted infection
• High-grade fever before rash
• Deep-seated vesicles/pustules
• Central umbilication
• Lymphadenopathy is a key differentiating feature from chickenpox

Differentials:

• Varicella: Superficial pleomorphic vesicles (“dewdrop on rose petal”), centripetal spread
• HFMD: Vesicles over palms, soles, buttocks, oral cavity due to Coxsackie A16/Enterovirus 71

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 28-year-old sexually active man presents with multiple asymptomatic lesions over the genital region and palms for 2 weeks. Examination reveals flat-topped moist papules in the perianal region, generalized non-tender lymphadenopathy, and symmetric non-pruritic papulosquamous lesions involving both palms and soles. Patchy “moth-eaten” non-scarring alopecia is also noted. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?
options: Painful vesicular lesions with inguinal buboes
Dark ground microscopy demonstrating corkscrew motility from a hard chancre
Buschke-Ollendorff sign due to endarteritis obliterans
Ascending aortic aneurysm involving the arch of aorta
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Buschke-Ollendorff sign due to endarteritis obliterans

This patient has secondary syphilis:

• Condyloma lata
• Palms and soles involvement
• Generalized lymphadenopathy
• Moth-eaten alopecia
• Symmetric non-pruritic polymorphic rash

Buschke-Ollendorff sign:

• Deep dermal tenderness on pressing lesions with a blunt object
• Due to endarteritis obliterans
• Seen in secondary syphilis

Why others are wrong:

• Dark ground microscopy + corkscrew motility → primary syphilis
• Ascending aortic aneurysm → tertiary cardiovascular syphilis
• Painful vesicles with buboes suggest herpes/chancroid rather than syphilis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman applied a potent topical steroid on her face for 6 months on advice from a friend. She now presents with flushing, papules, and pustules over her face without comedones. Which adverse effect of topical corticosteroids does this represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rosacea-like dermatitis

Prolonged facial topical steroid use causes a rosacea-like dermatitis — papules and pustules without comedones (distinguishing it from acne). This is part of the STEROID mnemonic of adverse effects. Topical steroids are therefore contraindicated in rosacea treatment.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair loss following COVID-19 infection 3 months ago. Hair pull test is positive. Trichoscopy shows no miniaturised hairs. The most likely underlying mechanism involves which phase of the hair cycle?
options: Premature termination of the catagen phase
Premature transition of anagen hairs to telogen phase
Abrupt disruption of mitotic activity in matrix cells
Autoimmune targeting of the hair bulb
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Premature transition of anagen hairs to telogen phase

Telogen effluvium follows a systemic stressor (infection, fever) 3-4 months prior. The stressor disrupts the hair follicle cycle, causing premature anagen-to-telogen transition, leading to diffuse shedding.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 3-week-old neonate is diagnosed with scabies. Most scabicidal agents carry risk of neurotoxicity in this age group. Which is the only recommended topical agent specifically approved for infants under 2 months?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Topical sulfur preparation

Topical sulfur (keratolytic) is the only recommended agent for infants under 2 months of age. Permethrin is approved from 2 months; ivermectin from >5 years (>15 kg); lindane is contraindicated in children under 10 years.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the OPD due to 2 days of fever and rash. Her mother says that she has also been refusing to eat or drink. She has no prior medical conditions and is up to date with recommended vaccinations. Physical examination shows multiple small vesicles and ulcers with an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa and tongue. There are similar vesicular lesions on the distal extremities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's rash?
options: Immune response to a bacterial toxin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Disseminated enteroviral infection

This child’s presentation is classic for hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD). Key features include fever, painful oral vesicles and ulcers (buccal mucosa, tongue), and vesicular lesions on distal extremities. HFMD is caused by enteroviruses, most commonly Coxsackievirus A16 or Enterovirus 71, which disseminate after initial replication in the oropharynx and GI tract. Painful oral lesions explain refusal to eat or drink. The disease is self-limited and common in young children.

Why the other options are incorrect:

• Autoantibody-mediated acantholysis – Seen in pemphigus vulgaris, not febrile viral illness in children.
• Idiosyncratic hypersensitivity reaction – Typically drug-related; lacks characteristic hand-foot-mouth distribution.
• Immune response to a bacterial toxin – Seen in scarlet fever or toxic shock, which do not cause vesicular oral lesions.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old individual presents with multiple blistering skin lesions. A skin biopsy reveals acantholysis, characterized by the loss of adhesion between keratinocytes. Which of the following conditions is least likely to display acantholytic cells on histological examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection

Acantholysis refers to loss of intercellular adhesion between keratinocytes, typically due to damage to desmosomes. It is a key histologic feature in several blistering disorders—but not HPV infection.

HPV infection causes koilocytosis (perinuclear clearing, nuclear atypia), not acantholysis.

Why other options are correct:

A. Pemphigus – Autoantibodies against desmogleins → classic acantholysis (“row of tombstones”).

C. Herpes simplex infection – Shows acantholysis with multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear.

D. Bullous impetigo – Caused by Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxins that cleave desmoglein-1, producing acantholysis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man has multiple tender, necrotic genital ulcers that bleed on touch, along with a unilateral painful fluctuant inguinal bubo with concomitant ulcer. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Azithromycin 1 g stat

Chancroid (H. ducreyi) presents with soft, tender, necrotic ulcers that bleed on touch, with a unilateral bubo and concomitant genital ulcer. School of fish pattern on smear is characteristic. Treatment: Azithromycin 1g single dose.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 31-year-old pregnant lady comes with dysuria and urethral discharge for 3 days. NAAT for gonorrhea was negative. What is the true statement regarding the condition the patient is most likely to have?
options: The elementary body is the infectious form of the causative organism.
Applying erythromycin to the newborn's eyes prevents the disease.
Infection in pregnant women is treated with doxycycline.
Genital disease is caused by serotypes A, B, and C
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The elementary body is the infectious form of the causative organism.

This pregnant woman has nongonococcal urethritis, most likely due to Chlamydia trachomatis, since NAAT for gonorrhea is negative. Key points about C. trachomatis:

• Elementary body (EB) – infectious, extracellular form that attaches to epithelial cells.
• Reticulate body (RB) – Intracellular, metabolically active, replicative form.
• Treatment in pregnancy – azithromycin is preferred; doxycycline is contraindicated.
• Neonatal prophylaxis – Erythromycin ointment prevents gonococcal ophthalmia, not chlamydial infection.
• Serotypes – Genital disease is caused by D–K, not A–C (which cause trachoma).

Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Applying erythromycin to newborn’s eyes prevents disease – Prevents gonococcal ophthalmia, not chlamydial infection.

C. Infection in pregnant women is treated with doxycycline – Contraindicated; use azithromycin instead.

D. Genital disease is caused by serotypes A, B, C – Cause ocular trachoma, not genital infection.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 32-year-old man with lepromatous leprosy presents with sudden onset of painful erythematous nodules over the face and extremities, accompanied by fever, malaise, and arthralgia. Examination shows multiple tender subcutaneous nodules. Laboratory tests reveal neutrophilia and elevated ESR. He also has orchitis and lymphadenitis. This condition is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type III hypersensitivity

This patient has erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), a type 2 lepra reaction, seen in lepromatous leprosy. Key features include:

• Sudden onset of tender erythematous nodules on face and extremities
• Systemic symptoms: fever, malaise, arthralgia
• Multisystem involvement: orchitis, lymphadenitis, eye involvement
• Laboratory: neutrophilia, elevated ESR

Pathophysiology:

• ENL is caused by immune complex deposition (antigen-antibody complexes) in tissues, activating complement and neutrophils → Type III hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of fatigue and yellowish discoloration of her skin. During this period, she has also had a 6 kg weight gain. She does not smoke and drinks one glass of wine daily. She follows a vegan diet that consists mainly of spinach, kale, and sweet potatoes. Physical examination shows yellowing of the skin. Her hands are cold to the touch and her nails appear brittle. Eye examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following findings is most likely in this patient's serum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased beta-carotene concentration

She has yellow skin without eye involvement (no scleral icterus) plus fatigue, weight gain, cold hands, brittle nails → consistent with hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism reduces conversion of β-carotene to vitamin A, causing carotenemia. A vegan diet high in spinach/ kale/sweet potatoes (β-carotene–rich) further increases this, leading to yellow-orange skin (often prominent on palms/soles) with normal sclera.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Decreased haptoglobin → hemolysis (would also raise indirect bilirubin; not diet- related; scleral icterus possible).

B. Increased alkaline phosphatase → cholestasis/biliary disease; typically jaundice with scleral icterus ± pruritus.

C. Positive antimitochondrial antibodies → primary biliary cholangitis; cholestatic labs, pruritus, scleral icterus.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with eczematous patches that worsened significantly after starting topical corticosteroids. Biopsy shows disruption of intercellular spaces with fluid accumulation between keratinocytes. Which layer of the epidermis is primarily affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stratum spinosum

Intraepidermal intercellular oedema (spongiosis) characteristically occurs in the stratum spinosum. It is the hallmark of acute eczema, where fluid separates keratinocytes in this layer.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 33-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of progressive hair loss from his scalp. He first noticed receding of the hairline over the bitemporal regions of his scalp 5 years ago. Since then, his hair has gradually become thinner over the crown of his head. He is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. Examination shows diffuse, nonscarring hair loss over the scalp with a bitemporal pattern of recession. Administration of which of the following systemic drugs is most appropriate to treat this patient's hair loss?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Finasteride

This patient has androgenetic alopecia, characterized by bitemporal recession and vertex thinning in a young man. The most appropriate systemic therapy is finasteride, a 5-α reductase inhibitor that blocks conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), the androgen responsible for follicular miniaturization. By lowering scalp DHT levels, finasteride slows hair loss and promotes regrowth, especially at the crown, making it the treatment of choice for male-pattern baldness.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Flutamide – An antiandrogen used in prostate cancer; not used due to toxicity.

B. Clomipramine – A tricyclic antidepressant; no role in alopecia.

C. Minoxidil – Effective but primarily topical; systemic use is not standard for alopecia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 34-year-old patient presents with multiple soft, pedunculated skin lesions on the trunk. On palpation, these lesions are compressible and invaginate into the skin upon gentle pressure, creating a characteristic "button-hole" appearance. This finding is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neurofibromatosis type 1

The description of multiple soft, pedunculated, compressible skin lesions that invaginate into the skin on pressure (“button-hole sign”) is classic for cutaneous neurofibromas.

This sign occurs because neurofibromas are unencapsulated tumors of peripheral nerve sheath origin that are loosely attached to surrounding tissue, allowing them to be pushed inward. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the NF1 gene (chromosome 17).

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Systemic lupus erythematosus – Causes photosensitive rashes, not compressible nodules.

B. Discoid lupus erythematosus – Produces scarring plaques, not pedunculated lesions.
