D. Psoriasis – Presents with erythematous plaques and silvery scales, no button-hole sign.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 35-year-old farmer from Bihar presents with 2 annular plaques with central clearing, loss of sensation within the lesion, and thickening of the superficial radial nerve. His lepromin test is positive. Which classification best describes his disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tuberculoid — TT type

TT leprosy presents with 1-3 lesions, annular plaques with central clearing, well-defined margins, associated anaesthesia and anhidrosis, and positive lepromin test (reflecting strong CMI). A saucer right-way-up side profile is characteristic.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent tender violaceous nodules over the posterior aspect of both calves. Some lesions have ulcerated and healed with depressed scars. A Mantoux test is strongly positive. Skin biopsy reveals granulomatous inflammation involving the subcutaneous fat with inflammation of medium-sized blood vessels. Which of the following histopathological findings is most characteristic of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lobular panniculitis with vasculitis

The patient has Erythema induratum of Bazin, a tuberculid caused by a hypersensitivity reaction to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens.

Histopathology

• ✔ Lobular panniculitis
• ✔ Granulomatous inflammation
• ✔ Vasculitis involving medium-sized vessels
• ✔ Fat necrosis may be present

Clinical features

• Tender nodules on the posterior calves
• Recurrent episodes
• Ulceration
• Healing with scars
• Associated with tuberculosis

Why the other options are incorrect?

A. Septal panniculitis without vasculitis ❌

• Characteristic of erythema nodosum.

C. Dermatitis with neutrophilic abscess ❌

• Seen in neutrophilic dermatoses such as Sweet syndrome.

D. Subepidermal blister with IgG deposition ❌

• Seen in bullous pemphigoid.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man with HIV presents with thick hyperkeratotic crusted plaques over the trunk and extremities. Surprisingly, itching is minimal. Skin scrapings reveal innumerable mites. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is most accurate?
options: Face is typically spared because of increased sebaceous activity
The condition usually contains only 10–12 mites per patient
It is the most severe form of scabies associated with immunosuppression
Permethrin alone is sufficient treatment in all cases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is the most severe form of scabies associated with immunosuppression

The patient has Norwegian/crusted scabies:

• Immunosuppressed host (HIV)
• Hyperkeratotic crusted lesions
• Minimal pruritus despite extensive disease
• Millions of mites present

Key facts:

• Most severe variant of scabies
• Seen in HIV, lepromatous leprosy, Down syndrome, neurologic disorders
• Highly contagious

Treatment:

• Combination therapy:

• Oral ivermectin
• Permethrin 5%
• Keratolytics (e.g., salicylic acid)

Why others are wrong?

• A. Face is typically spared because of increased sebaceous activity: Face sparing is typical of adult classical scabies, not crusted scabies
• B. The condition usually contains only 10–12 mites per patient: Classical scabies has \~10–12 mites; crusted scabies has millions
• D. Permethrin alone is sufficient treatment in all cases: Permethrin alone is usually inadequate in severe crusted scabies

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with porcelain-white papules and plaques over the vulva with a cellophane paper-like texture and atrophic changes. If untreated, which serious complication must be discussed during counselling?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Squamous cell carcinoma

Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory mucocutaneous disorder. The key long-term complication is development of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) from chronic inflammation, scarring, and atrophy — making it premalignant and requiring surveillance and topical corticosteroid treatment.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 43-year-old man comes to the clinic for evaluation of a healed forehead laceration. On examination, the scar is pink, firm, and mildly raised, without surrounding erythema or edema; it does not extend beyond the initial wound borders. The patient is reassured that the scar should flatten over the following months. The process by which this occurs relies mostly on enhanced cellular production of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Metalloproteinases

This patient has a hypertrophic scar—pink, firm, mildly raised, and confined to the original wound borders. Over months, hypertrophic scars flatten and soften due to remodeling of extracellular matrix, primarily through increased activity of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). MMPs degrade excess type III collagen deposited during early wound healing and help reorganize collagen fibers, leading to scar regression and flattening.

Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Plasminogen activator – Involved in fibrinolysis, not collagen remodeling.

C. Reactive oxygen species – Promote tissue injury and inflammation, not scar resolution.

D. TNF-α – Pro-inflammatory cytokine; excess would worsen fibrosis rather than remodel it.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 44-year-old woman has urticarial wheals persisting for 9 weeks with no identifiable trigger. She is already on maximum-dose second-generation antihistamines. What is the next appropriate treatment escalation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Omalizumab

For chronic spontaneous urticaria (>6 weeks, no trigger) unresponsive to 2nd generation antihistamines: step 2 escalation is Omalizumab (anti-IgE monoclonal antibody). Cyclosporine (calcineurin inhibitor) is the step 3 option.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old dermatologist develops an indurated, verrucous, hyperkeratotic plaque on his right hand dorsum after performing autopsies for 10 years. What is the mechanism of this cutaneous TB variant?
options: Haematogenous spread from primary pulmonary TB
Exogenous reinfection in a previously sensitised individual
Direct inoculation in immunologically naive individuals
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Exogenous reinfection in a previously sensitised individual

Tuberculosis verrucosa cutis (anatomist's wart/warty TB) occurs from exogenous reinfection with M. tuberculosis in previously sensitised individuals with moderate-high immunity — hence common in those occupationally exposed to infected tissue.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 52-year-old renal transplant recipient on long-term immunosuppressive therapy presents with a slowly enlarging yellowish-red plaque in the perianal region. Biopsy shows sheets of large foamy macrophages containing concentrically layered basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions with a targetoid appearance. Culture grows Escherichia coli. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?
options: The hallmark inclusion bodies are formed due to defective neutrophil oxidative burst activity
The condition most commonly occurs in immunocompetent individuals after fungal infection
The lesion represents a reactive vasculitis caused by immune complex deposition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Histology characteristically shows Michaelis–Gutmann bodies

This patient has cutaneous malakoplakia.

High-yield facts:

• Seen in immunocompromised patients

• HIV
• renal transplant
• malignancy
• immunosuppressive therapy

• Due to acquired bactericidal defect of macrophages
• Common organisms:

• E. coli (most common)
• Klebsiella
• Proteus

• Common site: perianal region
• Histology:

• Sheets of macrophages = Von Hansemann cells
• Intracytoplasmic concentric basophilic inclusions = Michaelis–Gutmann bodies (hallmark)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child develops fever and malaise for 2 days followed by an intensely pruritic rash. Examination reveals lesions in various stages of evolution including papules, vesicles, pustules, and crusts predominantly over the trunk. Which of the following statements regarding this illness is true?
options: Child is infectious only after appearance of rash until crusting occurs
The most common complication is bronchopneumonia
Secondary bacterial infection is commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes
Only intravenous therapy should be used
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Secondary bacterial infection is commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes

Diagnosis = Varicella (Chickenpox)

| Feature | Varicella

| ------- | ---------

| Rash | Pleomorphic vesicles

| Distribution | Centripetal

| Classic description | Dew drops on rose petals

| Infectivity | 24–48 hr before rash → crusting

| MC complication | Secondary bacterial infection

| Organisms | S. aureus, S. pyogenes

| Treatment | Oral/IV acyclovir within 24–48 hr

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with recurrent blisters on areas of minor trauma since infancy. The blisters heal with atrophic scarring and milia formation. Examination reveals nail dystrophy and mucosal involvement. Immunofluorescence mapping shows the level of cleavage at the sublamina densa of the basement membrane zone. Which protein defect explains this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Collagen VII

This child has dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB). Key clues are blistering since infancy after minor trauma, healing with atrophic scarring and milia, nail dystrophy, mucosal involvement, and cleavage below the basement membrane (sublamina densa) on immunofluorescence mapping. DEB is caused by defects in collagen VII, which forms anchoring fibrils that attach the basement membrane to the underlying dermis. Loss of these fibrils leads to deep blistering and scarring.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Collagen IV – Component of the basement membrane, not anchoring fibrils.

C. Laminin-332 – Defective in junctional epidermolysis bullosa (cleavage within lamina lucida).

D. Keratin 14 – Defect causes epidermolysis bullosa simplex (intraepidermal, no scarring).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of a painful rash on his right flank. Two years ago, he underwent cadaveric renal transplantation. Current medications include tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Examination shows an erythematous rash with grouped vesicles in a band-like distribution over the patient's right flank. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sensory neuropathy

This patient has herpes zoster (shingles), indicated by a painful, unilateral, dermatomal vesicular rash. His immunosuppressed state (renal transplant on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, prednisone) increases the risk of complications. The most common and greatest risk complication of herpes zoster—especially in older or immunocompromised patients—is postherpetic neuralgia, a form of chronic sensory neuropathy due to VZV- induced nerve damage. It presents as persistent burning or stabbing pain in the affected dermatome after rash resolution.

Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Ascending paralysis – Suggestive of Guillain–Barré syndrome, more often linked to Campylobacter or CMV.

C. Urinary retention – Occurs with sacral (S2–S4) zoster, not flank involvement.

D. Loss of vision – Seen in herpes zoster ophthalmicus (V1), not thoracic dermatomes.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 64-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to worsening left lower extremity pain, swelling, and redness over the past 3 days. The patient has had no trauma but reports feeling feverish. Medical history is significant for hypertension and obesity. Physical examination shows diffuse erythema extending up to the left midcalf with indistinct border. There is increased warmth, tenderness, and edema of the left leg. No areas of fluctuation or purulent exudate are present, but the interdigital skin of the feet is macerated and fissured. Laboratory testing shows neutrophilic leukocytosis, and Doppler ultrasonography is negative for deep venous thrombosis. Infection with which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for this patient's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Beta-hemolytic streptococci

This patient has acute cellulitis, suggested by diffuse erythema with indistinct borders, warmth, tenderness, edema, fever, and neutrophilic leukocytosis. The presence of macerated, fissured interdigital skin indicates tinea pedis, a common portal of entry for bacteria. Beta-hemolytic streptococci (especially Streptococcus pyogenes) are the most common cause of nonpurulent cellulitis, as they spread rapidly through dermis and subcutaneous tissue via lymphatics, producing ill-defined margins.

Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Candida albicans – Causes intertrigo or mucocutaneous candidiasis, not acute cellulitis.

C. Clostridium perfringens – Causes gas gangrene with severe pain, crepitus, and tissue necrosis after trauma.

D. Mycobacterium marinum – Causes chronic nodular skin lesions after aquatic exposure, not acute spreading erythema.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 68-year-old man on chemotherapy develops burning pain over the right side of chest, followed after 2 days by vesicles on an erythematous base. Which of the following findings would favor primary varicella rather than herpes zoster?
options: Lesions confined to one thoracic dermatome
Grouped vesicles preceded by localized neuralgic pain
Pleomorphic rash with lesions in different stages of evolution
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pleomorphic rash with lesions in different stages of evolution

| Feature | Varicella | Herpes zoster

| ------- | --------- | -------------

| Infection type | Primary VZV infection | Reactivation of VZV

| Distribution | Centripetal, starts on trunk | Unilateral dermatomal

| Lesions | Pleomorphic rash | Grouped vesicles

| Pain | Mild prodrome/fever | Pre-eruptive burning/shooting pain

| Complication | Infective till all lesions crust | Post-herpetic neuralgia

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 7-year-old girl has a congenital, stable, solitary hypopigmented patch on her left cheek that does not cross the midline. Wood's lamp shows off-white accentuation. Which best describes the underlying pathology?
options: Absent melanocytes due to autoimmune destruction
Neural crest migration defect causing absent melanocytes
Functional defect in melanocytes with defective melanosome transfer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Functional defect in melanocytes with defective melanosome transfer

Nevus depigmentosus results from a functional defect in melanocytes — melanosomes are produced but their transfer to keratinocytes is defective. Melanocytes are present in normal numbers but dysfunctional.

Histology

• Normal or slightly reduced melanocyte count.
• Reduced melanin within keratinocytes.
• Defective melanosome formation/transfer.

Key Features

• Present at birth or appears in early childhood.
• Stable in size relative to body growth.
• Non-progressive.
• Irregular hypopigmented patch with serrated borders.
• Does not show complete depigmentation as seen in vitiligo.

Differentiation from Vitiligo

| Feature | Nevus Depigmentosus | Vitiligo

| ------- | ------------------- | --------

| Onset | Congenital/early childhood | Acquired

| Progression | Stable | Progressive

| Melanocyte number | Normal | Reduced/absent

| Defect | Melanosome transfer/function | Autoimmune melanocyte destruction

| Color | Hypopigmented | Depigmented (chalk white)

| Wood's lamp | Off-white accentuation | Bright chalky-white fluorescence

Exam Pearl:

• Nevus depigmentosus = Normal melanocyte number + defective melanosome transfer.
• Vitiligo = Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes leading to absence/reduction of melanocytes.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with tense bullae on an erythematous base over flexural areas. Nikolsky sign is negative. Tzanck smear shows eosinophils. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. Which current medication is a recognised trigger?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pembrolizumab — immune checkpoint inhibitor

Bullous pemphigoid can be triggered by gliptins and immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g. pembrolizumab). Tense sub-epidermal bullae, flexural distribution, eosinophil-rich Tzanck smear, and linear DIF are all characteristic.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 72-year-old man on bortezomib for multiple myeloma develops painful grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. VZV reactivation

Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor used in multiple myeloma. It can reactivate VZV by interfering with proteasomal degradation pathways involved in antiviral immunity, leading to herpes zoster.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 78-year-old woman presents with persistent dryness and itching on her chin for the past few weeks. Examination shows erythematous exfoliated patches. Which of the following structures is primarily responsible for lipid secretion and maintaining skin barrier function?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lamellar granules

Lamellar granules (Odland bodies): found in keratinocytes of stratum granulosum.

• Function: Secrete lipids ( cholesterol, free fatty acids) into the stratum corneum. ---> forming epidermal permeability barrier.
• This lipid layer prevents transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and keeps the skin hydrated--> normal barrier function.

The question describesdryness and exfoliation, which indicatesbarrier dysfunction.

B. Birbeck granules

• Function: processing of antigen and immune response.--> No role skin barrier formation.

C. Keratohyalin granules

• Function is keratin aggregation, not lipid secretion.

D. Eleidin granules

• Found in stratum lucidum (mainly in thick skin like palms and soles).
• Helps in keratinization of epidermal cells. --> no role in lipid secretion/ skin barrier formation.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 79-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to bleeding from an ulcerative lesion on her right nipple that she first noticed several months ago. The lesion is itchy and is slowly increasing in size. Examination shows a crusty, thickened, erythematous, and ulcerated nodule with evidence of hyperpigmentation. Changes extend to the surrounding areola. Excisional biopsy reveals relatively well-circumscribed aggregates of large, polygonal, pleomorphic cells with abundant mitotic activity and surrounding necrosis. S-100 and HMB-45 stains are diffusely positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Melanoma

This elderly woman has a slowly enlarging, ulcerated, bleeding, hyperpigmented lesion of the nipple–areolar complex. Histology shows large pleomorphic polygonal cells with high mitotic activity and necrosis, and immunohistochemistry is strongly positive for S-100 and HMB-45, which are classic markers of melanocytic tumors. These findings are diagnostic of melanoma, which can rarely involve the nipple and may clinically mimic Paget disease.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Basal cell carcinoma – Shows basaloid cells with peripheral palisading; HMB-45 negative.

C. Paget disease of the breast – Involves malignant glandular cells (Paget cells) within epidermis; CK7 positive, not melanocytic markers.

D. Seborrheic keratosis – Benign “stuck-on” lesion; no ulceration, necrosis, or melanocytic markers.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy is brought with multiple pruritic brownish macules and papules over the trunk and proximal limbs for 2 years. On rubbing one of the lesions with a blunt instrument, the lesion becomes erythematous and develops a surrounding urticarial wheal within minutes. Skin biopsy stained with toluidine blue demonstrates metachromatic granules within dermal cells. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is most accurate?
options: The wheal formation occurs due to IgE-mediated degranulation of Langerhans cells causing leukotriene release
The positive sign elicited on rubbing is a form of dermographism seen over normal uninvolved skin
Histamine-mediated mast cell degranulation following mechanical stimulation produces the characteristic Darier sign
The disease is characterized by defective melanocyte transfer leading to post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Histamine-mediated mast cell degranulation following mechanical stimulation produces the characteristic Darier sign

This child has cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa):

• Multiple hyperpigmented lesions
• Positive Darier sign
• Toluidine blue stain showing metachromatic granules
• Mast cell proliferation in skin

Pathophysiology:

• Scratching/rubbing → mast cell degranulation → histamine release → erythema + urticarial wheal

Other options:

• A. The wheal formation occurs due to IgE-mediated degranulation of Langerhans cells causing leukotriene release → Mast cells, not Langerhans cells, are involved
• B. The positive sign elicited on rubbing is a form of dermographism seen over normal uninvolved skin → Dermographism occurs on normal skin; Darier sign is elicited on lesional skin
• D. The disease is characterized by defective melanocyte transfer leading to post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation → Hyperpigmentation is secondary to mast cell proliferation, not melanocyte transfer defect

High-yield pearl:

• Darier sign = whealing of lesional skin after rubbing
• Dermographism = wheal formation on normal skin after stroking

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A child presents with generalized hypopigmentation involving skin, hair, and eyes along with recurrent infections. Peripheral smear shows neutrophils with giant granules. Choose the correct statement regarding the underlying disorder:
options: The primary enzymatic defect in albinism is deficiency of tyrosine hydroxylase.
Chediak–Higashi syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with TYR gene mutation.
Oculocutaneous albinism involves eyes, skin, and hair and may be associated with LYST gene mutation in Chediak–Higashi syndrome.
Ocular albinism characteristically presents with giant granules in eosinophils due to actin gene mutation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oculocutaneous albinism involves eyes, skin, and hair and may be associated with LYST gene mutation in Chediak–Higashi syndrome.

| Feature | Fact

| ------- | ----

| Defect in albinism | Tyrosinase deficiency

| Types | Ocular and oculocutaneous

| Oculocutaneous albinism | Involves eyes + skin + hair

| Associated syndrome | Chediak–Higashi syndrome

| Inheritance | Autosomal recessive

| Gene mutation | LYST gene

| Additional features | Recurrent infections + neutrophils with giant granules

• A. The primary enzymatic defect in albinism is deficiency of tyrosine hydroxylase: Defect is in tyrosinase, not tyrosine hydroxylase.
• B. Chediak–Higashi syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with TYR gene mutation: Chediak–Higashi syndrome is autosomal recessive, not dominant.
• D. Ocular albinism characteristically presents with giant granules in eosinophils due to actin gene mutation: Giant granules are seen in neutrophils, and the mutation is in LYST gene, not actin gene.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A clinician is attempting to match the dermatologic condition in Column A with its most characteristic associated feature in Column B. Column A 1. Erythema nodosum 2. Acanthosis nigricans 3. Granuloma annulare 4. Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum 5. Pretibial myxedema Column B a. Waxy yellow atrophic plaques with telangiectasia over shin b. Velvety hyperpigmented plaques over neck folds associated with obesity c. Diffuse non-pitting edema over anterior leg associated with Graves disease d. Septal panniculitis with tender nodules over anterior shin e. Annular arrangement of papules associated with collagen degeneration Which of the following is the correct match?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1-d, 2-b, 3-e, 4-a, 5-c

• Erythema nodosum → septal panniculitis with tender shin nodules
• Acanthosis nigricans → velvety hyperpigmented plaques in flexures/neck, commonly obesity-associated
• Granuloma annulare → annular papules with collagen degeneration
• Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum → waxy yellow atrophic plaques with telangiectasia over shin
• Pretibial myxedema → non-pitting edema over anterior legs in Graves disease

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A construction worker develops vesicular eczema on his hands and forearms with dissemination beyond the contact site. Which mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type IV cell-mediated (delayed) hypersensitivity

Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV (cell-mediated, delayed) hypersensitivity reaction. Cement sensitisation via potassium dichromate is the classic occupational example. Patch test is read at 48-96 hours.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A dermatologist adds a biologic agent targeting the IL-17A pathway for a patient with severe plaque psoriasis. Which agent is correctly matched to this mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Secukinumab

Secukinumab and ixekizumab target IL-17A. Ustekinumab targets IL-12/23; guselkumab targets IL-23; adalimumab, etanercept, and infliximab are anti-TNF-alpha agents.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A dermatologist presses a glass slide over a red skin lesion on a patient's forearm. The redness disappears completely under pressure. This finding is most consistent with which pathological process?
options: Extravasation of red blood cells into dermis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vasodilation with intact vessel walls

Blanching on diascopy indicates erythema caused by vasodilation with intact vessel walls — blood can be pushed away by pressure. Non-blanching (purpura) implies RBC extravasation into the dermis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A dermatologist suspects leprosy and plans a nerve biopsy for a patient with pure neuritic type disease. Which nerve is preferred for unilateral (U/L) disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Radial cutaneous nerve

In pure neuritic leprosy, nerve biopsy is the IOC. The radial cutaneous nerve is preferred for unilateral disease, while the sural nerve is preferred for bilateral (L/L) disease.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient from Bihar presents with multiple hypopigmented macules over the trunk and infiltrated nodules over the face 2 years after treatment for prolonged febrile illness. Giemsa stain from skin lesions shows Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies. Which of the following findings is least likely to be associated with post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL)?
options: Symmetrical peripheral nerve thickening with sensory loss
Demonstration of amastigote forms on Giemsa stain
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Symmetrical peripheral nerve thickening with sensory loss

PKDL is a cutaneous sequela of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) and commonly occurs in endemic areas like Bihar.

Typical features include:

• History of prolonged fever/kala-azar
• Hypopigmented macules over trunk
• Infiltrated facial nodules
• Demonstration of LD bodies (amastigotes) on Giemsa stain

The major differential is lepromatous leprosy, which characteristically shows:

• Symmetrical peripheral nerve thickening
• Sensory impairment
• Positive slit-skin smear for M. leprae

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient shows brown-black pigmentation of nail with extension onto surrounding skin (Hutchinson sign). This indicates:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Subungual melanoma

(Hutchinson sign = periungual spread = melanoma until proven otherwise)

Hutchinson sign is the pigmentation of the proximal or lateral nail fold extending from the nail plate, seen in subungual melanoma. It indicates malignant melanocytic proliferation under the nail. This is a red flag for melanoma and requires prompt biopsy and excision, as early diagnosis is critical for prognosis.

Why the other options are incorrect:

• A. Benign nail nevus: Usually confined to the nail plate; does not involve the surrounding skin.
• B. Superficial spreading melanoma: Typically affects cutaneous surfaces, not subungual areas.
• D. Bowen disease: Squamous cell carcinoma in situ; rarely pigmented, not associated with Hutchinson sign.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient with Hansen disease presents with 10–30 polymorphic lesions showing a geographic map-like appearance. Examination reveals an inner punched-out margin (“Swiss cheese” appearance) with a sloping outer margin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mid-borderline (BB) leprosy

High-yield clues pointing to BB leprosy:

• Most unstable form
• Features of both TT and LL
• Geographic map-like lesions
• Swiss cheese appearance = inner punched-out margin
• Inverted saucer outer sloping margin
• 10–30 polymorphic lesions

Important differentiators

| Type | High-yield clue

| ---- | ---------------

| TT | “Saucer right way up”

| BT | Satellite lesions

| BB | Swiss cheese + geographic lesions

| BL | Almost symmetrical lesions + inverted saucer

| LL | Leonine facies, glove & stocking neuropathy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A previously healthy 3-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of fever, irritability, and rash for 3 days. The rash started around the mouth before spreading to the trunk and extremities. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). Examination shows a diffuse erythematous rash with flaccid bullae on the neck, flexural creases, and buttocks. Gentle pressure across the trunk with a gloved finger creates a blister. Oropharyngeal examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of these skin findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Toxin-induced cleavage of desmoglein-1

This infant has staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS), suggested by fever, irritability, diffuse erythema, flaccid bullae, and a positive Nikolsky sign, with no mucosal involvement. SSSS is caused by exfoliative toxins (ETA, ETB) from Staphylococcus aureus that cleave desmoglein-1, a desmosomal protein in the superficial epidermis (stratum granulosum). Loss of cell adhesion leads to superficial blistering and skin desquamation.

Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Bacterial production of erythrogenic toxin – Causes scarlet fever (sandpaper rash), not bullae or Nikolsky positivity.

C. Bacterial invasion of the epidermis – Seen in bullous impetigo; lesions are localized and contain bacteria.

D.Autoantibody deposition in stratum spinosum – Describes pemphigus vulgaris (anti-desmoglein-3) with mucosal involvement.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: All are caused by staphylococcal infection except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erysipelas

Staphylococcus aureus commonly causes pyogenic skin infections due to its toxin production and invasive properties. Conditions caused by Staphylococcus aureus:

• Impetigo contagiosa: Superficial skin infection producing honey-colored crusts (may also be caused by Streptococcus pyogenes).
• Ritter syndrome (Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome): Caused by exfoliative toxins of S. aureus.
• Ecthyma: A deeper ulcerative form of impetigo that may involve Staphylococcus or Streptococcus.

Exception:

• Erysipelas is classically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus), not Staphylococcus.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: All are correct regarding miliaria crystallina, except:
options: Obstruction occurs at the level of stratum corneum
Presents as superficial clear vesicles without inflammation
Obstruction occurs at the level of stratum spinosum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Obstruction occurs at the level of stratum spinosum

Miliaria crystallina is a superficial sweat gland obstruction disorder, often seen in hot, humid climates.

Miliaria types are classified by the depth of sweat duct obstruction:

• Crystallina → stratum corneum
• Rubra → stratum spinosum (pruritic, erythematous)
• Profunda → dermal-epidermal junction

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: All are true regarding Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction, except:
options: Occurs within 24 hours of penicillin therapy in syphilis
Due to lipoprotein release causing cytokine storm
Corticosteroids are indicated in pregnant women and neurosyphilis
It is a contraindication to penicillin therapy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is a contraindication to penicillin therapy

The Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (JHR) is an acute, transient reaction that occurs after antibiotic treatment of spirochetal infections, most commonly syphilis. Key points:

• Timing: Usually occurs within 24 hours of initiating therapy (A).
• Pathophysiology: Release of treponemal lipoproteins triggers a cytokine-mediated inflammatory response (B).
• Management: Supportive care is usually sufficient; corticosteroids may be used in pregnant women to reduce fetal risk and in severe cases like neurosyphilis (C).
• Penicillin is not contraindicated; in fact, it remains the drug of choice, despite the possibility of JHR (D is false).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: All are true regarding lupus vulgaris, except:
options: It is a form of cutaneous tuberculosis seen in previously sensitized individuals
Originates from an underlying focus of tuberculosis
Most common site in India is the buttock and trunk
Shows large numbers of acid-fast bacilli on biopsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Shows large numbers of acid-fast bacilli on biopsy

Lupus vulgaris is a chronic, progressive form of cutaneous tuberculosis that occurs in previously sensitized individuals.

Key points:

• A. It is a form of cutaneous tuberculosis seen in previously sensitized individuals. True – Occurs in previously sensitized individuals (type IV hypersensitivity).
• B. Originates from an underlying focus of tuberculosis. True – Often from contiguous focus of TB (bone, lymph nodes, lungs) or hematogenous spread.
• C. Most common site in India is the buttock and trunk. True – In India, common sites are buttock/trunk.
• Western/European countries: Lesions are usually solitary and more than 90% involve the head and neck.
• D. Shows large numbers of acid-fast bacilli on biopsy. False – Lupus vulgaris is paucibacillary, meaning few or no acid-fast bacilli are seen on biopsy.

Why the other options are correct:

• The disease is slow-growing, chronic, and shows granulomatous inflammation, but AFB are rarely demonstrable.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: All of the following are features of the secondary stage of lymphogranuloma venereum except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Esthiomene of vulva

Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3. The disease progresses through three stages:

1. Primary stage

• Small painless genital papule or ulcer
• Often transient and may go unnoticed

2. Secondary stage (inguinal stage)

Characterized by lymphatic spread and lymphadenitis, with features such as:

• Painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes)
• Groove sign – depression between inflamed inguinal and femoral lymph nodes
• Pelvic or intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy
• Fever and systemic symptoms

3. Tertiary stage (late stage)

• Chronic lymphatic obstruction
• Esthiomene of vulva (elephantiasis-like swelling of genitalia)
• Genital strictures and fibrosis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: All of the following can cause lesions on the glans penis, expect:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chlamydia

Genital ulcers/lesions on the glans penis are classically caused by specific sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and identifying the etiology is key for diagnosis and management.

Causes of lesions on glans penis:

• Haemophilus ducreyi → Causes chancroid: painful, soft ulcers with ragged edges
• Corynebacterium granulomatis → Causes donovanosis: painless, beefy red ulcers that bleed easily
• Herpes simplex virus → Causes multiple painful vesicles/ulcers

Exception:

• Chlamydia trachomatis

• Typically causes:

• Urethritis
• Cervicitis
• Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) → small transient lesion (often unnoticed) + lymphadenopathy

• Does NOT typically cause prominent ulcers on the glans penis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: All of the following conditions may present as a collodion baby, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ichthyosis vulgaris

The collodion baby phenotype is a presentation, not a diagnosis. It may evolve into:

•

Lamellar ichthyosis

•

Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma

•

Self-healing collodion baby (rare)

But Ichthyosis vulgaris does NOT present as a collodion baby.

Instead, it presents later in infancy or childhood with fine white scales on extensor surfaces

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: All of the following drugs are associated with lichenoid drug eruption except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Isotretinoin

Causes of lichenoid drug eruption

| Drug class | Example

| ---------- | -------

| Anti-hypertensives | ACE inhibitors, β-blockers, α-methyldopa

| Anti-arrhythmics | Quinidine

| Diuretics | Thiazides

| Anti-malarials | Chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine

| Metals | Gold salts

Important trigger associations:

• Dental amalgam (mercury)
• Hepatitis C virus (HCV)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: An 11-month-old child is evaluated for chronic diarrhea, abdominal distension, irritability, poor weight gain, and pallor. Symptoms started 3 months after complementary feeding was introduced. Screening shows: • Total IgA: Normal • Anti-tTG antibody strongly positive Further testing reveals anti-tTG levels more than 10 times the upper limit of normal. What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Duodenal biopsy looking for villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia
Contrast enema to exclude Hirschsprung disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endomysial antibody (EMA) assay

The child has classic celiac disease:

Diagnostic algorithm:

1. Total IgA + anti-tTG screening
2. If anti-tTG >10× normal →
3. EMA positive

• Diagnosis confirmed

If anti-tTG is positive but <10× normal, then:

• EGD with duodenal biopsy is required
• Findings: villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Arrange the following corticosteroids in the order of increasing t1/2 (low to high). 1. Dexamethasone 2. Hydrocortisone 3. Betamethasone 4. Prednisolone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 4, 1, 3

Corticosteroids are classified by biologic half-life (t½) into short-, intermediate-, and long- acting agents.

• Hydrocortisone is short-acting with the lowest t½.
• Prednisolone is intermediate-acting.
• Dexamethasone and betamethasone are long-acting, with betamethasone having a slightly longer t½ than dexamethasone.

Therefore, the order of increasing half-life (low → high) is: Hydrocortisone → Prednisolone → Dexamethasone → Betamethasone

| Drug | Potency | Half-life | Uses

| ---- | ------- | --------- | ----

| Hydrocortisone (similar to cortisol) | GC ×1 MC ×1 | 8–12 hours | DOC for replacement:

• Addison’s disease
• Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)

| Prednisone / Prednisolone | GC ×4 MC ×0.8 | 12–36 hours | ↓ Inflammation ↓ Immunity

| Methylprednisolone | GC ×5 MC ×0.8 | 12–36 hours | ↓ Inflammation ↓ Immunity

| Triamcinolone | GC ×5 MC = 0 | 12–36 hours | ↓ Inflammation ↓ Immunity

| Dexamethasone / Betamethasone | GC ×30 MC = 0 | 36–72 hours

• Surfactant maturation
• CAH in pregnancy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Choose the correct statement regarding psoriasis:
options: Munro microabscesses represent neutrophilic collections within the stratum spinosum.
Spongiform pustules of Kogoj are collections of eosinophils in the stratum corneum.
Systemic steroids are routinely indicated in pustular psoriasis except during pregnancy
Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative arthritis commonly involving the DIP joints.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative arthritis commonly involving the DIP joints.

Histopathology of psoriasis

| Finding | Description

| ------- | -----------

| Munro microabscess | Neutrophils in stratum corneum

| Spongiform pustule of Kogoj | Neutrophilic collection in stratum spinosum

| Parakeratosis | Retained nuclei in stratum corneum

| Acanthosis | Epidermal hyperplasia

| Dilated dermal papillary vessels | Responsible for Auspitz sign

Psoriatic arthritis

• Seronegative arthritis (RF negative)
• Classical joint: DIP joint
• Enthesitis positive

Treatment pearls

• Systemic steroids are generally contraindicated in psoriasis
• Exception: Pustular psoriasis of pregnancy
• PUVA adverse effects:

• Photoaging
• Lentigines
• Cataract
• SCC/BCC risk

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Choose the correct statement:
options: Mee’s lines are paired transverse white bands associated with hypoalbuminemia.
Lindsay’s nails show proximal 50% white discoloration and are associated with growth arrest.
Terry’s nails show proximal 90% white nail with distal brown band and are associated with chronic liver disease.
Muehrcke’s bands are associated with chronic arsenic poisoning.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Terry’s nails show proximal 90% white nail with distal brown band and are associated with chronic liver disease.

| Nail finding | Characteristic feature | Association

| ------------ | ---------------------- | -----------

| Mee’s lines | Transverse white bands | Chronic arsenic poisoning

| Muehrcke’s bands | Transverse paired white bands | Hypoalbuminemia

| Lindsay’s nails | Proximal 50% white + distal 50% brown | Chronic renal failure

| Terry’s nails | Proximal 90% white + distal 10% brown | Chronic liver disease

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Crisaborole is a topical agent used for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis. It acts by inhibiting which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phosphodiesterase-4

Crisaborole is a topical phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) inhibitor used for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis. By inhibiting PDE-4, it increases intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels, which reduces the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-2, IL-12), thereby decreasing inflammation and pruritus in eczematous skin.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Espundia refers to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis

Espundia is the term used for mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, classically caused by Leishmania braziliensis in the New World. It typically begins as a cutaneous lesion and later spreads to involve the mucous membranes of the nose, mouth, and pharynx, leading to destructive ulceration and tissue loss.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Cutaneous leishmaniasis – Causes localized skin ulcers (e.g., oriental sore), not Espundia.

B. Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) – Occurs after visceral leishmaniasis; presents with hypopigmented macules/nodules.

D. Visceral leishmaniasis – Kala-azar with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the correct kit for the clinical presentations: 1. Painful ulcers upon palpation, with suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy on the right side 2. Vaginal discharge in a CSW with cervical erosions 3. Painful, swollen, and tender inguinal lymph node in a truck driver 4. Painless ulcer in the genital area with non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy in CSW; past h/o treatment of a similar lesion resulted in fever, malaise, tachycardia and vomiting
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1-White, 2-Grey, 3-Black, 4-White

1. Painful genital ulcers with suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy → suggests chancroid → treated with Kit White.
2. Vaginal discharge in a CSW with cervical erosions → indicates cervicitis (GC + Chlamydia) → managed with Kit Grey
3. Painful, swollen, tender inguinal lymph node (bubo) in a truck driver → typical of LGV → treated with Kit Black.
4. Painless genital ulcer with non-tender lymphadenopathy and Jarisch– Herxheimer reaction history → classic primary syphilis → treated with Kit White (Not suggestive of allergy or a CI for future penicillin use)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: In a leprosy patient’s smear showing 1–10 Bacilli per field, the bacteriological index is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3+

In leprosy, the bacteriological index (BI) measures the density of Mycobacterium leprae in slit-skin smears on a logarithmic scale:

• 1+ → 1–10 bacilli per 100 fields
• 2+ → 1–10 bacilli per 10 fields
• 3+ → 1–10 bacilli per field (Correct)
• 4+ → 10–100 bacilli per field
• 5+ → 100–1000 bacilli per field
• 6+ → >1000 bacilli per field

So a smear showing 1–10 bacilli per field corresponds to BI = 3+.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Isotretinoin is associated with which of the following bone disorders?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH)

• Isotretinoin (a systemic retinoid, vitamin A derivative) used for severe acne is associated with skeletal adverse effects, especially with long-term or high-dose therapy.
• Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH):

• Characterized by calcification and ossification of ligaments and entheses, especially along the spine
• Leads to flowing anterior osteophytes and spinal stiffness
• Retinoids stimulate osteoblastic activity and new bone formation

Hence, isotretinoin → DISH-like changes

Why not other options:

B. Osteomalacia:

• Due to vitamin D deficiency
• Not linked to retinoids

C. Osteoporosis: Bone resorption disorder → not a typical isotretinoin effect

D. Osteogenesis Imperfecta:

• Genetic collagen disorder (Type I collagen defect)
• No association with isotretinoin

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Match the Following – Congenital Ichthyosis: Column A 1. Ichthyosis vulgaris 2. X-linked ichthyosis 3. Lamellar ichthyosis Column B a. Steroid sulfatase defect with brown-black scales and cryptorchidism b. Filaggrin defect with fine white scales c. Epidermal transglutaminase-1 defect with ectropion and plate-like adherent scales Which of the following is the correct match?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1–b, 2–a, 3–c

| Disorder | Defect / Inheritance | Key Clinical Features | Important Associations

| -------- | -------------------- | --------------------- | ----------------------

| Ichthyosis vulgaris | Filaggrin defect (AD) | Fine white scales | Commonest inherited ichthyosis

| X-linked ichthyosis | Steroid sulfatase deficiency (XLR) | Brown-black scales | Cryptorchidism, corneal opacities

| Lamellar ichthyosis | Epidermal transglutaminase-1 defect (AR) | Dark plate-like adherent scales | Collodion baby, ectropion, eclabium

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Partner treatment of STD is given to all while prescribing all of the following kits, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Red kit

Under NACO syndromic management guidelines, partner treatment is advised for almost all sexually transmitted infections to prevent reinfection—except when prescribing the Red kit.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Regarding diffuse pattern non-scarring alopecia, all of the following are true except:
options: Anagen effluvium commonly follows chemotherapy or radiotherapy
Telogen effluvium usually occurs after severe systemic stress
Telogen effluvium is due to disruption of mitotic activity of matrix cells
Anagen effluvium presents with abrupt diffuse hair loss
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Telogen effluvium is due to disruption of mitotic activity of matrix cells

• Anagen effluvium:

• Acute insult to hair matrix cells
• Seen after chemotherapy/radiotherapy
• Abrupt onset hair loss

• Telogen effluvium:

• Triggered by systemic stress/infection
• Causes premature transition of hair from anagen → telogen phase
• Typically occurs months after the stressor

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Regarding inflammatory tinea capitis, choose the correct statement:
options: Favus is commonly caused by T. mentagrophyte and shows coral red fluorescence on Wood’s lamp.
Kerion is caused by anthropophilic fungi and presents with non-inflammatory scaly alopecia without lymphadenopathy.
Favus presents with yellow cup-shaped crusts (scutula) and may show dull blue fluorescence on Wood’s lamp.
Kerion commonly presents in adults with fronto-temporal scarring alopecia and madarosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Favus presents with yellow cup-shaped crusts (scutula) and may show dull blue fluorescence on Wood’s lamp.

Favus

• Caused by T. schoenleinii
• Characterized by:

• Yellow cup-shaped crusts called scutula
• Scalp involvement
• Dull blue fluorescence on Wood’s lamp

Kerion

• Severe inflammatory tinea capitis caused by zoophilic fungi

• T. mentagrophyte
• T. verrucosum

• Features:

• Child with animal/pet exposure
• Boggy scalp swelling
• Easily pluckable hair
• Regional lymphadenopathy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: SAPHO syndrome includes all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seborrhea

SAPHO syndrome stands for Synovitis, Acne, Pustulosis, Hyperostosis, and Osteitis. It is a chronic inflammatory disorder involving skin and osteoarticular manifestations. The dermatologic features classically include severe acne (acne conglobata/fulminans) and palmoplantar pustulosis, while the skeletal features include hyperostosis and osteitis, especially of the anterior chest wall.

Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Acne – A core component of SAPHO.

C. Pustulosis – Palmoplantar pustulosis is characteristic.

D. Hyperostosis – One of the defining skeletal features.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the ratio of type-I to type-III collagen in adult human skin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 8:1

• More precise biochemical studies of adult human dermis place the ratio closer to 8:1 (Type I : Type III)
• In surgical texts (like Bailey and Love) they mention the ratio of Type I to Type III collagen is approximately 4:1 (but thats in context of wound healing)
• Some sources quote "80:20" which gets loosely interpreted as 4:1, but the actual molar/weight ratio of fibers in dermis is closer to 8:1
•

Collagen Ratio in Normal Adult Skin

| Source | Type I : Type III Ratio

| ------ | -----------------------

| Normal adult dermis | \~80–85% : 10–15% → approximately 8:1

| Fetal skin | Higher Type III proportion

| Early wound / granulation tissue | Type III increases temporarily

| Mature scar | Returns toward Type I dominance

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following are side effects of topical corticosteroids? 1. Hypertrichosis 2. Acneiform eruption 3. Atrophy 4. Bluish-grey skin discolouration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 3 only

Topical corticosteroids commonly cause local adverse effects due to their anti-mitotic and vasoconstrictive actions on the skin. Hypertrichosis occurs from stimulation of hair follicles, acneiform eruptions result from follicular occlusion and altered sebum dynamics, and skin atrophy develops due to inhibition of fibroblast activity and reduced collagen synthesis. These effects are more common with potent steroids, prolonged use, occlusion, and application on thin skin (face, groin).

• Bluish-grey skin discolouration – Seen with minocycline, amiodarone, silver (argyria), not topical steroids.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the histopathology of Erythema Induratum (Bazin)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lobular panniculitis with vasculitis

Erythema induratum of Bazin is considered a tuberculid, and it characteristically shows:

• Lobular panniculitis
• Granulomatous infiltrate
• Vasculitis of medium-sized vessels
• May ulcerate and heal with scars
• Usually on posterior legs (calves)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following correctly matches the hair cycle phase with its characteristic feature?
options: Catagen – Accounts for 80–90% of scalp follicles at any given time
Telogen – Active proliferation phase lasting several years
Anagen – Presence of angulated roots and longest growth period
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anagen – Presence of angulated roots and longest growth period

The hair cycle has three main phases:

1. Anagen (growth phase) – Longest phase, lasting 2–6 years on the scalp. Hair actively grows from the bulb; angulated roots are often seen in plucked anagen hairs.
2. Catagen (involution phase) – Short transitional phase (\~2–3 weeks), during which hair follicle regresses.
3. Telogen (resting phase) – Lasts \~3 months; hair is shed at the end of this phase.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is a poor prognostic factor for vitiligo?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mucosal involvement

In vitiligo, certain features are associated with a poorer prognosis (harder to treat, less likelihood of repigmentation):

• Mucosal involvement – Particularly lip, oral, or genital mucosa; these areas respond poorly to therapy.
• Bilateral, generalized, or acral/extremity involvement – Worse prognosis than localized lesions.
• Koebner phenomenon presence – Indicates active disease, often more refractory.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Unilateral, dermatomal macules – Typical of segmental vitiligo, usually stable and responds better.

B. Absence of Koebner phenomenon – Suggests less active disease → better prognosis.

D. Segmental pattern – Often localized and stable, with higher chance of repigmentation → favorable prognosis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of SAHA syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hyperostosis

SAHA syndrome is a constellation of cutaneous manifestations associated with hyperandrogenism.

SAHA stands for:

• S – Seborrhea
• A – Acne
• H – Hirsutism
• A – Androgenetic alopecia

In many dermatology texts, SAHA syndrome is extended to SAHA-AN syndrome, where AN = Acanthosis nigricans, reflecting the frequent coexistence of insulin resistance (especially in PCOS).

Why Option C is incorrect?

• Hyperostosis is not a feature of SAHA syndrome.

Hyperostosis refers to abnormal bone overgrowth and is seen in conditions such as:

• Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)
• Hypervitaminosis A
• Meningioma-associated hyperostosis
• SAPHO syndrome

It has no association with hyperandrogenic dermatoses.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of the triad of poikiloderma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lichenification

Poikiloderma is defined by a classic triad of skin atrophy, pigmentary changes (both hypo- and hyperpigmentation), and telangiectasia, giving the skin a mottled, thin, and fragile appearance. It is seen in conditions like dermatomyositis, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, chronic radiodermatitis, and genodermatoses.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a risk factor for developing a candidal infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypertension

Candidal infections occur when there is disruption of the normal host defense mechanisms or alteration of the local environment that favors Candida overgrowth. Important predisposing factors include pregnancy (high estrogen levels), oral contraceptive pills, obesity (warm, moist skin folds), diabetes mellitus, prolonged antibiotic use, corticosteroid therapy, immunosuppression (HIV), and occlusive clothing. Hypertension does not alter host immunity or local mucosal conditions and is not a recognized risk factor for candidiasis. Therefore, among the given options, hypertension is the least likely to predispose to Candida infection.

High-Yield Risk Factors for Candidiasis

• Pregnancy (↑ Estrogen)
• Oral contraceptive pills
• Obesity (intertriginous areas)
• Diabetes mellitus
• Broad-spectrum antibiotics
• Corticosteroids/immunosuppressants
• HIV/AIDS and other immunodeficiency states

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is not included in the Amsel criteria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vaginal pH <4.5

The Amsel criteria are used to diagnose bacterial vaginosis (BV). A diagnosis is made when ≥3 of the following 4 criteria are present:

1. Homogeneous, thin, white or gray vaginal discharge → C
2. Presence of clue cells on wet mount → D
3. Vaginal pH >4.5 → opposite of option A
4. Positive “whiff” test (fishy odor with addition of KOH) → B

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common cause of paraneoplastic pemphigus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

Paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP) is most commonly associated with non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, especially B-cell lymphomas. It is a severe autoimmune blistering disease caused by autoantibodies against desmogleins and plakin proteins, leading to painful mucosal erosions and polymorphic skin lesions. Among all associated malignancies, NHL is the most frequent, followed by CLL and Castleman disease.

Why others are less common:

A. Multiple myeloma – Rare association

C. Gastric adenocarcinoma – Solid tumors are uncommon causes

D. CLL – Important association, but less common than NHL

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is the vector of Chiclero ulcer (new world leishmaniasis)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lutzomyia

Chiclero ulcer is a form of New World cutaneous leishmaniasis, most commonly caused by Leishmania mexicana in Central America. The vector is the sandfly genus Lutzomyia, which transmits the parasite through its bite.

Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Reduviid – Triatomine bugs; vector for Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease).

B. Phlebotomus – Old World sandfly vector for Leishmania donovani and L. tropica.

C. Trombiculid – Chiggers; vectors for scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Consider the following regarding the human hair growth cycle: I. Anagen is a phase of active hair growth II. Telogen is a transitional phase III. Catagen is a resting phase Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I only

Human hair growth occurs in a cyclical pattern consisting of three main phases:

1. Anagen (Growth Phase)

• Phase of active hair growth
• Lasts 2–7 years on the scalp
• About 85–90% of scalp hairs are normally in this phase

2. Catagen (Transitional Phase)

• Short involution/regression phase
• Lasts about 2–3 weeks
• Hair follicle shrinks and detaches from the dermal papilla

3. Telogen (Resting Phase)

• Resting phase of the hair cycle
• Lasts about 2–3 months
• Followed by shedding of the hair (exogen phase)

Evaluation of Statements

• I. Anagen is a phase of active hair growth → Correct
• II. Telogen is a transitional phase → Incorrect (Telogen is the resting phase)
• III. Catagen is a resting phase → Incorrect (Catagen is the transitional/regression phase)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the cause(s) that result in non-scarring alopecia from the following options. 1. Alopecia areata 2. Telogen effluvium 3. Androgenic alopecia 4. Frontal fibrosing alopecia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, and 3

Non-scarring (non-cicatricial) alopecia is characterized by reversible hair loss with preservation of hair follicles, allowing potential regrowth.

Conditions causing non-scarring alopecia:

• Alopecia areata → autoimmune; patchy hair loss with exclamation mark hairs
• Telogen effluvium → diffuse shedding due to stress/illness; hair cycle shift
• Androgenetic alopecia → patterned hair loss due to androgen sensitivity

Scarring alopecia (contrast):

• Frontal fibrosing alopecia → permanent follicular destruction and fibrosis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of finasteride?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5-alpha reductase inhibition

Finasteride acts by inhibiting 5-α reductase (Type II), the enzyme that converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Since DHT is the principal androgen responsible for prostatic growth and hair follicle miniaturization, reducing DHT levels leads to shrinkage of the prostate and slows the progression of androgenetic alopecia.

Why not the other options?

• A. Adrenergic α₁A receptor antagonism: Mechanism of tamsulosin, alfuzosin, and silodosin, which relax smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck to improve urinary flow but do not reduce prostate size.
• C. Androgen receptor blockade: Mechanism of flutamide, bicalutamide, enzalutamide, and apalutamide, used primarily in prostate cancer.
• D. Phosphodiesterase inhibition: Mechanism of sildenafil and tadalafil; tadalafil is also approved for BPH by relaxing smooth muscle via increased cGMP.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs used as nail lacquer belongs to morpholines? (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amorolfine

Amorolfine is a morpholine antifungal commonly used as a topical nail lacquer for the treatment of onychomycosis (fungal nail infection). It acts by inhibiting fungal sterol synthesis through blockade of Δ14-reductase and Δ7–Δ8 isomerase, leading to disruption of the fungal cell membrane.

• Class: Morpholine antifungal
• Formulation: 5% nail lacquer
• Indication: Onychomycosis (especially distal and superficial infections)
• Application: Usually once or twice weekly
• Mechanism: Inhibits ergosterol synthesis at two different enzymatic steps

| Class | Drug Examples

| ----- | -------------

| Morpholines | Amorolfine

| Azoles | Oxiconazole, Tioconazole, Clotrimazole, Ketoconazole

| Hydroxypyridones | Ciclopirox olamine

| Allylamines | Terbinafine, Naftifine

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Oxiconazole → Imidazole antifungal
• Ciclopirox olamine → Hydroxypyridone antifungal
• Tioconazole → Imidazole antifungal

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is not considered a focal non-cicatricial cause of alopecia? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Discoid Lupus Erythematosus

Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) is a cicatricial (scarring) alopecia, making it the exception among the options listed. Chronic inflammation destroys hair follicles and replaces them with fibrous tissue, resulting in permanent hair loss.

In contrast, the following are causes of focal non-cicatricial alopecia, where hair follicles remain intact and regrowth is possible:

• Alopecia areata – autoimmune attack on hair follicles causing smooth, well-circumscribed patches of hair loss.
• Secondary syphilis – causes characteristic “moth-eaten” patchy alopecia.
• Black dot tinea capitis – fungal infection causing hair shaft breakage at the scalp surface, leaving black dots.

Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia = permanent follicular destruction

• DLE
• Lichen planopilaris
• Folliculitis decalvans

Non-scarring alopecia = follicles preserved

• Alopecia areata
• Tinea capitis
• Telogen effluvium
• Secondary syphilis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which one of the following is an example of non-scarring alopecia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Telogen effluvium

Non-scarring (non-cicatricial) alopecia is characterized by hair loss without permanent destruction of hair follicles, allowing the potential for complete hair regrowth once the underlying cause is corrected. Telogen effluvium is one of the most common causes and results from premature transition of hair follicles from the anagen (growth) phase to the telogen (resting) phase, leading to diffuse hair shedding.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Linear scleroderma: Causes scarring (cicatricial) alopecia due to fibrosis and permanent follicular destruction.
• B. Cutaneous metastases: Can infiltrate and destroy hair follicles, producing scarring alopecia.
• D. Sarcoidosis: Cutaneous sarcoidosis involving the scalp usually causes scarring alopecia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent painful nodules and foul-smelling discharge in the axilla. The lesions are located in areas rich in specialized sweat glands that become active after puberty and are associated with hair follicles. Which of the following sites predominantly contains these glands?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Axilla

Why this is classic for apocrine glands:

• Location: Axilla, areola, anogenital region
• Secretion: Viscous, protein-rich → odor after bacterial action
• Association: Open into hair follicles
• Activation: Puberty onward (androgen-dependent)
• Clinical correlate: Hidradenitis suppurativa (recurrent painful nodules, sinuses)

Option traps:

• A. Palms & soles → Eccrine only (thermoregulation)
• B. Forehead → Predominantly eccrine
• D. Scalp → Mainly sebaceous + eccrine, not apocrine-dominant

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man with a known case of chronic pancreatitis presents to the OPD with complaint of skin pigmentation over the abdomen. The patient gives a history of chronic use of a hot water bottle to relieve the abdominal discomfort. Which one of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Erythema ab igne

Erythema ab igne (“redness from fire”) is a localized skin condition caused by repeated or prolonged exposure to moderate heat (43–47°C) that is insufficient to cause burns. It classically presents as a reticulated (net-like), brownish hyperpigmented rash over the area of chronic heat exposure.

In patients with chronic pancreatitis, recurrent abdominal pain often leads to repeated use of hot water bottles or heating pads, making erythema ab igne a characteristic clinical finding.

Why not the other options?

• A. Erythema infectiosum: A viral exanthem caused by Parvovirus B19, characterized by a “slapped cheek” rash in children.
• B. Erythema marginatum: One of the major Jones criteria of acute rheumatic fever; presents as evanescent, serpiginous, non-pruritic annular lesions.
• C. Erythema nodosum: Painful, tender erythematous nodules over the anterior shins, associated with conditions such as tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and streptococcal infections.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The "Carpet Tack Sign" is observed in which of the following conditions? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE)

Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE) is a chronic cutaneous form of lupus characterized by well-defined erythematous plaques with adherent scales, follicular plugging, atrophy, and scarring.

Carpet Tack Sign

• Seen when the adherent scale is lifted from a DLE lesion.
• The undersurface of the scale shows multiple horny plugs corresponding to dilated hair follicles.
• This appearance resembles the underside of a carpet tack, hence the name Carpet Tack Sign (also called the Tin Tack Sign).

Clinical Features of DLE

• Erythematous scaly plaques
• Follicular plugging
• Central atrophy and scarring
• Dyspigmentation
• Commonly affects face, scalp, and ears

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

Pityriasis Versicolor

• Caused by Malassezia species.
• Shows fine branny scales and positive scratch sign.

Psoriasis: Characterized by silvery-white scales and Auspitz sign.

Lichen Planus: Characterized by violaceous papules with Wickham striae.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Where is tattoo ink present in the skin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dermis

Tattoo pigment is deposited into the dermis, mainly within dermal macrophages and fibroblasts.

Why dermis?

• The epidermis continuously undergoes desquamation.
• If ink were placed only in the epidermis, it would disappear with skin turnover.

Mechanism:

• Tattoo needle penetrates epidermis
• Pigment deposited in superficial/mid dermis
• Macrophages engulf pigment → long-term persistence

Clinical relevance:

• Laser tattoo removal works by fragmenting dermal pigment particles.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which glands are primarily affected in Bromhidrosis? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Both Apocrine and Eccrine Glands

Bromhidrosis (osmidrosis) is a condition characterized by offensive body odor resulting from the breakdown of sweat by skin bacteria.

Both apocrine and eccrine sweat glands contribute to bromhidrosis:

• Apocrine glands

• Located mainly in the axillae, areola, and anogenital region.
• Produce protein- and lipid-rich secretions.
• Bacterial degradation of these secretions is the major cause of body odor.

• Eccrine glands

• Distributed throughout the body.
• Excess sweating (hyperhidrosis) can promote bacterial growth and contribute to odor formation.

Types of Bromhidrosis

• Apocrine bromhidrosis – most common form
• Eccrine bromhidrosis – associated with hyperhidrosis, poor hygiene, certain foods, and metabolic disorders

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

• Apocrine glands alone: Major contributor but not the only glands involved.
• Eccrine glands alone: Can contribute but are not solely responsible.
• Sebaceous glands: Produce sebum and are not the primary glands involved in bromhidrosis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is a primary skin lesion? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Purpura

Primary skin lesions are the initial, directly observable manifestations of a skin disease. Purpura is considered a primary skin lesion and results from extravasation of blood into the skin or mucous membranes, producing non-blanching red, purple, or brown discolorations.

Primary Skin Lesions:

• Macule
• Papule
• Plaque
• Nodule
• Vesicle
• Bulla
• Pustule
• Wheal
• Cyst
• Purpura

Secondary Skin Lesions:

• Crust
• Scale
• Erosion
• Ulcer
• Fissure
• Scar
• Atrophy
• Lichenification

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

• Crust: Secondary lesion formed by dried serum, blood, or pus on the skin surface.
• Atrophy: Secondary lesion characterized by thinning of the epidermis, dermis, or subcutaneous tissue.
• Induration: Refers to hardening/thickening of the skin and is a descriptive clinical sign rather than a primary lesion.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is not related to sebaceous glands? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glands of Moll

Sebaceous glands are holocrine glands that secrete sebum, which lubricates the skin and hair. Sebaceous Gland Derivatives:

Glands of Zeis: Modified sebaceous glands associated with eyelash follicles.

Meibomian (Tarsal) Glands

• Specialized sebaceous glands located in the tarsal plate of the eyelids.
• Secrete the lipid layer of the tear film.

Fordyce Spots: Ectopic sebaceous glands found on the oral mucosa, lips, and genital mucosa.

Glands of Moll are not sebaceous glands.

• They are modified apocrine sweat glands located at the eyelid margin.
• Their secretion is sweat-like rather than sebaceous.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following signs is associated with Acantholysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nikolsky Sign

Acantholysis refers to the loss of intercellular connections (desmosomes) between keratinocytes, resulting in separation of epidermal cells and intraepidermal blister formation.

Nikolsky Sign

• Gentle lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin causes the epidermis to shear away.
• Indicates loss of cohesion between keratinocytes due to acantholysis.
• Classically seen in:

• Pemphigus vulgaris
• Pemphigus foliaceus

• Autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 and/or desmoglein 3
• Disruption of desmosomes
• Formation of flaccid intraepidermal bullae

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

Auspitz Sign

• Pinpoint bleeding on removal of scales
• Seen in psoriasis

Button-Hole Sign

• Soft neurofibroma invaginates into the skin on pressure
• Seen in neurofibromatosis type 1

Oil Drop Sign

• Yellow-brown discoloration beneath the nail plate
• Seen in nail psoriasis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct? a. Epidermis can regenerate from deeper follicular cells such as hair follicles and sebaceous glands b. Stratum corneum is the outermost cellular layer c. Epidermis is ectodermal in origin d. Dermis and hypodermis are endodermal in origin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. a and c

The epidermis has the capacity to regenerate and has a distinct embryological origin.

• Regeneration: Epidermis can regenerate not only from basal keratinocytes but also from epithelial stem cells in adnexal structures (hair follicles, sebaceous glands) → important in wound healing
• Embryology: Epidermis is derived from ectoderm
• Incorrect concepts:
• Stratum corneum = outermost layer but consists of dead (anucleate) cells, so not a true “cellular” layer
• Dermis and hypodermis arise from mesoderm, not endoderm

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which one of the following correctly denotes a flat, coloured lesion, < 2 cm in diameter, not raised above the surface of the surrounding skin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Macule

A macule is a flat, circumscribed, discolored lesion that is not palpable, typically <1 cm in diameter. In exam terminology, a flat lesion <2 cm is also classified as a macule, while a larger flat lesion is called a patch.

Why not other options?

• A. Macule: Correct. Flat, non-palpable, color change, <2 cm.
• B. Patch: Flat, non-palpable lesion >2 cm.
• C. Papule: Solid, raised, usually <1 cm.
• D. Nodule: Solid, raised and deeper, generally >1 cm.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 17-year-old male with severe acne vulgaris is planned for treatment with oral isotretinoin. Which of the following baseline investigations should be performed before initiating therapy?
options: Renal function test + Complete blood count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liver function test + Lipid profile

Oral isotretinoin is the most effective treatment for severe nodulocystic or treatment-resistant acne vulgaris, but it is associated with hepatotoxicity and hypertriglyceridemia. Therefore, baseline liver function tests (LFTs) and a fasting lipid profile should be obtained before starting therapy and monitored periodically during treatment.

• LFT: Detects baseline liver dysfunction, as isotretinoin can cause elevated transaminases.
• Lipid profile: Detects hypertriglyceridemia, the most common laboratory abnormality during therapy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Complete blood count + Lipid profile: CBC is not routinely required before isotretinoin.
• C. Renal function test + Complete blood count: Neither is routinely indicated unless clinically warranted.
• D. Liver function test + Serum electrolytes: Electrolytes are not routinely monitored with isotretinoin.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female presented in dermatology OPD with acne that is not resolving on oral isotretinoin and antibiotics therapy. Which of the following is the next best step among the following options?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Evaluate for hyperandrogenism

Refractory acne in females (not responding to isotretinoin + antibiotics) → always evaluate for underlying hyperandrogenism.

o    Persistent, severe, or treatment-resistant acne often indicates hormonal etiology

o    Common causes:

§  PCOS (most common)

§  Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

§  Androgen-secreting tumors (rare)

• Clinical clues suggesting hyperandrogenism:

o    Irregular menstrual cycles

o    Hirsutism

o    Androgenic alopecia

o    Sudden onset or severe acne

• Next steps in evaluation:

o    Serum testosterone

o    DHEAS

o    LH/FSH ratio (PCOS)

• Management implication: Add hormonal therapy (OCPs, spironolactone) rather than escalating antibiotics/isotretinoin

Why not others:

• Dietary triggers → mild/moderate acne, not resistant severe acne
• Antibiotic resistance → already on isotretinoin (not primarily antibiotic-dependent)
• Drug triggers → consider, but less likely in classic persistent female acne

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with annular lesions on the skin. Which of the following conditions is least likely to present with annular lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urticaria

Annular (ring-shaped) lesions are classically seen in several dermatological conditions due to central clearing with peripheral activity.

Common causes of annular lesions:

·         Tinea corporis → ringworm with central clearing and active scaly margin

·         Porokeratosis → annular plaques with keratotic ridge (cornoid lamella)

·         Pityriasis rosea → annular/oval lesions with collarette scaling

Least likely:

·         Urticaria → transient wheals, not true annular lesions; lesions are fleeting and change within hours

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young child is evaluated for a scaly, pruritic rash predominantly involving the face and extensor surfaces of the limbs. The itching is particularly intense at night. There is a family history of asthma in the father. The child has dry skin with eczematous lesions. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atopic dermatitis

Recognize atopic dermatitis by its chronic, intensely pruritic eczematous lesions, xerosis (dry skin), infantile distribution over the face and extensor surfaces, and association with a personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema). Pruritus is the hallmark feature, and scratching perpetuates the disease.

Why not the other options?

• A. Scabies: Intense nocturnal itching but typically involves finger webs, wrists, axillae, and genitalia with burrows; facial involvement is uncommon except in infants.
• C. Contact dermatitis: Localized rash confined to the site of allergen/irritant exposure; lacks a characteristic atopic history and chronic distribution.
• D. Cradle cap dermatitis (seborrheic dermatitis): Greasy yellow scales on the scalp and face with minimal or no pruritus.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Allergic contact dermatitis is a manifestation of:
questions.explanation:
