Correct answer: D. Type IV hypersensitivity

Allergic Contact Dermatitis (ACD) is a Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by T lymphocytes. It occurs after sensitization to an allergen, and on re-exposure, activated memory T cells produce an inflammatory response, resulting in pruritic, erythematous, vesicular eczema at the site of contact.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Type I hypersensitivity: IgE-mediated immediate reaction, seen in anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, and urticaria.
• B. Type II hypersensitivity: Antibody-mediated cytotoxic reaction involving IgG/IgM, e.g., autoimmune hemolytic anemia and Goodpasture syndrome.
• C. Type III hypersensitivity: Immune complex-mediated reaction, e.g., serum sickness, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and SLE.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old female comes with complaints of pain in her fingernail. On examination, nail folds were seen to be red and with erythema as shown in the picture.The most likely diagnosis is ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paronychia

Acute suppurative infection of the nail beds and folds is called acute paronychia. It is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

* It presents as tender, purulent swellings around the nail.

* Treatment of pyogenic paronychia consists mostly of protection against trauma and concentrated efforts to keep the affected fingernails dry.

* Acutely inflamed pyogenic abscesses should be incised and drained. The abscess may often be opened by pushing the nailfold away from the nail plate.

* In acute suppurative paronychia, especially if stains show pyogenic cocci, a semisynthetic penicillin or a cephalosporin with excellent staphylococcal activity should be given orally.

Chronic paronychia is caused by Candida species.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A sexually active male presented with warts on his penis as shown below. Similar lesions was present near the anal canal.What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Condyloma Accuminata

The most likely diagnosis is of Condyloma Accuminata.

Human papillomavirus 6 & 11 (6 >11) are the most common cause of anogenital warts (also known as Condyloma Accuminata).

* Giant Anogenital warts are known as Buschke Lowenstein Tumor.

* It is more common in males than in females.

* Most common site:

* In males: Frenulum, corona, glans penis

* In females: Posterior fourchette

* On histology koilocytes are seen.

These are squamous epithelial cells which have nuclear enlargement, irregular nuclear membrane, hyperchromasia, perinuclear halo.

* Most of these warts resolve spontaneously.

* Persistent warts might transform into malignancy most commonly when infected with HPV 16 and 18.

Treatment:

Provider administered:

* Podophyllin (25%) - Antimitotic drug

* Trichloroacetic acid

* Cryotherapy

Both trichloroacetic acid and cryotherapy are safe in pregnancy.

Patient administered:

* Purified podophyllin called podophyllotoxin

* Imiquimod - Immunomodulator which acts on toll-like receptor 7 and 8

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young man presents with a leg lesion as shown in the image below. On examination, the lesions are painful and the edges are well demarcated and raised. He also complains of blisters over his body. He is otherwise normal and does not have any other diseases. This infection is most likely to be caused by which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Group A Streptococcus

The given image shows the presence of erythematous skin lesions with well-demarcated borders. The edge is raised. This is the hallmark of erysipelas. In immunocompetent patients, it is caused by group A streptococcus.

Erysipelas is a bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Causative organisms

* Commonly caused by group A Streptococcus.

* Group B streptococcus- May cause infection under the age of 3 months and pelvic erysipelas after surgery

* Haemophilus influenzae type b- causes facial cellulitis

Patients will have erythema, heat, swelling, and pain or tenderness over the affected site. The edge of the lesion is well demarcated and raised. Blistering can also be seen. The most common site is the leg followed by the face. It can also affect the ear, referred to as Millan's ear sign.

It is treated with antibiotics like flucloxacillin, clarithromycin, clindamycin, and benzylpenicillin.

Another infection similar to erysipelas is cellulitis. It is the infection of loose connective tissue. It is also commonly caused by group A Streptococcus. Important differentiating features are

* The edges of the lesions are diffuse

* The ear is not involved due to a lack of subcutaneous tissue and deeper dermis in the ear.

Pearl PF1531: Skin and soft tissue lesions caused by Streptococcus

Streptococcus causes a variety of skin and soft tissue infections. These include:

a. Impetigo- Infection of superficial layers of the skin. It presents as superficial vesicles which break down and are then encrusted by honey-colored scab. It usually occurs in children.

The given image shows impetigo:

b. Erysipelas- Infection of the superficial epidermis. It presents as an erythematous raised lesion with sharply demarcated edges that differentiate it from the surrounding skin.

The given image shows erysipelas- note the clear demarcation at the nasolabial folds seen in facial erysipelas.

c. Cellulitis- Infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue. It presents with erythema and edema. It can be differentiated from erysipelas by - i. Erysipelas is a raised lesion whereas cellulitis is not, ii. Cellulitis is poorly demarcated from the surrounding skin whereas erysipelas is clearly demarcated.

The given image shows cellulitis:

d. Necrotizing fasciitis- Infection involving the fascial planes. It presents with dark areas of necrosis, erythema, and edema.

The given image shows necrotizing fasciitis with areas of erythema and necrosis:

d. Myositis and myonecrosis- Infection of the muscle.

The given image shows necrotizing myositis:

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Auspitz sign is seen in ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Psoriasis vulgaris

Auspitz sign is a characteristic feature seen in psoriasis.

The presence of silvery-white scaly lesions on the extensor aspect of the elbows and knee is a characteristic feature seen in psoriasis. The condition can be diagnosed clinically by demonstrating the Auspitz sign.

Demonstration of Auspitz Sign:

If superficial silvery scales are removed by scratching (grattage), then the scales come off attached together, as if one has scratched on a wax candle (wax candle scales).

Subsequently, a thin membrane, known as Bulkeley membrane, is seen.

Removal of Bulkeley membrane, reveals classical pinpoint bleeding known as Auspitz sign.

Auspitz sign is due to the elongated vessels in the dermal papilla, together with the thinning of supra papillary epidermis.

Silvery-white scales on the extensor aspect of the elbow seen in psoriasis are portrayed in the picture below:

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The girl seen in the image has had history of severe sunburns after just a few minutes in the sun, severe freckling in the sun exposed areas. The most likely diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Xeroderma Pigementosum

The image shows a girl with Xeroderma Pigmentosum. It is characterized by Defective Nucleotide Excision repair that is transmitted autosomal recessively.

Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by defective DNA repair which leads to clinical and cellular hypersensitivity to ultraviolet radiation and other carcinogenic agents.

Important clinical features are:

* Child is asymptomatic at birth. Diffuse erythema, scaling, and freckle like areas over the sun exposed regions of the body at around 6 months of age.

* Poikiloderma is a characteristic feature of the second stage. Poikiloderma results in skin atrophy, telangiectasias with mottled hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation.

* In the third stage appearance of cutaneous malignancies like squamous cell carcinomas, malignant melanoma, basal cell carcinoma,  and fibrosarcoma.

The final diagnosis of XP can be confirmed by special laboratory tests by examining the DNA damage repair in cells from cultures exposed to ultraviolet radiation. The most common tests are skin biopsy and culture of skin fibroblasts.

There is no cure for XP. Treatment consists of minimizing exposure to sunlight and regular dermatological care, as well as surgery for recurrent tumors excision. Patients should be followed up every 3 months.

Genetic counseling is important in a family that has an affected child and is considering having more children.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with the given rash after he had taken NSAIDs for his knee pain. He reported that he developed the same rash in the same location 6 months ago when he took the same drugs for back pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fixed drug eruption

The recurrence of hyperpigmentation occurring at the same site with the use of the same drug is characteristic of fixed drug eruption.

Fixed drug eruption is one of the most common drug-induced exanthems. The acute erythematous and bullous stages of fixed eruption characteristically settle leaving residual slate-brown hyperpigmentation, especially in those with darker skin types. The genitalia and perianal area are often affected.

Option A: Drug hypersensitivity is an immune-mediated reaction to a drug of which symptoms ranging from mild to severe include rash, anaphylaxis, and serum sickness.

Option B: Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH) is an acquired hypermelanosis occurring after cutaneous inflammation or injury e.g., acne vulgaris, atopic dermatitis, and impetigo.

Option D: Drug-induced hypermelanosis is localized or generalized hyperpigmentation that can be caused by a wide range of medications and chemicals. eg. busulphan.  It doesn't necessarily occur at the same site with the reintroduction of drugs.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presented to the outpatient department with a swelling over his palm as shown in the photo. A few months back he got injured with a thorn. What is the presentation given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Implantation dermoid

The given image shows an implantation dermoid which is caused due to traumatic injury.

Implantation dermoid:

* An acquired condition that occurs as the result of implantation of epidermal fragments into the dermis by a penetrating injury. The epidermis continues to grow and forms a cyst lined with stratified squamous epithelium and filled with keratin.

* Can occur with any skin puncture, laceration, or skin incision which has the potential to implant epidermal elements into the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, where continued production of keratin and other epidermal products produces a thick-walled cyst.

* Mostly seen in farmers, factory workers, carpenters, and tailors who are subject to repeated minor traumas to the hand.

* Risk factors of palmoplantar epidermoid cysts-HPV infection, ultraviolet exposure, and eccrine duct obstruction.

* Presents as asymptomatic, slowly enlarging, painless, superficial localized swellings over the volar aspect of the hand, especially the distal portion of the digits.

* Investigations-X-rays, Ultrasonography, FNAC(CT and MRI may be helpful in delineating the anatomy of the soft tissue tumors, although unnecessary to guide the treatment).

* Histologically, the inclusion epidermoid cysts are lined with stratified squamous epithelium with granular cell layer and are filled with eosinophilic lamellated keratinous material.

* Most of the hand dermoid cysts are benign and asymptomatic, and hence surgical intervention is not needed.

* The surgical treatment is needed for symptomatic cysts causing interference with hand function in which complete excision is done with regional anesthesia under a pneumatic tourniquet.

Dermoid cysts present as firm painless subcutaneous nodules and are of 4 types:

* Sequestration dermoid - sequestration of epithelium during embryological development

* Tubulodermoid - accumulation of secretions from ectodermal tube/duct

* Implantation dermoid - implantation of the epidermis due to trauma

* Teratomatous dermoid - having all 3 germ layers (ecto, meso, and endoderm)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the disease shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Elephantiasis

The given clinical picture is suggestive of lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis).

Lymphatic filariasis is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi.

Elephantiasis is a delayed sequel to repeated lymphangitis, obstruction, and lymphedema. Repeated leakage of lymph into tissues first results in lymphedema, then to elephantiasis.

The characteristic manifestations of filariasis are due to obstruction of lymph vessels and nodes. The essential features are lymphadenopathy, lymphangitis, lymphangiovarix, lymphorrhagia or chylorrhagia, hydrocoele, lymphoedema and elephantiasis, and chyluria. Sometimes the swelling involves the whole leg, the whole arm, the scrotum, the vulva, or the breast.

Occult Filariasis is a term given to hypersensitivity reactions to filarial antigens.Wuchereria bancrofti infection is usually asymptomatic.

Microfilaria of the Wuchereria bancrofti has a pointed tail that is free of nuclei.

The lymphatic vessels of the male genitalia are most commonly affected in bancroftian filariasis, producing episodic funiculitis, epididymitis, and orchitis. Adenolymphangitis of the extremities is less common.

DEC provocation test is used to demonstrate microfilaria during the day.

Diethylcarbamazine is the drug of choice.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The image shown below is a pathognomonic finding in Psoriasis. What is it called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subungual oil drop sign

The above clinical image depicting the Subungual oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature.

Image of Thinning of Nails.Most common sign Of Lichen Planus of the nails

Image of Dorsal Nail Pterygium.
It is the most specific nail change in Lichen planus. Fusion of dorsal nail fold and nail bed leads to pterygium.

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

Image: oil drops visible in the nail bed.

Image: pitting and salmon patches in fingernails.

Image: Leukonychia in a patient with psoriasis.

Features of Nail Psoriasis – Mnemonic

“Nail – POLISH”

* P – Pitting

* O – Oil drop sign, Onycholysis

* L – Leuconychia

* I – Irregular pitting pattern

* S – Splinter Hemorrhage

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the clinical sign shown in the below picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Koebner's phenomenon

The image shows Koebner’s phenomenon.

Koebner’s phenomenon/ isomorphic response is the development of lesions in previously normal skin that has been subjected to trauma. If the same response is seen from the spread of an infective agent ( like molluscum contagiosum, viral warts), it's called pseudo-koebner’s phenomenon.

Any of the following can elicit an isomorphic response: physical trauma, including friction, pressure, incision and laceration, skin grafting, bites, vaccination skin tests, burns, freezing, and ultraviolet (UV) and ionizing radiation.

It is seen commonly associated with psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo. Other associated disorders include Darrier’s disease, pityriasis rubra pilaris, lichen nidatus, DLE, necrobiosis lipoidica, and Grzybowski syndrome.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 7-year-old intellectually disabled boy was brought with large warty crusts on the trunk, hands, and feet as shown below. Severe fissuring and scaling of the skin are present over the soles. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Norwegian scabies

The clinical scenario is suggestive of Norwegian scabies or human-crusted scabies.

Individuals who are intellectually challenged, suffering from dementia, or with Down's syndrome are frequently associated with Norwegian scabies.  Lack of appreciation of pruritus could be a reason for this.

Crusted scabies (Norwegian or hyperkeratotic scabies) is seen in individuals who are immunocompromised due to any underlying disease or therapy, patients with HIV infection, and in people who use topical steroids and pimecrolimus.

Crusted scabies occurs in people with an inadequate immune response to the mite, allowing them to multiply. It is called 'Norwegian' because it was first described in lepers of Norway.

Large warty crusts form on the hands and feet. Palms and soles may be irregularly fissured and thickened. Horny debris get accumulates beneath the thickened and discolored nails. Erythema and scaling occur in the scalp face and seborrheic area. The itching will be absent often.

Scrappings teeming with mites and eggs confirms the diagnosis.

All patients should be hospitalized and isolated due to the risk of transmission due to physical contact. Treatment includes oral ivermectin, topical scabicide, and keratolytic agents for the crusting.

The images given below show hands in Norwegian scabies.

Other options:

Option A- If topical steroids are used on scabies lesions, the clinical picture modifies to mimic other conditions. This is termed as scabies incognito.

Option B-  Animal scabies transmission to humans is rare. Lesions are similar to human scabies with itchy papules except for the burrows. It is rare.

Option C-  Nodular scabies presents as violaceous, pruritic localized nodules over the groin, axilla, and genitalia. They represent a hypersensitivity reaction to the mite antigens and can persist after treatment.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presented with lesions as shown in the image below and later developed arthritis also. What is the treatment of choice for a patient who presented with the following findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Methotrexate

The patient has right knee effusion, dactylitis of multiple digits, sharply demarcated red papulosquamous lesions on both knees all of which point towards a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis.

Methotrexate and apremilast are the first-line drugs for the treatment of moderate to severe psoriasis associated with psoriatic arthritis.

Features of psoriatic arthritis are :

* Asymmetrical oligoarthritis

* associated with nail pitting/ onycholysis, or

* dactylitis, enthesitis

* Inflammation is prominent in the distal interphalangeal joints

* There is dactylitis with pronounced telescoping.

* Nail dystrophy (hyperkeratosis and onycholysis) affects each of the finger

* Axial involvement may occur

Radiological features:

* Pencil-in-cup deformity of DIP joint

* marginal erosions with adjacent bony proliferation "whiskering"

* small joint ankylosis

* Ray distribution of lesions

Note :

Indications for methotrexate (inflammatory conditions) include:

* Rheumatoid arthritis

* Psoriasis

* Psoriatic arthritis

* Ankylosing spondylitis

* Polymyositis

* Dermatomyositis

* Wegener’s granulomatosis

* Giant cell arteritis

* Systemic lupus erythematosus

* Other systemic vasculitis

* Graft versus host disease associated with organ transplantation.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following features are not associated with the condition shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Munro microabscesses

The image shows characteristic lesions of Lichen Planus and Munro microabscesses are not a feature of Lichen Planus but seen in Psoriasis.

Lichen planus (LP) is an idiopathic inflammatory disease affecting the skin and mucous membrane.

Patients present with pruritic, purple, polygonal, papules. The lesions have thin white lines on their surface known as Wickham’s striae. They are commonly seen on the volar aspect of the wrists, the lumbar region, and around the ankles.

The mucosal involvement is also seen. The commonest mucosal sites are buccal mucosa and tongue, rarely it can also be found on the buccal mucosa, anus, genitalia, etc.

Nail involvement can be seen as thinning of nail plate leading to an exaggeration of longitudinal lines, and linear depressions. The nails can also be destroyed leading to anonychia. Involvement of nail bed may give rise to longitudinal melanonychia, hyperpigmentation, subungual hyperkeratosis, or onycholysis.

Microscopy will show acanthosis of the epidermis, irregular thickening of the granular layer, and compact hyperkeratosis.  Degenerating basal epidermal cells are transformed into colloid bodies. The rete ridges can display a sawtooth pattern, and localized detachment from the dermis may form Max Joseph spaces. Active lichen planus is characterised by infiltration of lymphocytes arranged in the form of a band at the junction between the dermis and epidermis.

Other options:

Munro microabscess is the accumulation of neutrophils in the stratum corneum. The lesions present as red scaly plaques which are well demarcated with the surrounding normal skin. They might have a circle of clear zone around it which is known as the Woronoff ring.

Pearl PF1438: Nail changes in lichen planus

Nail involvement in lichen planus occurs in up to 10% of the cases but is usually a minor feature of the disease.

Dorsal Nail Pterygium is the most specific nail change in Lichen planus. The fusion of dorsal nail fold and nail bed leads to pterygium.

The most frequent nail change is the exaggeration of longitudinal lines and linear depressions due to a slight thinning of the nail plate.

Pup-tent sign - elevation of nail in shape of tent

Trachonychia - 20 nail dystrophy

Subungual Hyperkeratosis and Onycholysis

Longitudinal Melanonychia in Lichen Planus of the nail bed

Permanent destruction of several toenails with ulceration of soles (rare variant)

Image shows  Nails in Lichen planus presented with irregular longitudinal grooves and ridges .

Image : Dorsal Nail Pterygium

Image : Pup-tent sign

Image : Trachonychia

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following side effects are seen most commonly with Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Embryopathy

Isotretinoin is a vitamin A derivative which is highly teratogenic when orally administered. It is commonly used to treat cystic nodular acne. It inhibits the migration of neural crest cells during embryogenesis and affects the development of multiple organs. These defects are collectively termed retinoic acid embryopathy.

Embryopathy or developmental disorder of an embryo comprises a large variety of abnormalities and is more common than any individual defect. Specific anomalies may include ventriculomegaly, maldevelopment of the facial bones or cranium, microtia or anotia, micrognathia, cleft palate, conotruncal heart defects, and thymic aplasia or hypoplasia.

Isotretinoin also increases the risk of spontaneous abortions and stillbirths in pregnancies exposed in the first trimester of this medicine. Presenting with pregnancy during treatment with isotretinoin is a failure of prevention strategies.

The guidelines for isotretinoin usage are as follows:

* Isotretinoin is a teratogenic drug that should not be taken during pregnancy and nursing.

* Patients should take 2 pregnancy tests before starting isotretinoin and take a monthly pregnancy test while on the medication, and another test 1 month after stopping the medication.

* It is recommended to use two birth control methods concurrently, beginning one month before treatment to one month following the end of isotretinoin treatment.

* Isotretinoin should be reserved for the treatment of severe, nodulocystic acne and should not be used for milder forms of acne.

Other options:

Option B: Lithium is used in the treatment of bipolar disorder. It is a teratogen associated with Ebstein's anomaly which is a rare cardiac condition characterized by severe tricuspid regurgitation and right atrial enlargement.

Option C: Valproic acid is the anti-epileptic which confers the greatest risk to the developing fetus while used in pregnancy. It is associated with an increased risk of neural tube defects in the fetus.

Option D: Tetracyclines are associated with yellowish-brown discoloration of deciduous teeth when used after 25 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old male presented with erythematous plaques covered with silvery scales over the extensor surfaces of both arms. Punctate pitting was noted on examining the nails. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Psoriasis

The presentation of erythematous plaques with silvery scales over the extensor surfaces of arms and punctate pitting of the nails are suggestive of psoriasis.

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the skin with systemic manifestations. Plaque psoriasis is the most common type.

* The peak occurrence is between 16 to 22 years and between 57 to 62 years. They usually present with itching and a papulosquamous rash.

* The lesions are red, and scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin.

* They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone which is called the Woronoff ring.

* They commonly appear in the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs.

* Koebner or isomorphic phenomenon- describes the appearance of new lesions along the site of trauma (linear lesions)

Nail findings are commonly seen across all types of psoriasis. Patients present with pits, ridges, and grooves of the nail plate. In the case of nail bed involvement subungual oil drops, subungual hyperkeratosis, and distal onycholysis can be seen.

The characteristic histopathological finding in psoriasis consists of multiple neutrophilic foci in the parakeratotic stratum corneum i.e Munro’s microabscesses and spongiform neutrophils in the spinous layer of the epidermis i.e spongiform pustules of Kogoj.

The topical application of steroids, retinoids, vitamin D, and emollients is the mainstay of management. Phototherapy and oral methotrexate, acitretin, and cyclosporine can also be used.

Other options:

Option B: Lichen planus is an inflammatory disorder affecting the skin and mucosal membranes. The lesions of Lichen planus can be described as 5Ps — purple, polygonal, pruritic, plane-topped (flat), papules and are shown in the image below. White streaks forming a lacework in buccal mucosa is a characteristic feature and are known as Wickham’s striae. Nail involvement includes hyperpigmentation, subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis, and pterygium unguis due to adhesion between the dorsal nail fold and the nail bed.

Option C: Atopic dermatitis or eczema is a relapsing chronic inflammatory skin disease. Patients present with itchy erythematous papules/ papulovesicular lesions in flexural regions as shown below. Nail involvement is in the form of coarse pitting and ridging.

Option D: Pityriasis rosea is an acute self-limiting papulosquamous disorder. It is commonly seen in children and young adults. The first manifestation of the disease is usually the appearance of the herald patch, which is larger and more conspicuous than the lesions of the later eruption covered by fine scales. Later the center tends to clear and assumes a wrinkled, atrophic appearance and a tawny color, with a marginal collarette of scale attached peripherally, with the free edge of the scale internally - called a Hanging curtain sign.

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

Image: oil drops visible in the nail bed.

Image: pitting and salmon patches in fingernails.

Image: Leukonychia in a patient with psoriasis.

Features of Nail Psoriasis – Mnemonic

“Nail – POLISH”

* P – Pitting

* O – Oil drop sign, Onycholysis

* L – Leuconychia

* I – Irregular pitting pattern

* S – Splinter Hemorrhage

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

Pearl PF1460: Treatment Ladder for Psoriasis

Treatment Ladder for Psoriasis

I. In Mild Psoriasis Without Arthritis

First line

* Coal tar

* Dithranol

* Potent topical steroid

* Vitamin D analogue

Second line

* Local NB-UVB or PUVA

* Excimer laser

II. In Moderate or Severe Psoriasis Without Arthritis

First line

* NB-UVB or PUVA

Second line

* Acitretin

* Apremilast

* Ciclosporin

* Fumaric acid esters (where available)

* Methotrexate

Third line

* Adalimumab

* Etanercept

* Infliximab

* Secukinumab

* Ustekinumab

III. In Moderate or Severe Psoriasis with Psoriatic Arthritis

First line

* Apremilast

* Methotrexate

Second line

* Adalimumab

* Etanercept

* Infliximab

* Ustekinumab

Third line

* Combination therapy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old female patient, who is a known case of ovarian cancer, presents with difficulty in activities like climbing stairs, getting up from the chair, combing hair, etc. The following characteristic sign was found on examination. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dermatomyositis

The most probable diagnosis is dermatomyositis.

The given image shows upper eyelid lilac erythema or heliotrope rash which is pathognomonic of dermatomyositis. The clinical presentation of proximal myopathy with a rash in an elderly female, with a history of internal malignancy, is also suggestive of dermatomyositis.

Other classic cutaneous signs in dermatomyositis:

* Heliotrope rash/ eyelid erythema- Violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids

* V sign- Confluent macular erythema over the lower anterior neck and upper anterior chest

* Shawl sign- Confluent macular erythema over the upper back and lateral aspect of arms

* Gottron’s papules- Erythematous papules and plaques over extensor surface of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints

* Gottron's sign- Erythematous rash over the extensor surfaces of joints such as the knuckles, elbows, knees, and ankles.

* Mechanic’s hands- Rough, hyperkeratotic lines on the lateral and palmer areas of the fingers

Facial rash in dermatomyositis-

Shawl sign in dermatomyositis-

Flagellate erythema in dermatomyositis-

Poikilodermatous changes in dermatomyositis-

Other options:

Option A: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents with a malar rash as visualized in the image in the image below. It is characterized by a well-demarcated erythematous butterfly rash over the malar eminences with sparing of the nasolabial folds.

Option C: Scleroderma or systemic sclerosis has findings of mask-like facies with stretched, shiny skin, loss of normal facial lines, microstomia, and resorption of distal phalanges of the fingers.

Option D: Cushing's syndrome presents with easy bruisability and multiple purple striae over the abdomen. They may also have rounding, puffiness, fat deposition, and plethora in the face collectively called the moon facies.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A baby presents to the OPD and the findings are shown in the image below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Capillary hemangioma

The image shows a capillary hemangioma involving the left upper lid and periocular area. A capillary haemangioma is the most common tumor of the orbit and periorbital area in childhood.

Hemangioma is a benign tumor caused by the abnormal growth of blood vessels. Types of hemangioma are:

* Capillary hemangioma (most common)

* Juvenile/ strawberry hemangioma

* Cavernous hemangioma

* Pyogenic hemangioma

Capillary hemangioma may present as small isolated lesions or large masses that can cause visual impairment (due to mechanical ptosis and the resulting sensory deprivation amblyopia), systemic effects (severe thrombocytopenia), or exist as part of PHACE syndrome (Posterior fossa anomalies, Hemangioma, Arterial lesions, Cardiac abnormalities, Eye or Endocrine abnormalities)

30% of lesions resolve by the age of 3 years and about 75% by the age of 7. On histology, they show thin-walled capillaries with scant stroma as shown below.

Indications for treatment are:

* Visual (amblyopia, astigmatism, occlusion, strabismus)

* Cosmesis

* Optic nerve compression

* Exposure keratopathy

Capillary hemangioma regresses spontaneously very often. Treatment options include:

* Beta-blockers- oral propranolol, topical timolol.

* Steroids- intralesional triamcinolone or betamethasone, topical clobetasol, systemic steroids.

* Interferon alfa-2a and vincristine- for steroid-resistant sight-threatening lesions

* Local resection with cutting cautery or carbon dioxide laser.

Option A: Port wine stain is a congenital low-flow vascular malformation that may occur anywhere in the body and does not fade away with time. Visually they appear as partially or completely blanchable, pink to red or reddish brown patches, mostly on the head and neck. This lesion is associated with syndromes such as Sturge-Weber syndrome and occult spinal dysraphism.

Option B: Cavernous hemangiomas are large, cavernous blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue stroma. They are infiltrative and involve deep structures. They do not regress spontaneously. Von Hippel–Lindau disease is associated with cavernous hemangiomas. These vascular lesions are commonly found in the cerebellum, brain stem, retina, pancreas, and liver.

Option C: Salmon patches or naevus simplex (as shown below) are small, ill-defined, pink-colored macules commonly seen over the glabella, eyelids, upper lip, and nuchal area, which develop due to vascular ectasia. It is a common vascular birthmark and disappears within 1 year.

Pearl PF0879: Classification of Vascular Tumors and Tumor-like Conditions

Benign Neoplasms, Developmental and Acquired Conditions

• Hemangioma

• Capillary hemangioma

• Cavernous hemangioma

• Pyogenic granuloma

• Lymphangioma

• Simple/capillary lymphangioma
• Cavernous lymphangioma (cystic hygroma)

• Glomus tumor

• Vascular ectasias

• Nevus flammeus
• Spider telangiectasia (arterial spider)
• Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasis (Osler–Weber–Rendu disease)

• Reactive vascular proliferation

• Bacillary angiomatosis

Intermediate-grade Neoplasms

• Kaposi sarcoma

• Hemangioendothelioma

Malignant Neoplasm

• Angiosarcoma

• Hemangiopericytoma

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presented with itchy lesions as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lichen planus

The given image showing pruritic, purple, polygonal, papules are characteristic of lichen planus.

Lichen planus is a type of lichenoid disorder affecting the papillary dermis. It is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune disease against the basal keratinocytes. It is a chronic disease with a number of relapses and remissions.

The most common presentation of lichen planus is a well-defined area of purple-colored, itchy, flat-topped papules. This description is known as the characteristic "6 P"s of lichen planus: planar (flat-topped), purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, and plaques.

Clinically, oral lichen planus can present as Wickham striae (image below), white papules, white plaque, erythema, erosion, or blisters. They may be symmetrical and bilateral. Buccal mucosa, dorsum of the tongue, and gingivae are commonly affected. Early diagnosis and management play an important role in the prevention of progression to malignancy.

Complications of lichen planus include:

* Hair: Patches of cicatricial scarring alopecia

* Nails: Various nail changes are seen associated with lichen planus.

* Dorsal Nail Pterygium: The most specific nail change in lichen planus where the fusion of dorsal nail fold and nail bed leads to pterygium formation.

* Thinning of the nail plate: The most common nail change is the exaggeration of longitudinal lines and linear depressions.

* Pup-tent sign: Elevation of the nail in the shape of a tent

* Trachonychia: All 20 nails of hands and feet undergo dystrophy

* Subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis

* Longitudinal melanonychia in lichen planus of the nail bed

* Permanent destruction of several toenails with ulceration of soles (rare variant)

* Mucous membranes: Squamous cell carcinoma may occur on the lip, buccal mucosa, or gum margin.

Other options:

Option A: Scabies is an ectoparasitic infestation caused in humans by the Sarcoptes scabiei var. Hominis. The characteristic symptoms of a scabies infection include intense itching and superficial burrows usually in the area of the finger webs, feet, ventral wrists, elbows, back, breasts, buttocks, and external genitals. Burrows presents as slightly raised brownish linear or s-shaped tracks in the skin created by the excavation of the adult mite in the epidermis as depicted below.

Option C: Psoriasis is characterized by erythematous plaques covered with silver scales. It generally affects the extensor surfaces.

Option D: Warts are verrucous growths that may appear discrete or coalesce to form large cauliflower-like growths (as shown in the image below). Human papillomaviruses are implicated in causing this condition.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: An 18-year-old female patient comes with the following findings. Which of the following is pathognomic of the primary stage of this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Comedone

Comedones are pathognomic of the primary stage.

Acne is a polymorphic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit, frequently affecting the face, back, and chest. Comedonal lesions are the earliest lesions of acne. They represent the keratin plugs of the pilosebaceous duct. When the keratin plug is inside the follicle, it is called a closed comedone (Whitehead). When the keratin plug is exposed to the environment, it gets oxidized by the air and turns black which is known as an open comedone (blackhead).

Precipitating factors include:

* Lifestyle and environmental factors, diet, BMI, smoking and alcohol use, menstrual cycle, stress, and sleep deprivation

* Drugs like corticosteroids, anticonvulsants, etc

The severity of acne according to lesion type and extent:

Type of acne
Description

1. Comedonal

- Non‐inflamed lesions
- Open comedones/blackheads
- Closed (whiteheads) comedones

2. Mild

- Non‐inflamed lesions
- Inflammatory lesions <5 mm

3. Moderate

- Non‐inflamed lesions
- Papulopustular lesions

4. Severe

- Deep-seated inflammatory lesions
- Nodules and deep pustules
- Small nodules are >5 mm; large nodules are >1 cm
- Painful lesions with exudative sinus tracts, disfiguring tissue destruction, and scarring
Acne conglabata:

- Multiple-grouped comedones
- Papules, tender inflammatory nodules of varying sizes, suppurative and coalesce to form sinus tract
- Extensive scarring

Assessment of acne includes:

* Leed's photometric grading scale

* Comprehensive acne severity system (CASS)

Management:

* Mild acne -

* Comedonal acne - topical retinoid

* Papular and pustular acne - topical retinoid and topical antibiotics

* Moderate papular or pustular acne and nodular acne - oral antibiotic + topical retinoid ± benzoyl peroxide

* Severe nodular and conglobate acne - oral isotretinoin

* Other therapies -  topical niacinamide, salicylic acid, chemical peels, lasers, and photodynamic therapy

* Novel drugs -

* Drugs that target both retinoic acid receptors -beta and -gamma -

* Adapalene

* Tazarotene

* Tretinoin

* Topical androgen receptor inhibitor - 1% clascoterone cream

Pearl PF1661: Global Alliance Algorithm for Acne Treatment

Global Alliance Algorithm for Acne Treatment

Image: Global Alliance Algorithm for Improving Outcomes in acne

BPO - Benzoyl peroxide

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 60-year-old female patient presented with purplish, itchy, flat-topped lesions on his shins for the past 3 months. The patient also gives a history of chewing tobacco for 20 years. She occasionally drinks alcohol and smokes. On examination, the lesions are seen as in the image below. Which of the following is the first line of management for the condition seen in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Topical corticosteroids

The clinical features and characteristic lesions showing fine white lacework in buccal mucosa called Wickham's striae shown in the image are diagnostic of lichen planus. The first line of management is potent topical corticosteroids like clobetasol propionate ointment 0.05%.

Lichen planus is a type of lichenoid disorder affecting the papillary dermis. It is a T-cell mediated autoimmune disease against the basal keratinocytes. The primary lesions of lichen planus are described by the characteristic "6 Ps": planar (flat-topped), purple, polygonal, pruritic, papules, and plaques. These well-defined areas of purple-coloured, itchy, flat-topped papules may be with interspersed lacy white lines known as Wickham's striae(shown below). It may present with mucous membrane lesions in the absence of skin lesions, commonly involving the tongue and buccal mucosa.

Various factors that can precipitate the disease are:

* Viruses like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, Human herpesviruses (HHV-6, HHV-8), Varicella zoster

* Betel quid which contains areca nut and tobacco leaf

* Environmental factors like:

* Drugs like antimicrobials, antihypertensives, antimalarials, antidepressants, anticonvulsants

* Radiotherapy

* Anxiety, depression, stress

Histology: Most useful investigation to confirm the diagnosis. Basal epidermal cell degeneration/destruction by dermal CD8+ T lymphocytes is characteristically seen in lichen planus. Other findings are:

* Hyperkeratosis

* The degeneration leads to the formation of spaces in the epidermis known as Max-Joseph spaces.

* Saw-toothed appearance of the Rete ridges

* Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate is present at the dermo-epidermal junction.

Other options:

Options A and C: Ciclosporin, and methotrexate are used in third-line management and not first-line management of the disease.

Option D: Oral corticosteroids are used in the second-line management of the disease.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young woman was suspected to have bacterial vaginosis. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?
options: Gardnerella vaginalis is a causative agent
Amsel’s criteria is used for diagnosis
Oral metronidazole is given for treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vaginal itching is prominent

The false statement about bacterial vaginosis among the following is 'vaginal itching is prominent'.

Bacterial vaginosis is a condition associated with alteration in the normal vaginal flora. There is a decrease in the number of lactobacilli in the vaginal discharge and an increase in other anaerobic bacteria mainly, Gardnerella vaginalis (Mobiluncus and Mycoplasma hominins are others organisms). It is not sexually transmitted.

About half of the women having bacterial vaginosis are asymptomatic. Symptomatic women mostly present with a profuse, fishy vaginal discharge. It does not cause pruritus, dysuria, and dyspareunia.

Bacterial vaginosis is diagnosed by the Amsel criteria. At least three of the four are needed to confirm the diagnosis

* White, milky, nonviscous discharge adherent to the vaginal wall.

* The pH of the discharge more than 4.5. (pH 5-7).

* Amine or Whiff test-Fishy odour when discharge is mixed with 10% KOH

* Presence of clue cells - the epithelial cells have a fuzzy border due to adherence of bacteria.

Oral metronidazole (500 mg twice daily for 7 days) or oral clindamycin (300 mg twice daily for 7 days) is given for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis. Partners do not need to be treated. Metronidazole may be avoided in first trimester.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Inguinal bubo is caused by which of the microorganisms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Haemophilus ducreyi

The presence of inguinal bubo is a characteristic feature of chancroid, which is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi.

Inguinal bubo refers to swollen and tender lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy) in the inguinal (groin) region, which is a common presentation of chancroid due to regional lymph node involvement.

Other Options:

Diphtheria, caused by Corynebacterium diphtheria causes and the typical lesion early in the disease is a superficial ulcer, oval, rounded, or irregularly linear in shape with a clearly defined, overhanging edge. The ulcer may later become deeper and the edge becomes rolled, raised, and avascular. It is usually seen around the umbilicus, behind the ears, genito-crural flexure, or in the clefts.

Donovanosis, Klebsiella granulomatis previously known as Calymmatobacterium granulomatis causes a sexually transmitted disease. The incubation period is 1–12 weeks. It presents as a painless beefy red ulcer that bleeds readily on touch. Lymph node involvement is rare. However, pseudo buboes (subcutaneous granulomas) may be seen in the inguinal region in 10% of cases due to subcutaneous abscess.

Gonorrhea is caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae and can lead to various symptoms, including genital discharge and inflammation. While gonorrhea can involve the inguinal lymph nodes, it is not typically associated with the term "inguinal bubo." The major symptoms include urethritis, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia, and dysuria.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: This finding in the groin region on Wood's lamp examination is seen in _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Erythrasma

Coral pink fluorescence in groin region on Wood's Lamp examination is characteristically seen in Erythrasma.

* Coral pink fluorescence is due to the presence of porphyrins.

* Corynebacterium minutissimum is the bacterium responsible for erythrasma and conversion of aminolaevulinic acid to protoporphyrin.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is seen on the microscopy in patients with lichen planus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Colloid bodies

Colloid bodies can be seen on microscopy in patients with lichen planus.

Lichen planus (LP) is an idiopathic inflammatory disease affecting the skin and mucous membrane. Microscopy will show :

* Acanthosis of the epidermis.

* Irregular thickening of the granular layer.

* Hyperkeratosis.

* Colloid (civatte) bodies due to degenerating basal epidermal cells.

* Sawtooth appearance of rete ridges.

* Max Joseph spaces due to focal separation from the dermis.

* Band‐like infiltrate of lymphocytes and histiocytes near the dermo-epidermal junction.

Patients present with pruritic, purple, polygonal, papules. The lesions have thin white lines on their surface known as Wickham’s striae. They are commonly seen on the volar aspect of the wrists, the lumbar region, and around the ankles.

The mucosal involvement is also seen. The commonest mucosal sites are buccal mucosa and tongue, rarely it can also be found on the anus and genitalia.

Nail involvement can be seen as thinning of nail plate leading to an exaggeration of longitudinal lines, and linear depressions. The nails can also be destroyed leading to anonychia. Involvement of nail bed may give rise to longitudinal melanonychia, hyperpigmentation, subungual hyperkeratosis, or onycholysis.

Other options

Option A- Pautrier's microabscess is the intraepidermal lymphocytic microabscess in the absence of marked spongiosis. The cells within the epidermis may show nuclear hyperchromatism or atypia. It is seen in Mycosis fungoides.

The image below shows atypical lymphocytes showing epidermotropism and the formation of Pautrier's microabscesses in mycosis fungoides.

Option B- Munro microabscess is the accumulation of neutrophils in the stratum corneum. The lesions present as well-demarcated red scaly plaques. They might have a circle of clear zone around it which is known as the Woronoff ring. This finding is seen in psoriasis.

Option D- Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are large, foamy macrophages mixed with occasional multinucleate giant cells and lymphocytes. It occurs due to defective phagosomes presenting as basophilic concretions. These are pathognomonic of malakoplakia. Grossly, malakoplakia appears as soft, yellow, slightly raised mucosal plaques.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with painful genital ulcers on vulva accompanied by bilateral lymphadenopathy. She has a history of multiple partners over the years. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chancroid

Multiple painful genital ulcers with bilateral lymphadenopathy are indicative of chancroid or soft chancre.

Chancroid is a type of sexually transmitted infection (STI) that is caused by the bacteria Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative coccobacillus. It presents with painful genital ulceration along with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy that may develop into buboes. Auto-inoculation by the organism can result in new ulcers merging with the older ones. Hence, they are called "kissing ulcers".

The diagnosis is made clinically and can be supported by the Gram stain findings. A typical "school of fish"/"railroad track" appearance is noted.

Treatment is recommended with a single dose of azithromycin (1g) or ceftriaxone (250mg).

Chancroid has gained clinical significance because it can increase the risk of HIV transmission. Hence, it is important to identify and treat these patients and to inform and treat their sexual partners from the last 3 months.

Image: Chancroidal penile ulceration

Other Options:

Option B: Granuloma inguinale (also known as donovanosis) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. It presents with a painless papule or nodule that erodes into a beefy red granulomatous ulcer with rolled edges and often no lymphadenopathy.

Option C: In Lymphogranuloma venerum, a transient primary painless ulcer presents after 3–30 days of exposure and it usually presents on coronal sulcus in men and posterior vaginal wall in women.

Option D: Gonorrhoea is primarily a sexually transmitted bacterial infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae but vertical transmission during childbirth can occur. In men, it often presents as acute urethritis accompanied by a profuse urethral purulent discharge. Most women with early gonorrhea are asymptomatic. The primary site of infection in women is the cervix.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with following finding. Which of the following clinical tests will aid in diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Grattage Test

The image depicts silvery white scaly plaques on the back which is a charateristic feature of Psoriasis. Grattage test will aid in its diagnosis.

Grattage Test:

* Scratching (grattage) scales in psoriasis makes the scale appear more silver in colour by introducing air–keratin interfaces.

* When the scales are completely scraped off, the stratum mucosum (basement membrane) is exposed and is seen as a moist red surface (membrane of Bulkeley) through which dilated capillaries at the tip of elongated dermal papillae are torn, leading to multiple bleeding points.This classical pinpoint bleeding is known as Auspitz sign.

* Auspitz sign is due to the elongated, dilated, tortuous vessels in the dermal papilla along with supra papillary thinning of epidermis.

However Auspitz sign is neither sensitive nor specific for Psoriasis.

* It is not seen in Pustular, Guttate, Erythrodermic or Inverse psoriasis.

* It is also seen in non-psoriatic scaling disorders like Darier's disease and Actinic Keratosis.

Psoriasis is a group of common chronic inflammatory and proliferative conditions of the skin, associated with systemic manifestations in many organ systems. The most characteristic lesions consist of red, scaly, sharply demarcated, indurated plaques, present particularly over the extensor surfaces and scalp.

Other Options:

Option B: Nikolsky's sign: Firm tangential sliding pressure with a finger will separate normal‐looking epidermis from dermis, producing an erosion. Lateral pressure on the normal skin around the blister results in separation between the layers of epidermis and the epidermis moves under the finger and shears off.

Nikolsky's sign is positive in the following:

* Pemphigus

* Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome(SSSS)

* Pemphigus foliaceus

The following image shows Nikolsky's sign, where the application of gentle lateral pressure causes sliding of the epidermis.

Option C: The Asboe-Hansen sign is a dermatological test that involves applying pressure to a blister to see if it spreads to the surrounding skin. It's used to help diagnose blistering diseases like pemphigus vulgaris and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).

Option D: The standard patch test units are applied in two sets (on either side of the spine) and kept covered. One set of patches is removed and exposed to UVA. After irradiation, the other set of patches are also removed and both the sites are covered again for 48 hours. A positive reaction on the irradiated side only is an indication of photoallergy. Negative reaction is seen in phototoxic reaction.

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

Image: oil drops visible in the nail bed.

Image: pitting and salmon patches in fingernails.

Image: Leukonychia in a patient with psoriasis.

Features of Nail Psoriasis – Mnemonic

“Nail – POLISH”

* P – Pitting

* O – Oil drop sign, Onycholysis

* L – Leuconychia

* I – Irregular pitting pattern

* S – Splinter Hemorrhage

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 4-month-old child was brought to the hospital with an abdominal lesion, as shown in the image. What is the appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Observation

The given clinical picture is suggestive of infantile hemangioma. Only observation of the lesion is required as in 50% of cases, complete involution is seen by 5 years of age.

Hemangioma growth frequently peaks before the first year, and then the lesions enter the involuting phase. The involution phase begins in 50% of children by 5 years of age and in 70% by 7 years of age. It continues until 10 years of age.

Indications for immediate treatment are complications such as ulceration or those pertaining to the location of the mass (e.g. visual issues due to large hemangioma over eyelid).

Other treatment options include:

* Beta blockers - oral propranolol

* Steroids - intralesional triamcinolone, topical clobetasol, systemic steroids (Option B).

* Interferon alfa-2a and vincristine - for steroid-resistant lesions

* Local resection with cutting cautery or carbon dioxide laser (Option C).

Other options:

Option A: Betaxolol is a beta-1 selective blocker that is used in glaucoma and has a lower propensity to precipitate bronchial asthma.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old lady diagnosed with breast carcinoma who underwent chemotherapy presents with hair loss after 3 weeks. What is this pattern of hair loss known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anagen effluvium

Anagen effluvium arises from the disruption of the anagen phase of the hair cycle, primarily occurring after chemotherapy.

It is due to the disruption of the anagen or proliferating phase of the hair cycle. Hair shedding typically occurs within 1–3 weeks and it is complete within 1–2 months after the initiation of chemotherapy.

The most important drugs implicated in the order of decreasing frequency of association causing anagen effluvium:

* Anti-microtubule agents (e.g., paclitaxel)

* Topo-isomerase inhibitors (e.g., doxorubicin)

* Alkylating agents (e.g., cyclophosphamide)

* Anti-metabolites (e.g., 5-Fluorouracil)

The image below depicts the pattern of hair loss seen in anagen effluvium.

Other options:

Option A: Alopecia areata causes patchy, well-circumscribed hair loss, as shown below.

Option B: Telogen effluvium is a type of nonscarring alopecia that is marked by diffuse shedding of normal hair. This occurs due to premature termination of the anagen phase of the hair cycle.  It can be either acute or chronic.

The pattern of hair loss in telogen effluvium is given below.

Option D: Trichotillomania (trichotillosis) is considered an obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) spectrum disorder, marked by gratification from pulling one's own hair. It could be associated with underlying anxieties or depression. The vertex region of the scalp is most commonly involved. Scalp histology will show perifollicular haemorrhages and intrafollicular pigment casts.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with multiple nodulocystic lesions on the face. Which among the following is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Isotretinoin

The likely diagnosis in this patient is nodular acne and the drug of choice for this condition is oral isotretinoin.

Isotretinoin is an orally administered systemic retinoid that is used in the management of severe acne.

Commonly seen adverse effects of isotretinoin are cheilitis (dry lips), xerosis (dry skin), xerostomia (dry mouth), dry nose, and increased sun sensitivity.

Oral isotretinoin is contraindicated in pregnant patients and patients who may be pregnant.

Other Options:

Option A: Steroids are not indicated in cases of acne as they can exacerbate the condition due to increased sebum production and skin cell turnover disruption.

Options B and C: Nodulocystic acne is a severe form of acne that often requires more aggressive treatment options, such as isotretinoin. While antibiotics may be used in some cases of nodulocystic acne, they are not the first-line treatment option.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The given picture shows lesions found on the glans penis and pigmentation in the chin and oral cavity. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lichen sclerosis

White atrophic patches on the glans penis along with extragenital manifestations like hyperpigmentation of the face and oral mucosa are suggestive of lichen sclerosis.

Lichen sclerosis is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects the anogenital area. On the glans penis, it presents as white, atrophic patches that can become porcelain-white in appearance. The condition often shows extragenital manifestations, particularly hyperpigmentation in areas like the face and oral cavity. The disease process involves dermal sclerosis and atrophy of the epidermis, leading to characteristic whitish patches.

Treatment typically involves potent topical corticosteroids, and regular monitoring is necessary as there's a small risk of malignant transformation in longstanding cases.

Other options:

Option B: Condyloma acuminata is a genital infection caused by the human papillomavirus(HPV) commonly HPV‐6 and HPV‐11. HPV‐1 and HPV‐2 may also occur in genital warts. The lesions present as soft, pink, fleshy, anogenital warts. These growths may be pedunculated discrete or verrucous that coalesce to form large cauliflower-like growths. It commonly occurs on the glans, corona, and frenulum in men and the posterior fourchette in women.

Option C: Peyronie's disease is characterized by penile deformity, palpable penile plaques within the penis, erectile dysfunction, and pain on erection. It causes the penis to bend, usually towards the side of the plaque. It can be associated with Dupuytren's contracture.

Option D: Syphilis is primarily a sexually transmitted disease caused by Treponema palladium but vertical transmission is also possible. It commonly presents as a hard, painless genital ulcer with induration, followed by the development of rubbery enlargement of inguinal lymph nodes.

questions.text: A female patient presented with a lesion as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Malignant melanoma

An asymmetrical lesion, with an irregular border, with black/brown pigmentation points towards a diagnosis of malignant melanoma.

Types of melanoma:

* Superficial spreading

* Acral lentiginous

Histopathology of melanoma:

* Individual melanoma cells are larger than normal melanocytes

* They have large nuclei with irregular contours, chromatin is characteristically clumped at the periphery of the nuclear membrane with prominent red eosinophilic nucleoli

* All tumors have a vertical and radial phase of growth. The appearance of melanocytes is similar in both phases. The vertical growth has is often heralded by the appearance of a nodule.

* The possibility of metastasis correlates with the depth of invasion which is called the Breslow thickness.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female presented a few weeks ago to the OPD with an itchy skin rash. She was prescribed a topical ointment that relieved the itching. However, after a few days of stopping the ointment application, she presented to the OPD again with the same complaints. The lesions are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tinea incognito

In this case, the patient presented with an itchy skin rash and was most likely given topical corticosteroids. The image shows atypical lesions of tinea, which is a fungal infection. Although steroids could have provided initial relief, it is not the appropriate treatment for this condition. Therefore, the skin rash reappeared when the patient stopped using the ointment. This scenario is suggestive of tinea incognito.

Tinea corporis/ ringworm infection is caused by the dermatophyte Trichophyton rubrum. It results from the invasion and proliferation of the causal fungi in the stratum corneum with lesions on the trunk and limbs.

Characteristic lesions are circular, usually sharply marginated with a raised edge with central resolution. Scaling is a common but not a constant finding. The diagnosis is mostly clinical. In case of doubt, skin scrapings from site of lesion examined under a microscope may show fungal mycelium.

Steroids suppress inflammation without eliminating the fungus; so the typical raised margin is diminished, scaling is lost, and inflammation is reduced. Hence, diagnosis becomes difficult. Once steroid dosage is decreased or stopped, scaling reappears and shows fungal mycelium.

Pharmacological treatment of fungal Tinea infection is :

Localised disease, recent onset

* Topical terbinafine twice daily for 2 weeks

* Topical azole once or twice daily for 2–4 weeks

Widespread disease

* First-line:
Oral terbinafine 250 mg/day 2–3 weeks
Oral Itraconazole 100 mg/day 2–4 weeks

* Second line:
Oral Griseofulvin 1 g/day for 4 weeks

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with a hypopigmented lesion on his back. On examination, there is a complete loss of fine touch and temperature sensation over the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hansen's disease

The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy/ Hansen's disease.

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve, followed by the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve.

Leprosy has a long incubation period, usually ranging from 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

Ridley-Jopling classification of leprosy:

*

* Tuberculoid (TT)

* Borderline tubercular (BT)

* Borderline (BB)

* Borderline lepromatous (BL)

* Lepromatous (LL)

Indeterminate (IL)

One or a few hypopigmented or faintly erythematous, ill-defined to well-defined macular lesions with mild to moderate impairment of touch and/or thermal sensations. No thickening of peripheral nerves.

Borderline tuberculoid (BT)

Macular or plaque-type lesions numbering three to nine or more and asymmetrically located on any part of the body, with variable sizes and contours. Satellite lesions may be present. Loss of sensation is less intense than it is in TT lesions.

Several peripheral nerves are likely to be enlarged in an asymmetrical pattern, with sensory and motor deficits. Increased susceptibility to develop Type 1 leprosy reaction.

Tuberculoid (TT)
Well-defined, hypopigmented macule or as a raised, erythematous/brown/copper-colored plaque with a well-defined edge up to three in number.

Complete loss of fine touch and temperature sensations over the lesion.

Larger corresponding cutaneous nerves are thickened in a limited number of case

Mid-borderline (BB)

An unstable form of leprosy. Multiple plaque lesions and macular lesions; lesions are of various shapes and sizes, are bilateral, and usually occur in a more or less symmetrical. Minimal loss of sensation over the lesions.

Many nerves may be thickened, and this effect may be asymmetrical.

Borderline lepromatous (BL)

Numerous bilateral, round or oval, macular, diffusely infiltrated, erythematous, or hypopigmented lesions with moderately defined borders. Some loss of sensation may be detected, particularly over older lesions.

Widespread but asymmetrical thickening of peripheral nerves

Lepromatous (LL)

Innumerable bilateral, symmetrically distributed, diffusely indurated, erythematous, copper-colored, or skin-colored patches or plaques. There is no loss of sensation over these lesions.

Bilateral earlobe thickening and eyebrow loss occur. Coarse induration on the face gives rise to leonine facies.

Involvement of peripheral nerves occurs late and is bilateral and symmetrical, with sensory loss in a “glove-and-stocking” distribution.

Cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy:

* Characteristic skin lesions- hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation.

* Peripheral nerve involvement- thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen.

* Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR.

The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases with low bacterial load.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with joint pain which increases in the early morning when he wakes up and decreases with activity. Examination reveals the following picture (given below) along with inflammation of the wrist. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Psoriathic arthritis

The condition depicted in the above image with nail pitting and yellowing of the nails and inflammation of the DIP joints, point to a diagnosis of psoriatic arthritis.

Psoriasis is a papulosquamous disease with joint and nail manifestations apart from the skin. It has silvery scales.

The joint manifestations in psoriasis are referred to as psoriatic arthritis. It is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy and hence it is associated with HLA-B27. It is seen in 5-30% of patients with cutaneous manifestations. Nail involvement increases the risk of concomitant joint involvement.

Other features:

* Psoriatic nail changes like yellowing and hypertrophy

* Inflammation of the toes- dactylitis

* Shortening of toes- telescoping (because of osteolysis)

* Severe deformity- suggestive of arthritis mutilans

* Associated heel pain- suggestive of enthesitis (pain at the sites of ligament/tendon attachment)

The x-ray shows 'pencil in cup' deformity due to tapering of phalanges with cupping of proximal parts. Also all the bones of a single digit maybe involved refered to as ray deformity.

The drug of choice for different types of psoriasis is shown in the pearl below.

The most likely diagnosis for this patient's joint pain, which worsens in the early morning and improves with activity, along with the given picture showing nail changes and inflammation of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints, is Psoriatic Arthritis.

Psoriatic arthritis is a type of inflammatory arthritis associated with psoriasis. It is categorized under the seronegative spondyloarthropathies and is often linked to the presence of HLA-B27. It is seen in 5-30% of patients with cutaneous manifestations. Nail involvement increases the risk of concomitant joint involvement.

Some key features associated with psoriatic arthritis:

* Psoriatic nail changes like yellowing and hypertrophy

* Inflammation of the toes - dactylitis (sausage appearance).

* Shortening of toes - telescoping (because of osteolysis)

* Severe deformity - suggestive of arthritis mutilans

* Associated heel pain - suggestive of enthesitis (pain at the sites of ligament/tendon attachment)

* Radiographic findings, including the "pencil-in-cup" deformity, which results from the tapering of phalanges and cupping of proximal parts.

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

Image: oil drops visible in the nail bed.

Image: pitting and salmon patches in fingernails.

Image: Leukonychia in a patient with psoriasis.

Features of Nail Psoriasis – Mnemonic

“Nail – POLISH”

* P – Pitting

* O – Oil drop sign, Onycholysis

* L – Leuconychia

* I – Irregular pitting pattern

* S – Splinter Hemorrhage

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presents with complaints of nocturnal pruritus. Examination shows burrows over intertriginous areas, axilla, umbilicus, and in between the digits. Which of the following vectors is responsible for transmitting this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sarcoptes scabiei

The given clinical history of nocturnal pruritis and borrows over intertriginous areas, axilla, umbilicus, and in between digits is suggestive of scabies. It is caused by the itch mite also called Sarcoptes scabiei.

Scabies is caused by an infestation of Sarcoptes scabiei. It is transmitted by direct skin-to-skin contact and less frequently via contaminated clothes and bedding. They are seen more commonly in overcrowded areas, hostels, and schools, especially in unhygienic environments.

Clinically, these patients present with superficial excoriated papules or vesicles that are intensely pruritic. They are usually present on the volar surface of the wrists, interdigital spaces, penis, scrotum, navel, and skin folds and creases in the axillae, buttocks, and thigh regions. Burrows may be visualized in the superficial dermis in the above mentioned regions. Pruritis is typically intense and increases after showers and during the night.

Diagnosis is established considering the characteristic history and by dermatoscopic imaging or microscopy of the skin scrapings or cellophane tape lifted from lesions.

Permethrin cream - 5% is the treatment of choice. It is preferred over 1% lindane preparation and ivermectin. These preparations are applied once, all over the body below the jawline, following a bath. It should be washed off with soap and water after 8-14 hours.

It is imperative to treat close contacts simultaneously and wash bedding and clothing to prevent reinfestations.

The image given below shows itch mite.

Other options:

Option A: Crab louse infestation causes pediculosis pubis.

Option C: Rat fleas are vectors for endemic typhus, bubonic plague, and hymenolepis diminuta.

Option D: Ixodes ticks (hard ticks) transmit rocky mountain spotted fever, Russian spring-summer encephalitis, Colorado tick fever, tularemia, tick paralysis, and human babesiosis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presented with the following findings on her face. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acne vulgaris

The age of the patient and the presence of papules and pustules with an erythematous base on the face are suggestive of acne vulgaris.

Acne vulgaris is a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit. It is commonly seen in teenagers and young adults.

Comedonal lesions are the earliest lesions of acne. They represent the keratin plugs of the pilosebaceous duct and are non-inflammatory.

When the keratin plug is inside the follicle, it is called a closed comedone/whitehead.
When the keratin plug in the pilosebaceous unit is exposed to the environment, it gets oxidized by the air and turns black, known as open comedones/blackheads.
Inflammatory changes lead to the formation of papules, which may become pustules that rupture superficially or else spread deeper and form cystic lesions.

Management is directed at minimizing inflammation, decreasing keratin production, antibiotics, and antiandrogens to diminish sebum production.

The FDA has recently approved the drug Clascoterone, an androgen receptor inhibitor for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients aged 12 years and older.

Other options:

Option A: Acne rosacea or Rosacea is predominantly a disease with onset in middle‐aged adults (30–50 years old) and involves the convexities of the face.

Option C: Eczema presents more over the flexures and extremities from early adulthood. Features of pruritus and excoriations are predominant.

Option D: Tinea faciei is a fungal infection of the face and presents with a scaly lesion.
