questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 21-year-old female presented to OPD with complaints of recurrent lesions on her lips as shown below. Which of the following characteristic feature is seen on Tzanck smear?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mutlinucleated giant cell

The above image shows multiple vesicles & crusts clustered on an inflamed base around the lips which is characteristic of herpes labialis or cold sore caused by HSV-1 virus. Tzanck smear of this patient will show multinucleated giant cells.

Herpes labialis is commonly caused by herpes simplex virus type 1(HSV-1) and rarely by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2). It begins with a prodrome of pain, burning, and tingling followed by the appearance of erythematous papules. The papules then become vesicular and may ulcerate.

Tzanck cells or multinucleated giant cells are seen in microscopy. Multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogeneously stained ground glass chromatin-Tzanck cells are seen.

It is treated with oral acyclovir 200 mg and 5% topical acyclovir.

Other options:

Option B: Molluscum bodies or Henderson–Patterson bodies are large, eosinophilic, hyaline, intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies caused by Molluscum contagiosum. These bodies are composed of a large number of virus particles embedded in a protein matrix.

Option C: Owl’s eye inclusion bodies are intranuclear basophilic inclusion bodies seen in cytomegalovirus infection.

Option D: Donovan bodies are seen in granuloma inguinale, which is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. They are seen inside large, mononuclear cells (pund cells) as gram-negative intracytoplasmic cysts filled with deeply staining bodies. They can have a characteristic safety pin appearance due to bipolar staining of the chromatin material.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 38-year-old lady, who was recently started on OCPs is referred to the dermatology OPD with hyperpigmented macules on the upper lip, malar region, and forehead as shown below. It is exacerbated by sun exposure. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Melasma

The given clinical scenario of a woman on OCPs, who has hyperpigmented macules on her face, exacerbated by sun exposure is suggestive of melasma.

Melasma is the most common cause of facial melanosis that manifests as hyperpigmented macules on the face. It is exacerbated by sun exposure and oral contraceptive pills. The condition is predominantly seen in females. Melasma presents as hypermelanosis of the upper lip, malar regions, forehead, and chin. There may also be darkening of the nipples, linea alba, and groin. The lesions are usually bilateral and symmetrical.

In a pregnant woman, melasma is called chloasma (also known as mask of pregnancy). Chloasma is very common in the 3rd trimester of pregnancy. The pigmentation usually fades after parturition, but the course is variable.

Treatment for melasma:

* First-line - Sun protection, changing oral contraceptives to low estrogen formulation, or triple therapy with topical hydroquinone, tretinoin, and corticosteroid cream.

* Second-line - Chemical peels, azelaic acid alone or in combination with tretinoin.

* Third line - Laser therapy, pulsed light therapy, dermabrasion, topical liquiritin, topical rucinol, kojic acid, and hydroquinone.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child with a sore throat develops skin lesions, as shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely type of psoriasis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Guttate

The picture shows scattered drop-like papules and plaques suggestive of guttate psoriasis.

Guttate psoriasis is a distinct variant of psoriasis that is classically triggered by streptococcal infection (pharyngitis or perianal) and is more common in children and adolescents than adults.

On examination, guttate psoriasis manifests as numerous, small scattered papules and plaques. These are often referred to as “drop-like” and typically manifest as round or slightly oval 2 to 10 mm papules. They are scattered more or less evenly over the body, particularly on the trunk and proximal part of the limbs as shown below.

The image below shows a typical lesion of psoriasis characterised by erythematous plaque covered with silvery scales, particularly over the extensor surfaces.

Other options:

Option B: Erythrodermic psoriasis - an uncommon type where almost the entire body is affected, and the patient is systemically ill.

Option C: Pustular psoriasis: - Appearance of macroscopic pustules within lesions.

Option D: Flexural/inverse psoriasis - Plaques affecting intertriginous folds, and scaling may be less prominent. It is shown in the image given below

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: An 8-year-old child was evaluated for multiple skin tumors. The workup revealed defective nucleotide excision repair. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Xeroderma pigmentosum

The given clinical history of skin tumors with defective DNA nucleotide excision repair is suggestive of xeroderma pigmentosum.

Xeroderma pigmentosum is an example of defective DNA nucleotide excision repair where there is an inability to repair DNA pyrimidine dimers caused by UV exposure.

UV radiation leads to pyrimidine dimerization in DNA strands, preventing further replication by DNA polymerase. The nucleotide excision repair mechanism corrects the dimer formation in DNA. There is an inability to repair DNA pyrimidine dimers caused by UV exposure.

Given below is the image of a patient diagnosed with xeroderma pigmentosum.

Other options:

Option B: Bloom syndrome is a rare congenital autosomal recessive disorder associated with defective homologous repair caused by the loss of function mutations in a helicase.

Option C: Werner syndrome is associated with defective homologous repair.

Option D: Severe combined immunodeficiency disease is caused due to defective nonhomologous end-joining repair.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 28-year-old dentist presents with painful grouped vesicular lesions on the distal phalanx of her right index finger. She reports a burning sensation followed by the appearance of fluid-filled blisters that ruptured into shallow ulcers. She denies systemic symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herpetic whitlow

The given clinical vignette of a dentist with fluid-filled, painful grouped vesicular lesions, with a burning sensation on the distal phalanx of a dentist, is suggestive of herpetic whitlow infection.

Clinical features include painful, deep vesicles at the site of inoculation (in this case, the fingertips), which coalesce to form large bullae or a honeycomb appearance, which is most commonly contracted by dental workers and medical workers exposed to oral secretions. Fever and constitutional symptoms are mild. HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause this condition.

Whitlow can lead to necrosis of the distal 4/5th of the terminal phalanx. It does not cause necrosis of the entire phalanx because the proximal 1/5th escapes, as in this part, the artery does not cross the fibrous septa.The pulp space of fingers contains subcutaneous fat arranged in tight compartments. These compartments are formed by fibrous septa extending from the skin to the periosteum of the terminal phalanx.

Diagnosis of herpes simplex virus:

* Most sensitive test- HSV DNA- PCR (can differentiate between HSV 1 and 2)

* Most definitive test- virus isolation using human diploid fibroblast in which cytopathic changes can be observed as early as 24 - 48 hours.

* Microscopy - Tzanck smear, which is a rapid, diagnostic method, shows Tzanck cells. These are multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogenously stained ground-glass chromatin. Intranuclear type A inclusion bodies may also be seen.

The image given below shows Tzanck cells:

The image below shows the characteristic lesions of herpetic whitlow (The presence of vesicles and cloudy blisters at the pulp of fingers)

Topical acyclovir therapy can be initiated in cases of primary herpetic whitlow. Primary HSV infection at multiple sites and recurrent herpetic whitlow require oral acyclovir therapy. Intravenous acyclovir is recommended in immunocompromised patients.

Other options:

Option A: Molluscum contagiosum is a common, self-limiting viral disease of the skin caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus(MCV), which is classified within the poxvirus family. Usually, it occurs as scattered lesions on discrete areas of the body, appearing as shiny, pearly white, umbilicated papules(shown below).

Option B: Paronychia refers to an infection of the proximal & lateral nail folds. It results from the disruption of the protective barrier between the nail and the nail fold, introducing pathogens and predisposing the area to infection. Most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus(shown below).

Option C: Verruca vulgaris or common wart is caused by human papilloma virus 2 (HPV-2), but is also closely related to types 27 and 57 as well as types 1 and 4. These present as firm papules with a rough, horny surface and are most commonly situated on the backs of the hands and fingers, and in children, frequently on the knees, though they may occur anywhere on the skin.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 35-year-old male presents with the lesion shown below in the axillary region. He reports that a similar rash occurs at the same site every time he takes Cotrimoxazole(a sulfa-containing antibiotic). The lesion is mildly itchy and heals with darkening of the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fixed Drug Eruption

The clinical scenario of a patient having well-defined, dusky lesions that recur at the same spot, with hyperpigmentation after healing, points towards the diagnosis of a fixed drug eruption (FDE). The most likely implicated agent here is Cotrimoxazole.

Fixed drug eruptions/reactions are characterized by sharply demarcated, dull red to brown lesions. But new lesions can occur on different body parts on re-exposure to the offending drug. FDE is a type of delayed hypersensitivity reaction. Cotrimoxazole (sulfa-containing agents) is one of the most common drugs causing FDE.

Drug‐specific clinical patterns have been reported. These include the following:

* NSAID‐induced FDE - lips and genitals

* Tetracycline and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole‐induced FDE - genitals

* Metamizole‐induced FDE - trunk and extremities

* Carbocysteine‐induced FDE - face

Diagnosis is based on history and lesion morphology. Discontinuation of the offending drug is the first step in management.

Other options:

Option A: Drug Allergy usually presents with Drug-induced urticaria, angioedema, and anaphylaxis. There are different clinical features of anaphylaxis identified in different organs. On withdrawal of the offending drug, clinical improvement arises within 24–48h.

Option B: Immunological Drug reaction usually presents with SJS, TEN, DRESS, which are predominantly a T-cell mediated reaction.

Option D: Contact dermatitis is an eczematous reaction with itchy, erythematous papules and papulovesicles that occurs as an immunological response following exposure to a substance to which the immune system has previously sensitized. It is diagnosed using a Patch test. The image below shows Bindi dermatitis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 6-year-old girl presents with multiple small skin colored papules with central umbilication over the trunk and face. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Molluscum Contagiosum

The given clinical vignette of multiple small skin colored papules with central umbilication over the trunk and face is suggestive of infection with Molluscum Contagiosum.

It belongs to the Family Pox virus and is transmitted via autoinoculation, sexual or nonsexual contact. The condition is usually self-limiting, but treatment is required for non-resolving symptomatic lesions. Incubation period is 2 weeks - 6 months.

The age of peak incidence is between 2 and 5 years. In children, it is mainly caused by the type I molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV-1). There is a relatively higher incidence of MCV‐2 type in adults and HIV infection. Sexually transmitted molluscum contagiosum may be present over the genital area.

The lesions are shiny, pearly white, hemispherical, umbilicated papules that may show a central pore. These may enlarge slowly. Widespread and refractory lesions are seen most commonly in HIV or patients on immunosuppressive therapy.

Intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies called Henderson-Patterson bodies are seen. There are eosinophilic and are also called molluscum bodies.

Pseudo-Koebner phenomenon is seen i.e., new lesions develop along a line of trauma.

The diagnosis is usually clear when multiple lesions at different stages of evolution are seen and the classical umbilicated papule is observed. Diagnosis can be confirmed by direct microscopy, histopathology, or molecular analysis.

Treatment is usually not required, and lesions are likely to resolve spontaneously. Stimulation of the immune response can be done after destructive or inflammatory therapies with salicylic acid, trichloroacetic acid, and imiquimod. Cryotherapy when done needs to be repeated at 3-4 week intervals. Extensive lesions are treated with an antiviral agent like cidofovir.

The image below shows a characteristic lesion of Molluscum Contagiosum.

Option A: Impetigo contagiosa is a type of bacterial skin infection, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes. It presents as honey-colored crusts.

Option C: Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, intensely pruritic, skin condition associated with Celiac disease. It includes intensely pruritic inflammatory papules and vesicles on the forearms, knees, scalp, or buttocks.

Option D: Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular and proliferative infection caused by Bartonella henselae or Bartonella quintana. It mainly occurs in immunocompromised individuals.  It is the second-most-common cause of angiomatous skin lesions in persons infected with HIV.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A full-term neonate, delivered via an uncomplicated vaginal birth, is noted to have bullae and abrasions over the shoulder, knees, and legs shortly after delivery, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epidermolysis Bullosa

The above clinical scenario of the neonate having blisters and abrasions on the shoulder, buttocks, and knee after an uneventful vaginal delivery (due to minor handling/care)  points toward Epidermolysis bullosa.

Epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EBS) is a type of blistering disease. It occurs due to the mutation in the Keratin gene (KRT5 or KRT14) encoding for Keratin 5 or 14 expressed in the basal cell layer. This mutation causes the production of defective intermediate filaments. This makes epidermal basal cells fragile and subsequently causes blisters on physical pressure. The separation in EBS is within the epidermis (basal cell layer). The child is affected at birth, and caregivers present the baby with blisters on the hands, elbows, feet, and ankles. More blisters will appear as the baby starts crawling.

Option A: Erythema is superficial reddening of skin, which happens due to dilatation of capillaries secondary to an insult; it does not present as skin peeling in neonates.

Option C: Pustular melanosis are benign lesions seen predominantly in black neonates, contains neutrophils, and is present at birth as vesiculopustular eruption around the chin, neck, back, extremities, palms and soles.

Option D: Erythema toxicum is a self-limiting lesion that commonly occurs around day two of life and is a normal newborn phenomenon. It appears as firm, yellow-white, 1-2mm papules or pustules with surrounding erythema. They can be clustered or sparse and usually spare the palms and soles.

Pearl PF2200: Benign findings in a newborn

1. Erythema toxicum – small, white papules on an erythematous base that usually present on the face, trunk, and extremities. They contain eosinophils and may persist for a week.

2. Mongolian spots – Slate-blue, demarcated areas of pigmentation seen over the buttocks and back. This is also called dermal melanocytosis.

3. Pustular melanosis – Benign lesions seen predominantly in black neonates, contains neutrophils, and is present at birth as vesiculopustular eruption around the chin, neck, back, extremities, palms and soles.

4. Sebaceous Hyperplasia - White-Yellow papules on nose of a newborn due to hyperplastic sebaceous glands

5. Milia - Pearly opalescent white, epidermal inclusion cysts usually over the face.

6. Epstein Pearls - nests of epithelial cells, that appear as whitish/yellowish spots on hard palate. Usually, resolve by 3 months.

7. Cutis Marmorata - Transient lacy reticular vascular pattern of skin caused due to exaggerated physiologic vasomotor response on exposure to low environmental temperature.

8. Sucking Blisters - Solitary or scattered superficial bullae present at birth on the upper limbs of infants, which are caused by vigorous sucking on the affected part in-utero.

9. Salmon patch or naevus simplex - Small, ill-defined, pink-coloured macules commonly seen over glabella, eyelids, upper lip, and nuchal area, which develop due to vascular ectasia.

10. Harlequin colour change - A transient, well-demarcated colour change, with one half of the body displaying erythema and the other half pallor, usually occurring between two and five days of age.

11. Vaginal bleeding in the newborn at 2–3 days of age and enlargement and secretion of the breasts in both sexes.

12. Hymenal tags

13. Physiological phimosis

14. Conjunctival hemorrhage

15. Peeling of skin (especially in post terms)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the characteristic lesion of kaposi sarcoma in the oral cavity?
options: A white striated lesion that cannot be scraped off
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Purpulish red elevated lesions

Kaposi sarcoma(KS) is characterized by purplish-red elevated lesions. It is an AIDS defining illness due to multifocal endothelial proliferation with low-grade malignant potential, and the gammaherpesvirus HHV-8.

Classic KS typically affects older men of Eastern European and Mediterranean descent and progresses through three clinical stages: the patch stage, the plaque stage, and the nodular/tumour stage. Histopathological examination reveals a circumscribed tumour nodule within the dermis, characterized by a dense, whorled arrangement of spindle cells. Erythrocyte extravasation within slit-like spaces is often prominent, accompanied by readily observable mitoses and eosinophilic globules.

AIDS-associated KS is an AIDS-defining illness and is the most common malignancy associated with HIV infection. Involvement of the oral cavity is most common in AIDS-related KS, but it can be seen in other variants also. Oral KS (OKS) most often involves the hard and soft palate, gingiva, and dorsal tongue with plaques or tumors. The color of the lesions may range from non-pigmented to brownish-red or violaceous.

Other forms of KS include

* Classic Kaposi sarcoma: It has the following three clinical stages patches, plaques, and nodules.

* Endemic African KS

* Transplant-associated KS is more common after solid organ transplant patients receive immunosuppression as compared to the marrow or stem-cell transplant patients.

There is no definitive cure for KS, but it is highly radiosensitive, achieving complete responses in many cases. Treatment options include highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), which can lead to regression of lesions, as well as localized treatments such as excision, cryotherapy, and intra-lesional administration of agents like vinblastine and interferon-α2b.

The given images show coalescent red-purple macules and plaques of the skin and the violaceous growth on hard palate:

Other options:

Option A: A yellowish lesion containing pus describes an abscess or a pustular infection, bacterial in origin. Kaposi sarcoma is a neoplastic lesion with vascular proliferation not an abcess.

Option C: A white striated lesion that cannot be scraped off is more characteristic of Oral Lichen planus especially reticular form.

Option D: Small red erosions are more characteristic of herpetic stomatitis, traumatic ulcers, or aphthous ulcers, which are ulcerative.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 22-year-old college student presents with small depigmented lesions which have been there for over 2 years now as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitiligo

The image is suggestive of vitiligo. The pathological basis of vitiligo is the loss of melanocytes.

Vitiligo is a common form of localized depigmentation. It is characterized by milky‐white sharply demarcated macules. It is an acquired condition resulting from the autoimmune destruction of dopa-positive melanocytes in the basal layer of the epidermis. It can begin at any age but in the majority of cases becomes apparent in the third decade. The prevalence is most probably the same in both sexes or a slight female preponderance.

Electron microscopy studies confirm the loss of melanocytes. Wood's lamp examination shows milky-white fluorescence. Koebner phenomenon defined as the development of lesions at sites of trauma to uninvolved skin of patients with cutaneous diseases is a well‐known phenomenon in vitiligo.

World Vitiligo day is celebrated every year on 25th June to promote understanding and help vitiligo patients avoid discrimination and become more optimistic in life. The theme for the year 2021 is "Embracing Life with Vitiligo".

Other options:

Option A: Melasma is the most common cause of facial melanosis that manifests as hyperpigmented macules on the face. It is exacerbated by sun exposure and oral contraceptive pills. The condition is predominantly seen in females

Option C: Psoriasis:

* The peak on occurrence is between 16 to 22 years and between 57 to 62 years. They usually present with itching and a papulosquamous rash.

* The lesions are red, and scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin.

* They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone which is called the Woronoff ring.

* They commonly appear in the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs.

Option D: Dermatitis herpetiformis:

* Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, intensely pruritic, skin condition associated with gluten‐sensitive enteropathy.

* It typically appears in the 4th decade,  most typically over the extensor surfaces of the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp.

* On examination, multiple erythematous papules and vesicles can be seen over the extensor aspects. They appear symmetrical and heal without scarring. The oral cavity may show mucosal abnormalities and enamel pits.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presents with lacy lesions in oral cavity and genitals. Her proximal nail fold has extended onto the nail bed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lichen planus

Based on the given history, the patient has mucous membrane changes and pterygium of nail. Both are features of lichen planus.

* Mucus membrane lesions are very common in lichen planus, occuring in almost 30–70% of cases. It is mostly seen on tongue and buccal mucosa and also on genitals and anal mucosa.

* White streaks forming a lacework in buccal mucosa is a characteristic feature and are known as Wickham’s striae.

Image: Wickham’s Striae on the buccal mucosa.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man has come with complaints of hair loss. Examination findings are given below. The most likely diagnosis in this man is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alopecia areata

The image above shows circumscribed, hairless, smooth patch. Short, easily extractable broken hairs, known as exclamation mark hairs, are seen at the margins of the bald patch. This is characteristic of alopecia areata.

It is characterized by a circumscribed, smooth patch of hair loss. Exclamation mark hairs are often seen at the margins of the bald patches during active phases of the disease. Follicular orifices may appear as yellow dots on dermoscopy.

Alopecia areata is a chronic, inflammatory, autoimmune disease that causes non-scarring hair loss.

Other options:

Option A: Tinea capitis (as shown in the images below): The appearance may vary from dull grey, broken‐off hairs with a little scaling to a severe, painful, inflammatory mass covering the entire scalp. Predominantly seen in children, however, adults can also be affected due to infection by T.tonsurans.

Option B: Kerion (T. verrucosum and T. mentagrophytes) is a severe inflammatory type that presents with an inflammatory mass with thick crusting and matting of hair with pus and sinus formation.

Option D: Androgenic alopecia is a disorder characterized by a reduction of hair fiber production by follicles and miniaturization. Dihydrotestosterone, an androgenic metabolite, is implicated in the etiology. It is of two types: male-pattern and female-pattern hair loss. Male-pattern hair loss causes frontal hairline recession and thinning of the vertex.  Female-pattern hair loss involves the mid-frontal scalp diffusely. There is no or minimal involvement of the temporal region.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a swollen foot and multiple sinuses as shown in the below image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mycetoma

The most likely diagnosis here is Mycetoma which is caused by Eumycetoma.

Mycetoma:-

* Mycetoma is a chronic, granulomatous infection of the skin, subcutaneous tissues, fascia and bone, which most often affects the foot or the hand. It is, therefore, commonly known as Maduramycosis or Madura foot. Mycetoma occurs worldwide.

* Etiology:  It can be divided into three types, eumycetomas, actinomycetomas and botryomycosis.

Pathogenesis:-

* Triad of symptoms: Infection follows traumatic inoculation of the organism into the subcutaneous tissue from soil or vegetable sources, usually on thorns or splinters and results in tumefactions, deformities and draining sinuses discharging fungal colonies called grains or granules (triad of symptoms).

* Subcutaneous tissues of the feet, lower extremities, hands, and exposed areas are most often involved.

* Grains: Within host tissues the organisms develop to form compacted colonies (grains) 0.5–2 mm in diameter, the color of which depends on the organism responsible.

Laboratory Diagnosis

* A. Direct Examination: The presence of grains in pus collected from draining sinuses or in biopsy material is diagnostic.

* B. Culture Samples should also be cultured, at both 25–30°C and 37°C, on brain-heart infusion agar or blood agar for actinomycetes and on Sabouraud agar (without cycloheximide) for fungi.

Treatment:-

The management of eumycetoma is difficult, involving surgical debridement or excision and chemotherapy. Actinomycetoma responds well to rifampicin in combination with sulfonamides or cotrimoxazole.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Painless lesions over the vulval area as below is suggestive of ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Condylomata acuminata

The probable diagnosis is Condylomata acuminata.
It is also called as venereal warts. It is a sexually transmitted disease caused by Human Papilloma Virus 6 or 11.
Verrucous, exophytic cauliflower like growths can be seen over the skin of vulval region, perineum, perianal region which are usually non tender.

Treatment -
local application of Podophyllin 25% in alcohol or Podophyllin 20% in tincture benzoin for 6 hour daily,
Podofilox 0.5% solution
Trichloroacetic acid and bichloroacetic acid applied serially
Intralesional injection of Interferon

Vaccination - Cervarix at 0, 1 and 6 months; Gardasil at 0, 2 and 6 months.

Genital herpes - presents with painful blisters/ genital ulcer. It is caused by Herpes simplex virus 2.
Gonococcal vulvovaginitis - caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The patient usually presents with swollen, painful external genitalia and erythema around external urinary meatus along with foul smelling vaginal discharge.
Condyloma lata - these are infectious plaques which are broad, pink or gray-white present in warm, moist body areas. It is hallmark of secondary syphilis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old male presented with a skin lesion as shown below. Biopsy shows the presence of multiple neutrophilic foci in the stratum corneum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Psoriasis

The given image represents plaque psoriasis. The characteristic histopathological finding in psoriasis consists of multiple neutrophilic foci in the parakeratotic stratum corneum i.e Munro’s microabscesses and spongiform neutrophils in the spinous layer of the epidermis i.e spongiform pustules of Kogoj.

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the skin with systemic manifestations. Plaque psoriasis is the most common type. The nails are frequently involved and punctate pitting is the most common finding seen. Psoriasis is associated with Koebner or isomorphic phenomenon. It describes the appearance of new lesions along the site of trauma (linear lesions)

* The peak on occurrence is between 16 to 22 years and between 57 to 62 years. They usually present with itching and a papulosquamous rash.

* The lesions are red, scaly, and have well demarcation from the normal skin.

* They can also be encircled by a clear peripheral zone which is called the Woronoff ring.

* They commonly appear in the scalp, trunk, and extensor surfaces of the limbs.

Topical application of steroids, retinoids, vitamin D, and emollients is the mainstay of management. Phototherapy and oral methotrexate, acitretin, and cyclosporine can also be used.

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30 year old pregnant female presents to dermatology OPD with the given condition. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Chloasma

The woman here is presenting with chloasma or mask of pregnancy. The same facial melanosis in non-pregnant women is called melasma. Only the terms used differ.

* Melasma is the most common cause of facial melanosis and is manifested by hyperpigmented macules on the face which become more pronounced after sun exposure. Hypermelanosis affects mainly the upper lip, the malar regions, forehead, and chin.

* It is more common in women (90%) and in ages between 20-40 years.

* Chloasma is very common in the 3rd trimester of pregnancy and melasma is frequently seen in women on oral contraceptives.

Wood's Lamp examination is useful to differentiate the level of pigmentation and therefore the response to treatment.

Chloasma self resolves after pregnancy but melasma is more chronic and requires treatment with depigmenting agents like

* Kligman's triple combination - Topical hydroquinone + tretinoin + corticosteroid compound cream [First line]

* Hydroquinone (reduces tyrosinase activity)

* Kojic acid (tyrosinase inhibitor)

* Chemical peels

Pearl PF1989: Key Chart to help differentiate lesions on face

Key Chart to help Differentiate Lesions on face

The following images show the findings in -

* Melasma

* Rosacea

* Butterfly-shaped malar rash in SLE

* Acne

* Nevus of Ota

* Portwine stain

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the type of psoriasis in the given picture.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Guttate

The picture shows scattered drop-like papules and plaques suggestive of guttate psoriasis.

Guttate psoriasis is a distinct variant of psoriasis that is classically triggered by streptococcal infection (pharyngitis or perianal) and is more common in children and adolescents than adults.

On examination, guttate psoriasis manifests as numerous, small scattered papules and plaques. These are often referred to as “drop-like” and typically manifest as round or slightly oval 2 to 10 mm papules. They are scattered more or less evenly over the body, particularly on the trunk and proximal part of the limbs as shown below.

The image below shows a typical lesion of psoriasis characterised by erythematous plaque covered with silvery scales, particularly over the extensor surfaces.

Other options:

Option B: Erythrodermic psoriasis is an uncommon type where almost the entire body is affected, and the patient is systemically ill.

Option C: Pustular psoriasis is associated with the appearance of macroscopic pustules within lesions.

Option D: Flexural/ inverse psoriasis has plaques affecting intertriginous folds, and scaling may be less prominent. It is shown in the image given below

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Koebner's phenomenon is seen in all of the following, except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Herpes

Koebner's phenomenon is not seen in herpes.

Koebner’s phenomenon/ isomorphic response is the development of lesions in previously normal skin that has been subjected to trauma. If the same response is seen from the spread of an infective agent ( like molluscum contagiosum, viral warts), it's called pseudo-Koebner’s phenomenon.

Any of the following can elicit an isomorphic response: physical trauma, including friction, pressure, incision and laceration, skin grafting, bites, vaccination skin tests, burns, freezing, and ultraviolet (UV) and ionizing radiation.

It is seen commonly associated with psoriasis, lichen planus, and vitiligo. Other associated disorders include Darrier’s disease, pityriasis rubra pilaris, lichen nitidus, DLE, necrobiosis lipoidica, and Grzybowski syndrome.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is used to diagnose the condition given in the below image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wood's lamp examination

The given image shows sharply demarcated hypopigmented macules coalescing into patches over the trunk, pointing to a likely diagnosis of tinea versicolor or pityriasis versicolor. A Wood's lamp is used to diagnose the condition. Lesions show a pale yellow fluorescence when examined under the lamp.

Tinea versicolor is characterized by asymptomatic hypopigmented or hyperpigmented macules and patches and produces fine scales (branny/furfuraceous). The site most commonly affected is the upper trunk, but there is often spread to the upper arms, neck, and abdomen (seborrheic areas).

Pearl PF1216: Wood's lamp examination

Wood's Lamp Examination

Wood's lamp examination is a diagnostic test wherein the skin or hair is examined under exposure to the black light emitted by the Wood lamp. Black light is invisible to the naked eye because it is in the ultraviolet spectrum, with wavelength just shorter than the color violet. The lamp glows violet in a dark environment because it also emits some light in the violet part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

A traditional Wood lamp is a low-output mercury arc covered by a Wood filter (barium silicate and 9% nickel oxide) and emits light at wavelength 320–450 nm (peak 365 nm).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is the causative agent for acne fulminans?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Propionibacterium

Propionibacterium acnes is believed to be responsible for acne fulminans.

Acne fulminans is a severe destructive form of acne. It is predominantly seen in white, adolescent males.

The exact etiopathogenesis of this disease is unknown. However, the presence of elevated testosterone levels and infection by Propionibacterium acnes has been implicated.

The patient clinically presents with sudden onset of multiple ulcerative and hemorrhagic nodules over the face, back, and trunk. In addition, the lesions may be accompanied by various signs and symptoms of systemic inflammation like fever and arthralgia.

The onset of these symptoms is commonly heralded by the presence of mild to moderate acne for 6 months to 2 years. Treatment failure to antimicrobial therapy is seen.

The diagnosis is clinical and the management entails:

* Removal of crusts by soaking the crusts in an emollient oil.

* Applying a potent steroidal/antimicrobial cream over the lesions for 2-3 weeks after the removal of crusts.

* Oral prednisolone(0.5-1 mg/kg) therapy should be started and tapered over 2-3 months.

Systemic symptoms like fever and arthralgia are treated using oral salicylates or oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman in her second trimester of pregnancy presents with multiple symmetrical hypopigmented skin lesions, diffuse peripheral nerve thickening, and a positive slit-skin smear for Mycobacterium leprae. She is diagnosed with multibacillary leprosy. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Standard multidrug therapy (MDT)

Pregnancy is not a contraindication to the treatment of leprosy. Patients with multibacillary (MB) leprosy should receive the standard WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen during pregnancy. Early treatment reduces bacterial load, prevents nerve damage and disability, and decreases the risk of disease progression and lepra reactions.

The standard MB-MDT consists of:

• Rifampicin (monthly supervised)
• Clofazimine (monthly supervised + daily)
• Dapsone (daily)

These drugs are generally considered safe during pregnancy. Clofazimine may cause reversible skin discoloration in the mother and infant but is not a reason to withhold treatment.

Why not the other options?

• A. Postpone treatment until after childbirth: Incorrect. Delaying therapy increases the risk of irreversible nerve damage, deformities, and disease progression.
• B. Rifampicin monotherapy: Incorrect. Monotherapy promotes drug resistance and is never recommended for leprosy.
• D. Dapsone monotherapy: Incorrect. Dapsone monotherapy was abandoned because of widespread resistance; combination MDT is the standard of care.

High-yield pearl

• Leprosy in pregnancy → Treat with standard WHO MDT; do not delay therapy.
• Never use monotherapy for leprosy because of the high risk of developing resistant M. leprae.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with multiple hypopigmented anesthetic patches, thickened peripheral nerves, and a positive slit-skin smear. He is diagnosed with multibacillary leprosy. Which of the following is the correct WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen for an adult?
options: Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly, Dapsone 100 mg daily, Duration: 6 months
Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised), Clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised) + 50 mg daily, Dapsone 100 mg daily, Duration: 12 months
Rifampicin 600 mg daily, Clofazimine 100 mg daily, Dapsone 100 mg daily
Dapsone 100 mg daily, Clofazimine 50 mg daily
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised), Clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised) + 50 mg daily, Dapsone 100 mg daily, Duration: 12 months

The patient has:

• Positive slit-skin smear
• Multiple anesthetic skin lesions
• Thickened peripheral nerves

These findings are diagnostic of multibacillary leprosy, for which the WHO adult MDT regimen is:

• Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised)
• Clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised) + 50 mg daily
• Dapsone 100 mg daily
• Duration: 12 months

Why not the other options?

• A. Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly, Dapsone 100 mg daily, Duration: 6 months: This is the regimen for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy, not multibacillary disease.
• C. Rifampicin 600 mg daily, Clofazimine 100 mg daily, Dapsone 100 mg daily: Incorrect; rifampicin is not given daily in the standard WHO MDT regimen.
• D. Dapsone 100 mg daily, Clofazimine 50 mg daily: Inadequate because rifampicin, the most potent bactericidal drug against M. leprae, is omitted.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the dermatology OPD with intense itching, especially at night. On examination, there are multiple excoriated papules and burrows seen over the palms, soles, and trunk. A clinical diagnosis of scabies is made. The pediatrician plans to initiate topical therapy. Which of the following drugs are appropriate and safe for use in infants with scabies? 1. Permethrin 5% cream 2. Benzyl benzoate 25% lotion 3. Crotamiton 10% cream 4. Ivermectin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 and 3

Sarcoptes scabiei-

• Intense nocturnal pruritus
• Burrows + excoriated papules
•

Infants: involve palms, soles, face, trunk (unlike adults)Permethrin 5% cream

Mechanism

• Blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels in parasite
• Causes:

• Paralysis
• Death of mite

In infants, permethrin 5% is the first-line topical scabicide and is safe above 2 months of age. Crotamiton 10% is another safe topical option for young infants. Benzyl benzoate is irritant and avoided in infants, while ivermectin is not routinely used in children <15 kg. Hence only permethrin and crotamiton are appropriate.

| Drug | Mechanism | Safety in Infants | Role

| ---- | --------- | ----------------- | ----

| Permethrin | Na⁺ channel blocker | Safe (>2 months) | ✔ DOC

| Benzyl benzoate | Neurotoxic to mite | Not safe; Irritant | Avoid

| Crotamiton | Weak scabicide | Safe | Adjunct

| Ivermectin | Cl⁻ channel activator | Not safe | Severe cases only (older pts)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 42-year-old male farmer from a rural hilly region of Himachal Pradesh presents with a slowly progressive swelling of the foot over 1 year. He reports walking barefoot regularly. Examination reveals a painless, firm swelling with multiple discharging sinuses exuding black granules. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Madurella mycetomatis

Walking barefoot in soil (e.g., gardeners, farmers) predisposes to traumatic implantation of fungi, leading to mycetoma (Madura foot).

• Causative organism: Madurella mycetomatis (fungal eumycetoma)
• Mode of infection: Entry through minor trauma (thorns, splinters)
•

Clinical triad:

•

Tumefaction (swelling)

• Multiple sinus tracts
• Discharge with granules (“grains”)

Why not others:

• Cryptococcosis → inhalation (lungs/CNS), not via foot trauma
• Toxocara canis → visceral/ocular larva migrans (ingestion of eggs)
• Coccidioides immitis → inhalation causing pulmonary infection

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child presents with intensely itchy vesicular lesions over palms and soles. Itchy lesions were also present in periumbilical region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scabies

This is a classic presentation of infantile scabies caused by Sarcoptes scabiei.

Key clues:

• Intense itching, especially at night
• Palms and soles involved in children
• Periumbilical lesions
• Vesicles/papules with excoriation

Typical distribution (“Circle of Hebra”):

• Finger webs
• Flexor wrist
• Axilla
• Umbilicus
• Groin

Important point:

In adults, face is usually spared, but in infants: Face, Palms, Soles may all be involved.

Why other options are wrong?

• B. Atopic dermatitis: Flexural eczema, not burrows/periumbilical pattern.
• C. Bullous impetigo: Flaccid bullae with honey-colored crusts.
• D. Psoriasis: Well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales.

Treatment:

• Permethrin 5% cream is first line.
• Treat close contacts simultaneously.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man presents with the sudden onset of fever, malaise, and a painful, intensely burning rash over his left leg. Examination reveals a bright red, edematous plaque with well-defined, raised margins and tenderness. The lesion rapidly spreads along the superficial lymphatics. Medieval physicians referred to this condition as "St. Anthony's Fire." Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Streptococcus pyogenes

St. Anthony's Fire is the historical name for erysipelas, an acute infection involving the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics. It is classically caused by Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes).

Key clues:

• Sudden onset of fever and systemic symptoms
• Bright red, shiny plaque
• Raised, sharply demarcated borders (distinguishes it from cellulitis)
• Burning pain and rapid spread through superficial lymphatics

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Staphylococcus aureus ❌: More commonly causes furuncles, carbuncles, abscesses, impetigo, and purulent cellulitis. It does not typically produce the classic sharply demarcated erysipelas.
• C. Klebsiella pneumoniae ❌: Primarily causes pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and liver abscesses, especially in diabetics and hospitalized patients.
• D. Nocardia asteroides ❌: Causes nocardiosis, presenting with pulmonary disease, brain abscesses, or chronic cutaneous infections such as mycetoma—not erysipelas.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer with a history of prick injury came with the complaint: swelling of the foot with sinus tracts showing pus discharge, which showed white granules and gram-positive filamentous structures were noted on microscopy. What is the most likely causative organism associated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nocardia brasiliensis

A farmer with prick injury → chronic swelling of foot + multiple sinus tracts + granular discharge (“grains”) is typical of mycetoma (Madura foot).

• White granules + gram-positive filamentous bacteria → Actinomycetoma
• Causative organism: Nocardia brasiliensis (aerobic, weakly acid-fast, gram-positive filamentous bacteria)

Types of mycetoma:

• Actinomycetoma (bacterial):

o    Nocardia, Actinomadura

o    White/yellow granules

• Eumycetoma (fungal):

o    Madurella mycetomatis

o    Black granules

Why not others:

• Sporothrix → sporotrichosis (lymphocutaneous spread)
• Staphylococcus → abscess, no granules
• Aspergillus → not typical mycetoma cause here

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with a long-standing, progressively enlarging swelling of the foot associated with multiple discharging sinuses. The discharge contains black granules, and microscopic examination demonstrates fungal hyphae. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
options: Antifungal therapy combined with surgical debridement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Antifungal therapy combined with surgical debridement

The patient has eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma/Madura foot), characterized by the triad of painless subcutaneous swelling, multiple discharging sinuses, and colored granules. Black granules with demonstration of fungal hyphae indicate eumycetoma, which requires prolonged antifungal therapy combined with surgical debridement. Extensive disease may require amputation only as a last resort.

• Black granules + fungal hyphae = Eumycetoma
• Standard treatment is long-term antifungal therapy (e.g., itraconazole or terbinafine) with surgical excision/debridement of localized lesions.

Why not the other options?

• A. Amputation of the affected limb: Reserved only for advanced, extensive, or refractory disease.
• B. Antibiotic therapy without surgical intervention: Antibiotics are indicated for actinomycetoma, not eumycetoma.
• D. Oral corticosteroid therapy alone: Has no role in the treatment of mycetoma.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient with borderline leprosy who is on multidrug therapy (MDT) develops sudden redness and swelling of the existing skin lesions along with pain and tenderness of the peripheral nerves. What change in treatment is required?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Continue MDT, add steroids

The patient is experiencing a Type 1 (Reversal) lepra reaction, which occurs in borderline forms of leprosy (BT, BB, BL) due to an increase in cell-mediated immunity (Type IV hypersensitivity). It presents with acute inflammation of pre-existing skin lesions and painful, tender neuritis, which can rapidly lead to permanent nerve damage if untreated.

• MDT should be continued because the reaction is immune-mediated, not due to treatment failure.
• Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone) are the treatment of choice to reduce inflammation and prevent irreversible nerve damage.

Why not the other options?

• A. Continue MDT, start thalidomide: Thalidomide is indicated for Type 2 lepra reaction (ENL), not Type 1.
• C. Stop MDT, start thalidomide: Incorrect; MDT should never be stopped during lepra reactions.
• D. Stop MDT, start high-dose steroids: Steroids are appropriate, but MDT must be continued.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding gas gangrene: 1. It is caused by clostridial species, e.g., Clostridium perfringens. 2. It is characterized by a foul-smelling, painful wound containing serosanguineous discharge and gas bubbles. 3. It requires an aerobic environment and affects sites which are richly supplied with blood. 4. Radical amputation carries a high risk of advancing the infection to healthy tissue and is strictly contraindicated. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2

1. Clostridial species cause gas gangrene: Correct.

• Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is most commonly caused by Clostridium perfringens.

2. Foul-smelling, painful wound with serosanguineous discharge and gas: Correct.

• Characteristic findings include severe pain, tissue necrosis, edema, foul-smelling serosanguineous discharge, and gas production.

3. Requires an aerobic environment and affects well-vascularized tissue: Incorrect.

• Clostridia are anaerobic organisms.
• Gas gangrene typically develops in poorly oxygenated/devitalized tissue, often following traumatic injury.

4. Radical amputation is strictly contraindicated: Incorrect.

• Urgent aggressive surgical debridement or amputation, when necessary, is a cornerstone of treatment and should not be delayed.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Molluscum contagiosum: 1. It is caused by Papilloma virus skin infection. 2. It occurs frequently in immunosuppressed patients. 3. Lesions are dome-shaped, umbilicated, skin-coloured papules with central punctum. 4. Gently squeezing the lesions with forceps after bathing can hasten resolution. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

1. Papilloma virus infection: Incorrect

• Molluscum contagiosum is caused by the Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), a Poxvirus, not HPV.

2. Frequent in immunosuppressed patients: Correct

• It is particularly common and often more extensive in HIV/AIDS and other immunocompromised states.

3. Dome-shaped, umbilicated, skin-coloured papules: Correct

• The classic lesions are smooth, pearly, flesh-coloured, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication.

4. Squeezing lesions with forceps can hasten resolution: Correct

• Mechanical expression/removal of the central molluscum material can hasten clearance, although it should be performed carefully because of the risk of autoinoculation and secondary infection.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: In a case where a patient undergoing multi-drug therapy (MDT) experiences a deterioration of existing lesions and nerve complications, what course of action would you consider taking next? (NEET PG 2021)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Continue MDT, start systemic steroids

A patient on multidrug therapy (MDT) for leprosy who develops worsening of existing skin lesions and nerve involvement is most likely experiencing a Type 1 (Reversal) Lepra Reaction. This reaction is due to an increase in cell-mediated immunity against Mycobacterium leprae antigens and is a major cause of nerve damage and disability.

MDT should never be stopped during lepra reactions, as the reaction is an immunological event and not a drug toxicity or treatment failure.

Type 1 (Reversal) Reaction

• Sudden erythema and edema of existing lesions
• Enlargement of lesions
• Neuritis (painful, tender nerves)
• New sensory or motor deficits
• Nerve function impairment

Treatment

• Continue MDT
• Prednisolone is the drug of choice
• Early treatment prevents permanent nerve damage and deformities

| Feature | Type 1 (Reversal) Reaction | Type 2 Reaction (ENL)

| ------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------

| Immunity | Cell-mediated immunity ↑ | Immune complex-mediated

| Lesions | Existing lesions worsen | New tender erythematous nodules

| Nerve involvement | Prominent | May occur

| Common in | Borderline leprosy | Lepromatous/Borderline lepromatous

| Treatment | Corticosteroids | Thalidomide (if not contraindicated), steroids

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Nail lacquer used in treatment of Onychomycosis among the given options:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tavaborole

Onychomycosis (fungal nail infection) can be treated with topical nail lacquers in mild or superficial disease.\

• Tavaborole → a topical nail lacquer (oxaborole antifungal) that inhibits fungal protein synthesis
• Applied directly to the nail → good for distal/subungual mild infections

Drug classification:

• Topical nail lacquer: Tavaborole
• Systemic therapy (moderate–severe cases): Itraconazole, Griseofulvin
• Not used for onychomycosis: Caspofungin (IV echinocandin for systemic fungal infections)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Necrotizing fasciitis caused by fungi such as mucoraceous moulds is classified as which one of the following types?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Type 4

Necrotizing fasciitis is classified microbiologically into four types:

• Type 1: Polymicrobial infection — aerobic + anaerobic organisms
• Type 2: Monomicrobial infection — usually Group A Streptococcus ± Staphylococcus aureus
• Type 3: Gram-negative/anaerobic organisms, including Vibrio and other specific organisms
• Type 4: Fungal necrotizing fasciitis, most commonly caused by Mucorales (mucormycosis) or Candida

Therefore, necrotizing fasciitis caused by mucoraceous moulds is Type 4.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Type-2 necrotizing fasciitis is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Group A Streptococcus

Classification of necrotizing fasciitis:

• Type I: Polymicrobial (mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms) – most common overall.
• Type II: Monomicrobial – Group A Streptococcus ± Staphylococcus aureus.
• Type III: Marine organisms (Vibrio vulnificus) or Clostridium species (gas gangrene variants in some classifications).

Why not the other options?

• B. Vibrio vulnificus: Causes Type III necrotizing fasciitis, usually after exposure to seawater or raw seafood.
• C. Clostridium septicum: Causes clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene) and spontaneous infections, often associated with colonic malignancy or neutropenia, not classic Type II necrotizing fasciitis.
• D. Staphylococcus aureus: May coexist with Group A Streptococcus in Type II disease but is not the classic primary causative organism.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Varicella-zoster virus remains dormant in the: (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dorsal root ganglion

Varicella-zoster virus (VZV), a member of the herpesvirus family, causes varicella (chickenpox) during primary infection. After recovery, the virus is not eliminated; instead, it remains latent in the sensory dorsal root ganglia (and cranial nerve ganglia).

Years later, when cell-mediated immunity declines (due to aging, stress, immunosuppression, etc.), the virus can reactivate and travel along sensory nerves to the skin, producing herpes zoster (shingles).

• Primary infection: Varicella (chickenpox)
• Latent site: Dorsal root ganglion
• Reactivation: Herpes zoster (shingles)
• Lesions: Painful unilateral vesicular eruption in a dermatomal distribution

Pathogenesis

1. Primary VZV infection → Chickenpox
2. Virus migrates to sensory dorsal root ganglia
3. Latent infection persists for years
4. Reactivation → Viral spread along sensory nerves
5. Dermatomal vesicular rash (shingles)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What compound is responsible for the "coral-red" fluorescence observed under Wood's lamp examination in cases of Erythrasma? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coproporphyrin III

Erythrasma is a superficial bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, commonly affecting intertriginous areas such as the groin, axillae, and toe webs.

Wood’s Lamp Finding

• Erythrasma shows a characteristic coral-red fluorescence under Wood’s lamp examination.
• This fluorescence is due to the production of coproporphyrin III by Corynebacterium minutissimum.

Clinical Features

• Well-defined brownish-red patches
• Fine scaling
• Mild or absent pruritus
• Common in diabetic, obese, and immunocompromised individuals

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

Aminolevulinic Acid (ALA): A precursor in heme synthesis; not responsible for Wood’s lamp fluorescence in erythrasma.

Protoporphyrin IX: Accumulates in certain porphyrias and erythropoietic disorders.

Uroporphyrin I: Associated with congenital erythropoietic porphyria.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the most accurate description of Eczema marginatum? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tinea cruris

Eczema marginatum is the older clinical term for Tinea cruris, a superficial dermatophyte infection involving the groin, perineum, and adjacent upper thighs. It is most commonly caused by dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum and presents as pruritic, well-demarcated, erythematous plaques with an active scaly border and central clearing.

• Involves the inguinal folds and groin
• Intense itching (jock itch)
• Annular or arcuate plaques with raised, scaly margins
• Central clearing is common
• More frequent in men and in hot, humid climates

| Condition | Site Involved

| --------- | -------------

| Tinea cruris (Eczema marginatum) | Groin and inguinal region

| Tinea capitis | Scalp and hair

| Tinea barbae | Beard area

| Tinea unguium (Onychomycosis) | Nails

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the most common causative organism for verruca vulgaris? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Human papillomavirus-2

Verruca vulgaris (common wart) is the most common cutaneous wart and is caused primarily by Human Papillomavirus (HPV) type 2. It presents as firm, hyperkeratotic, rough-surfaced papules or nodules, commonly occurring on the hands, fingers, knees, and periungual regions.

• Rough, cauliflower-like surface
• Hyperkeratotic papules or nodules
• Commonly seen on hands and fingers
• May show black dots (thrombosed capillaries) on paring
• Spread by direct contact and autoinoculation

| HPV Type | Clinical Association

| -------- | --------------------

| HPV 2 | Verruca vulgaris (common wart)

| HPV 1 | Plantar warts (deep palmoplantar warts)

| HPV 3, 10 | Verruca plana (flat warts)

| HPV 6, 11 | Condyloma acuminata (genital warts)

| HPV 16, 18 | High-risk oncogenic HPV; cervical and anogenital cancers

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which condition is typically characterized by lesions described as "dew drop on rose petal"?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chicken Pox

Varicella (Chickenpox) is an acute viral infection caused by the Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) and is characterized by a distinctive vesicular rash.

“Dew Drop on a Rose Petal” Appearance

• Refers to a clear vesicle (dew drop) on an erythematous base (rose petal).
• Considered the classic skin lesion of chickenpox.
• Lesions appear in successive crops, resulting in papules, vesicles, pustules, and crusts being present simultaneously.

Clinical Features of Chickenpox

• Fever and malaise
• Pruritic vesicular rash
• Centripetal distribution (trunk > extremities)
• Lesions at different stages of evolution

Why Other Options Are Incorrect

Molluscum Contagiosum: Umbilicated pearly papules caused by a poxvirus.

Measles: Maculopapular rash with Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa.

Pityriasis Rosea: Herald patch followed by a “Christmas tree” pattern rash and collarette scaling.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which form of cutaneous tuberculosis is typically contracted from direct skin inoculation in individuals with good immunity? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tuberculosis Verrucosa Cutis

Tuberculosis Verrucosa Cutis (TBVC) results from direct inoculation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis into the skin of a previously sensitized individual with good cell-mediated immunity. Because of the strong immune response, the infection remains localized, producing warty (verrucous), hyperkeratotic plaques with a low bacillary load (paucibacillary form).

| Type | Mode of Infection | Immunity Status

| ---- | ----------------- | ---------------

| Tuberculosis Verrucosa Cutis (TBVC) | Direct exogenous inoculation | Good immunity

| Lupus Vulgaris | Hematogenous, lymphatic, or contiguous spread | Moderate to high immunity

| Scrofuloderma | Direct extension from underlying tuberculous lymph nodes, bone, or joints | Lower immunity than TBVC

Clinical Features of TBVC

• Solitary verrucous or warty plaque
• Commonly affects hands, fingers, knees, ankles, or buttocks
• Slow-growing lesion
• Paucibacillary disease
• Strongly positive tuberculin test

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs in leprosy treatment cause hyperpigmentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clofazimine

Clofazimine, a key drug in multibacillary leprosy (MDT), characteristically causes skin hyperpigmentation.

• Type of pigmentation: Red brown to black discoloration
• Mechanism: Drug deposition in skin and macrophages
• Clinical relevance: May lead to cosmetic concern and poor compliance

Other drug effects (for contrast):

• Dapsone → hemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency), methemoglobinemia
• Rifampicin → orange discoloration of body fluids
• Ofloxacin → GI/CNS side effects (no pigmentation)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding scabies? (NEET PG 2017)
options: Presence of Circle of Hebra lesions
Scalp and face are spared in infants
Norwegian scabies is the most severe form
Burrows are found in the stratum corneum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Scalp and face are spared in infants

Scabies is an infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. The female mite burrows into the stratum corneum, producing intense pruritus (especially at night) and characteristic skin lesions.

Why Option B is Incorrect:

• In adults, the scalp and face are usually spared.
• In infants and young children, however, the scalp, face, neck, palms, and soles are commonly involved.
• Therefore, the statement “Scalp and face are spared in infants” is incorrect.

Important Features of Scabies:

• Burrows are thin, wavy, grayish lines found in the stratum corneum.
• Circle of Hebra: Ring of papules and vesicles around affected areas, a classical sign of scabies.
• Norwegian (Crusted) Scabies: A severe, highly contagious form characterized by extensive hyperkeratotic crusted lesions and a very high mite burden, often seen in immunocompromised patients.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct in respect of scabies? 1. Male mite Sarcoptes scabiei are commonly transferred from an infected person to a non-infected person. 2. Norwegian scabies occur in immunodeficient patients. 3. Permethrin cream (5%) is used for treatment. 4. Pruritus intensifies at night and after hot shower. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Scabies is a contagious skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. It presents with intense nocturnal pruritus and characteristic burrows in the interdigital spaces, wrists, axillae, waistline, and genitalia. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies occurs in immunocompromised individuals and is highly contagious due to the heavy mite burden.

Why is D correct?

• 1. Male mite Sarcoptes scabiei are commonly transferred from an infected person to a non-infected person. ❌

• Fertilized female mites are primarily responsible for transmission and burrow into the skin.

• 2. Norwegian scabies occur in immunodeficient patients. ✅

• Seen in HIV infection, elderly, transplant recipients, and other immunocompromised states.

• 3. Permethrin cream (5%) is used for treatment. ✅

• 5% Permethrin cream is the drug of choice for scabies.

• 4. Pruritus intensifies at night and after hot shower. ✅

• Nocturnal itching is a hallmark of scabies and is often aggravated by warmth.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is characteristic of Purpura fulminans?
options: Non-hemorrhagic bullae usually present over extremities.
Present as large ecchymosis with irregular shapes.
Autoimmune disorder and never associated with any infection.
Asplenic patients are protected and do not develop this disease.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Present as large ecchymosis with irregular shapes.

Purpura fulminans is a life-threatening thrombotic disorder characterized by disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with rapidly progressive hemorrhagic skin necrosis. It typically presents as large, irregularly shaped ecchymotic purpuric lesions, which may progress to hemorrhagic bullae, necrosis, and gangrene. It is most commonly associated with severe bacterial sepsis, especially meningococcemia.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Non-hemorrhagic bullae usually present over extremities.

• Bullae, when present, are typically hemorrhagic, not non-hemorrhagic.

• C. Autoimmune disorder and never associated with any infection.

• Purpura fulminans is commonly triggered by severe infections, particularly Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus.

• D. Asplenic patients are protected and do not develop this disease.

• Asplenic patients are at increased risk of overwhelming sepsis with encapsulated organisms and are therefore more susceptible to purpura fulminans.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding leprosy?
options: Type 1 Leprosy Reaction is also called erythema nodosum leprosum
Type 2 Leprosy Reaction is an immune complex mediated syndrome called Arthus phenomenon
‘Lion face’ appearance is seen in tuberculoid leprosy
Nose is the last site of involvement in lepromatous leprosy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 2 Leprosy Reaction is an immune complex mediated syndrome called Arthus phenomenon

Leprosy reactions are acute inflammatory episodes occurring during the chronic course of leprosy. They are classified into Type 1 (Reversal reaction) and Type 2 (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum, ENL) based on the underlying immune mechanism.

Type 2 reaction (ENL) is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction (immune complex-mediated), also known as the Arthus phenomenon, and occurs mainly in patients with lepromatous or borderline lepromatous leprosy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Type 1 Leprosy Reaction is also called erythema nodosum leprosum: Incorrect.

• Type 1 reaction = Reversal reaction = Type IV (cell-mediated) hypersensitivity.
• ENL refers to Type 2 reaction.

• C. ‘Lion face’ appearance is seen in tuberculoid leprosy: Incorrect.

• Leonine facies is characteristic of lepromatous leprosy, due to diffuse dermal infiltration and skin thickening.

• D. Nose is the last site of involvement in lepromatous leprosy: Incorrect.

• The nose is one of the earliest sites involved because Mycobacterium leprae prefers cooler temperatures.
• Nasal stuffiness, epistaxis, and septal involvement are common early features.

| Feature | Type 1 Reaction | Type 2 Reaction (ENL)

| ------- | --------------- | ---------------------

| Other name | Reversal reaction | Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL)

| Hypersensitivity | Type IV (cell-mediated) | Type III (immune complex-mediated)

| Seen in | Borderline leprosy | Lepromatous/Borderline lepromatous leprosy

| Skin lesions | Existing lesions become swollen and erythematous | New painful erythematous nodules

| Neuritis | Prominent | May occur

| Treatment | Corticosteroids | Thalidomide (except in pregnancy), corticosteroids, clofazimine

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient from Bihar presented with normoanesthetic hypopigmented lesion as shown below. He had a history of fever for a long duration in his childhood. No thickened nerves were present. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Post kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis

The case presenting with hypopigmented lesions with normal sensations and a history of fever in childhood suggests a diagnosis of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis.

Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a condition when Leishmania donovani is found in the skin and manifests as dermal lesions. It is usually seen in the kala-azar endemic zones i.e. Bihar, Jharkhand, U.P, West Bengal (Northeastern states of India)

These patients present with erythematous rash and hypopigmented macules similar in appearance and distribution to those of lepromatous leprosy but normally less than 1cm. After a variable period of years or months, diffuse nodulation begins to develop in these macules.

The rash is progressive over many years and seldom heals spontaneously.

The image below shows post-kala-azar cutaneous leishmaniasis.

Other options:

Options A and B: The presence of hypopigmented macules over the trunk and face, suggests a differential of leprosy, but the nerves and sensations are normal, hence ruling it out.

Option C: Mycosis fungoides is characterized by polymorphic erythematous patches and plaques which are usually associated with severe pruritus. They could be asymptomatic too. The image below shows characteristic lesions in mycosis fungoides.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man presents with itchy tense bullae over the limbs. The roof of the bullae collapsed after a few days. A clinical image is shown below, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bullous pemphigoid

The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of bullous pemphigoid.

Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense itchy bulla in the flexor areas and trunk which do not rupture easily. Elderly aged people are usually affected. It is a subepidermal immunobullous disorder, which occurs due to the production of autoantibodies (IgG) against BP180 (BPAG2) and BP 230 (BPAG1) antigens on hemidesmosomes.

Mucosal membrane involvement is rare in this disease. Most of the lesions heal without a scar. Since these bullae are subepidermal, pressure over the lesions does not separate the epidermis from the dermis. (Nikolsky sign is negative).

Immunofluorescent microscopy will show the presence of subepidermal split and deposition of IgG antibodies at the dermo-epidermal junction. Histopathology will show the presence of subepidermal bullae with eosinophils.

It is mainly treated with corticosteroids. Other drugs used are azathioprine, dapsone, doxycycline, etc.

The above image (immunofluorescence microscopy) shows linear IgG deposits at the dermo-epidermal junction seen in the bullous pemphigoid.

Other options:

Option B: Pemphigus Vulgaris is an intraepidermal immunobullous disease. It occurs commonly between the 4th to 6th decade. They present with flaccid blisters, unlike bullous pemphigoid. Firm pressure over the lesion separates the epidermis from the dermis. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Mucosal involvement is seen in the form of buccal and palatal erosions.

Option C: Dermatitis herpetiformis typically appears in the 4th decade, and the patients present with itching and rash, most typically over the extensor surfaces. The majority of the patient have symptoms related to gluten-sensitive enteropathies, like bloating, diarrhea, and other gastrointestinal complaints. Immunofluorescence microscopy will show the deposition of IgA antibodies in the papillary dermis in a granular or fibrillar pattern(as shown in the below image).

Option D: Linear Ig A dermatosis (Chronic bullous dermatosis of childhood) is an autoimmune blistering disease seen in infants and children. The disease can also be seen in adults and is known as Linear IgA disease of adults or IgA bullous pemphigoid. The blisters are arranged in an annular pattern commonly known as the crown of jewels appearance (image below).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A child presented with asymptomatic lesions on the forearm and on the shaft of the penis. The lesions on the forearm are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lichen nitidus

The image shows an aggregate of pinhead-sized papules over the forearm of a child which is suggestive of lichen nitidus.

Lichen nitidus presents with tiny pinhead-sized flesh-colored papules and has a flat or dome‐shaped, shiny surface. They are found on any part of the body but the sites of predilection are the forearms, penis, abdomen, chest, and buttocks.

Lichen nitidus is considered to be a variant of Lichen planus as both are histologically similar in early stages. It has a "claw clutching a ball' appearance on histopathological examination. It refers to a sharply circumscribed inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis, that spans 4-5 dermal papillae.

The diagnosis can be made clinically, but skin biopsy provides a definitive diagnosis. Lesions are usually asymptomatic and rarely require any treatment. Symptomatic or generalized lesions can be treated with fluorinated topical steroids, PUVA, narrow‐band UVB phototherapy, astemizole, or acitretin.

Other options:

Option A: Lichen planus is an idiopathic inflammatory disease affecting the skin and mucous membrane. It usually presents with pruritic, purple, polygonal, papules. The lesions have thin white lines on their surface known as Wickham’s striae.

Option C: Scabies has typical distribution in the interdigital spaces and burrows are the characteristic lesions. The below image shows a magnified view of a burrowing trail of the scabies mite.

Option D: Scrofuloderma results from the direct invasion of the tubercle bacillus into the skin from underlying tuberculous foci.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A child presented with itchy plaques over the neck, the bilateral popliteal and cubital fossa. What could be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atopic dermatitis

The given clinical history of itchy plaques over the neck, cubital fossa and popliteal fossa suggests the diagnosis of ‘atopic dermatitis’.

Atopic dermatitis is the cutaneous expression of the atopic state, characterised by a family history of asthma, allergic rhinitis or eczema.

The etiology is only partially defined, but there is a clear genetic predisposition. A characteristic defect is impaired epidermal barrier. In many patients a mutation in gene encoding filaggrin (a structural protein in the stratum corneum) is responsible. The lesions are distributed in the flexural aspects.(as shown in the image).

Patients may display many immunoregulatory abnormalities, including increased IgE synthesis, increased serum IgE levels, delayed type hypersensitivity reactions.

The cardinal symptom is itching, along with rash.

Atopic Eczema can be divided into 3 phases: Infantile, Childhood, and Adult phases.

Infantile phase: The lesions of Atopic Eczema most frequently start on the face but may occur anywhere on the skin surface. Often, the napkin area is relatively spared.

• When the child begins to crawl, the exposed surfaces, especially the extensor aspect of the knees and elbows are most involved.
• The lesions consist of erythema and discrete or confluent oedematous papules. The papules are intensely itchy and may become exudative and crusted as a result of rubbing.
• Secondary infection and lymphadenopathy are common.

Childhood Phase: From 18 to 24 months onwards, the sites most characteristically involved are the elbow and knee flexures, a mixture of erythema, crusting, excoriation, hyper‐ and hypopigmentation, and warty lichenification may be seen depending on the skin type on the sides of the neck, wrists, and ankles.

• The sides of the neck may show a striking reticulate pigmentation, sometimes referred to as atopic dirty neck.
• The erythematous and oedematous papules tend to be replaced by lichenification.

Adult Phase: The picture is essentially similar to that in later childhood, with lichenification, especially of the flexures and hands.

Other options:

B) Dermatitis herpetiformis:

• Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic, intensely pruritic, skin condition associated with gluten‐sensitive enteropathy.
• It typically appears in the 4th decade, and the patients present with itching and rash, most typically over the extensor surfaces of the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp.
• They may also have symptoms associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathies, like bloating, diarrhea and other gastrointestinal complaints.
• On examination, multiple erythematous papules and vesicles can be seen over the extensor aspects. They appear symmetrical and heal without scarring. The oral cavity may show mucosal abnormalities and enamel pits.

C) Pemphigus vegetans:

It is a rare form of the bullous disorder that presents with large, moist, verrucous, vegetating plaques studded with pustules on the groin, axillae and flexural surfaces.

Predominant cell

Name of microabscess

Disease

Neutrophilic microabscess

Papillary tip microabscess

Munroe's microabscess (superficial)

Spongiform pustules of Kogoj (deep)

Dermatitis Herpetiformis

Psoriasis

Psoriasis

Lymphocytic microabscess
Pautrier's microabscess
Mycosis fungoides
